AI Bias and Fairness

Two product leaders discover in the same quarter that their models are lopsided. They do not have the same problem, and the mathematics says both cannot be fixed the same way.

1. Two decisions, five weeks apart

On 3 February 2026, Vikram Rathi, VP of Product at Sutradhar Clinical Systems in Bengaluru, receives a tender from a nine-hospital chain in Maharashtra. Clause 11.4 requires an "algorithmic fairness attestation" for clinical decision-support software, signed by an officer of the vendor. Sutradhar's flagship product reads vitals, labs and nursing notes and alerts a ward when a patient is likely to need intensive care within forty-eight hours. It runs in thirty-four hospitals. Rathi has never had to sign anything about it.

He asks his clinical lead, Dr Latika Bose, to split the quarter by admission pathway — Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY scheme versus private insurance or self-pay. It is crude, but in Indian hospital data it is the closest stand-in for income recorded on every admission. The result surprises him. The model does not flag PM-JAY patients less often; it flags them more, because they arrive sicker. What it does is miss them more. Of the two thousand PM-JAY patients who genuinely deteriorated it caught 1,220; of the thousand private patients who deteriorated it caught 780. Sixty-one percent against seventy-eight. And the precision of the alerts is nearly identical in both cohorts, which is exactly why nobody had noticed.

Exhibit 1 — Sutradhar deterioration score, Q4 FY26, 20,000 admissions, single threshold

PM-JAY pathway10,0002,0002,3461,22078052.0%61.0%

Catch-rate ratio 61.0 ÷ 78.0 = 0.782. Precision ratio 50.0 ÷ 52.0 = 0.962. One model, one threshold, passing one fairness test and failing another.

Five weeks later, Aparna Sridhar, Director of Product for Discovery at Reshmi Circle, a Mumbai social-commerce app with forty-six million monthly users, is handed a different problem. A creator collective in Coimbatore has published an open letter alleging that sellers who write listings in Tamil are being buried. Her data science lead, Zoya Ahmed, reconstructs a week of 4.2 million feed impressions. Creators posting in English or Hinglish hold thirty-one percent of the quality-matched catalogue and receive fifty-eight percent of position-weighted exposure; those posting in Tamil, Telugu, Bengali or Marathi hold sixty-nine percent of supply and receive forty-two. Conversion per impression, once an item is seen, is 2.9 percent against 2.8 — indistinguishable. The feed is not sorting on quality, and with conversion equal, Reshmi Circle cannot claim the gap belongs to the market.

Rathi's model is well calibrated and unequally accurate. Sridhar's ranker allocates attention unequally to items of equal value. Both are called bias. That one word covers both cases is the source of most confusion in this field.

2. The idea, and the six positions people actually hold

A system exhibits bias when its behaviour differs systematically across groups in a way the product's own stated objective cannot justify; fairness is having chosen, declared and met a specific criterion for what counts as justified. The definition is deliberately incomplete: no criterion-free notion of fairness is available to a product team, and the central skill is choosing one and defending the choice.

The legal root is Griggs v. Duke Power (1971), which made effect rather than intent the test, and the 1978 US Uniform Guidelines, which supplied the four-fifths convention. The mathematics arrived from elsewhere. Between 1968 and 1976, psychometricians arguing about culturally fair aptitude testing — Cleary, Thorndike, Darlington, Petersen and Novick — established that the competing definitions of a fair test are mutually inconsistent whenever two groups differ in the underlying rate of what is predicted; Darlington's 1971 paper listed four and showed that satisfying one violates the others. The field forgot this for forty years, rediscovering it in 2016 when ProPublica and the vendor Northpointe disagreed publicly about a recidivism score, each correct under its own criterion, and Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan — and independently Chouldechova — proved the impossibility formally. The machine-learning work in between (Dwork and colleagues, 2012; Barocas and Selbst, and Hardt, Price and Srebro, 2016) is scaffolding on an older foundation.

Six positions are held by serious practitioners. An expert can state each in its strongest form, and can usually tell which one a colleague is arguing from before the colleague can.

Exhibit 2 — the six schools, with the proposition each signs and the one it refuses
SchoolSignsRefuses
Anti-classificationNo model may take a protected attribute, or a near-substitute, as input.That an unequal outcome is itself evidence of unfairness.
Distributive parityUnequal allocation is a harm whatever the mechanism; the deployer carries the burden.That historical data supporting a gap makes it fair.
Equal opportunityAmong those who deserved the good outcome, errors must fall equally.Equal selection rates where true rates differ.
Actuarial / calibrationA score of 0.7 must mean a 70 percent chance for everyone.Equalising error rates at the cost of miscalibration.
CausalAsk whether the outcome changes if group membership changes, legitimate paths held fixed.That an observational statistic settles it.
Structural critiqueMetrics can launder a deployment that should not exist; ask first whether to build."We fixed it by swapping a feature."

Rathi's tender clause was drafted by lawyers holding the distributive position. His model is defensible under the actuarial one and indefensible under equal opportunity. Sridhar's critics are distributive; her growth team is anti-classification ("we don't use language as a feature"); her own instinct, once conversion parity was established, is causal. Naming the position each party occupies is not a debating trick; it is how the argument gets had once instead of four times.

3. Mechanics: the arithmetic of the wall

The impossibility result is usually stated abstractly and therefore not believed. On Rathi's numbers it is unavoidable. Take three criteria a hospital might demand: precision parity, equal catch rate, equal false-alarm rate. Suppose a vendor achieved the first two exactly, at 50 percent precision and 75 percent catch rate. In the PM-JAY cohort, 2,000 events at 75 percent gives 1,500 true positives; 50 percent precision forces 1,500 false positives out of 8,000 non-events — 18.75 percent. In the private cohort, 1,000 events give 750 true positives and 750 false positives out of 9,000 non-events: 8.33 percent. The rates differ by a factor of 2.25, and no engineering closes them, because the gap is produced by prevalence alone. Two of three, never three.

The step most teams skip is what follows the choice. Bose's first proposal is the obvious one: lower the threshold for PM-JAY patients until catch rates match. Arithmetically it works — 61 percent rises to 78, some 340 additional deteriorations detected. But dropping a threshold across a fixed score distribution drags in false positives faster than true ones. Alerts rise from 2,346 to roughly 3,600 and precision falls from 52 to 43 percent. A three-week pilot then measures what the spreadsheet did not: median acknowledgement latency rises from 41 seconds to 96, and the share of alerts acted on within ten minutes falls from 88 percent to 71. Multiply through. Before, 1,220 catches at 88 percent acted on is 1,074 patients escalated; after, 1,560 at 71 percent is 1,108. A seventeen-point gain in a fairness metric buys thirty-four patients. The nurses recalibrated faster than the model did.

This is the second-order effect that separates people who have run a fairness intervention from people who have read about one: a model's output is an input to a human process with its own priors, and equalising a statistic while degrading signal quality transfers the harm rather than removing it. Bose's second proposal goes upstream. The model's most influential feature is the count of laboratory investigations ordered in the first twelve hours — which tracks the payer pathway rather than severity, because PM-JAY package rates cap reimbursable investigations: a proxy for who pays, dressed as a proxy for how sick. Replacing it with severity-only vital-sign trajectories, and adding a sparsity indicator that widens the score's uncertainty band rather than lowering the score, moves catch rates to 74 and 77 percent — a ratio of 0.96 — with precision at 49 and 50, and alert volume up nine percent rather than fifty-three.

4. When the frame applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are testable claims, not assumptions. One: a group-rate comparison is meaningful only on a pool the product itself constructed. Sutradhar passes — both cohorts sit in the same hospitals under the same clinicians. Reshmi Circle passes on exposure but fails on a naive comparison of total sales, where catalogue composition differs. Two: the outcome must be one the system allocates, not one it observes. Rathi's model allocates clinical attention. Sridhar's generative captioning tool produces something else — a representational effect, where the harm lies in how a group is depicted rather than in what it receives, and which no selection-rate arithmetic captures. Three: a criterion means nothing unless someone can be held to it. Rathi signs personally; Sridhar's commitment is a published ratio her creators can check.

Where the frame actively misleads deserves saying plainly. When base rates differ for reasons the product should respond to, parity is harmful: equal alert rates across Rathi's wards would deliberately under-serve the sicker cohort. When the group taxonomy is imported from another jurisdiction, the metric measures the taxonomy rather than the harm. When the disparity is large and entirely upstream, a model-layer fix avoids the expensive thing — Taanabaana Learning, in section eight, spent fourteen months proving it. And when a product should not be deployed in the form proposed, a good fairness score is an argument for shipping it.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Two-sided, where fairness to one side is unfairness to the other. Reshmi Circle's remedy takes attention from established creators and gives it to under-exposed ones. Weekly exposure is conserved; no version exists where everyone gains. The honest framing is that the platform is choosing a distribution policy — state the rule in advance, publish the measurement, accept that the losing side has a real grievance.

Regulated, where the data you need is the data you may not hold. Jamdani Money, a Chennai NBFC lending under RBI's digital lending guidelines, cannot lawfully or decently collect caste or religion, and the DPDP Act 2023 pushes toward minimisation. It therefore cannot directly measure the disparities people most worry about. Its answer — a separate team imputing group membership from surname and geography, of the kind the US CFPB formalised, returning only aggregate rates from behind a wall that never emits an individual label — closed the measurement gap and opened an ethical one: the firm now computes something it promised not to know. The approval-rate ratio came out at 0.73; a pincode-cluster feature accounted for six of the eleven percentage points; removing it cost 0.9 points of AUC and eight basis points of portfolio default. The credit committee kept the feature — documented, arguable, unresolved.

Hardware plus software, where the fix is a three-year-old bill of materials. Patola Devices sells a voice-driven billing terminal to kirana stores with on-device speech recognition. Word error rate is 8.1 percent for Delhi-accented Hindi, 19.6 for Bhojpuri-influenced speech and 22.3 for Malayalam-accented Hindi. The better acoustic model needs memory that 38,000 of 140,000 fielded units lack, and those units sit in exactly the districts with the highest error rates, because the cheap SKU sold where margins were thinnest. For eligible units, median time to reach ninety percent of the fleet over shop Wi-Fi is seventy-one days. This problem was created by a 2023 procurement decision and cannot be patched in a sprint.

AI-native, where there is no baseline. Kalabattu Labs' legal-drafting copilot has no legacy process to compare against, so the team substitutes public benchmark scores for deployment evidence — a category error, since a model scoring well on a stereotype benchmark can still write thinner first drafts for one class of client.

What mature companies actually do, as distinct from what their responsible-AI pages claim, is narrower than a framework: they put one named person on the seam. At Sutradhar the review is now chaired by the clinical lead, because the failure lay in the label's relationship to the payer system and only a clinician would have recognised the investigation-count feature. The published policy says "cross-functional review board"; what works is one person whose promotion depends on catching it.

6. Nine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The label is more often biased than the model. The competent practitioner audits predictions; the expert audits what the model was asked to predict. The tell is a target that is a convenient operational record standing in for the thing cared about — cost for need, in Obermeyer and colleagues' 2019 Science finding, or "eighty percent of sessions from one device" for learning itself. The obvious reading is that the model learned a bad pattern; the correct one is that it learned the right pattern for the wrong question, and no reweighting repairs a mis-specified target.

Missingness is a feature, and usually the biased one. Where one group's records are sparser — fewer labs, shorter notes, no bureau history — a model trained on complete cases learns that sparsity predicts the negative class. The tell is high overall accuracy with errors clustered on low-density rows. The immediate move is to represent uncertainty explicitly rather than let absence of evidence score as evidence of absence.

Aggregate parity coexists with subgroup harm. Kearns and colleagues named this fairness gerrymandering in 2018: a model can be balanced across gender and across region while badly skewed against women in one of them. The tell is a remedy that hits its target ratio suspiciously fast. The expert checks intersections, knowing cells shrink quickly, that below roughly two hundred observations a ratio is noise, and that the discipline is to pre-register which intersections matter.

Exposure is not selection. In a ranked feed nothing is rejected; items are placed where nobody looks. Because attention decays roughly logarithmically with position, the top three slots of a ten-item screen carry about forty-seven percent of exposure. The tell is a team insisting it filters nobody out. The expert measures position-weighted exposure against a relevance baseline, and knows the criterion in ranking is amortised across sessions, not enforced inside one list.

An intervention changes behaviour, and behaviour changes the data. The Sutradhar alert-fatigue result is the general case: the system measured before a fix is not the system that exists after it. The tell is a projected benefit computed by multiplying a model-level gain by an unchanged downstream conversion rate. The expert puts the fairness metric and the human-response metric on one slide, because the product is the pair.

Calibration and error-rate balance are two customers, not two views. The actuarial position protects whoever reads the score — clinician, credit officer — from being misled. The equal-opportunity position protects the person the score is about. The tell is a meeting where one side says "but the score is accurate" and the other "but they're being missed," both with correct arithmetic. Naming the two customers ends the loop.

Generation has two harm surfaces and teams audit one. The allocative question is whether the artefact helps one group less: Reshmi Circle's captions were accepted without edit 81 percent of the time in English and 58 in Tamil, a quality gap with revenue consequences. The representational question is what the text implies about people. The tell is a team with a toxicity filter and no quality-parity measurement, because the filter can be bought. A quieter third surface: guardrails are classifiers too, and a benign-caption false-block rate of 0.6 percent in English against 3.1 in transliterated Bhojpuri is bias manufactured by the safety layer.

Benchmark scores are evidence about benchmarks. Blodgett and colleagues' 2020 survey of bias work in natural-language processing found most papers did not state what harm was measured or to whom. The tell is a vendor answering a fairness question with a leaderboard number. The expert asks for disparity on the deployment's own traffic, population and decision, preferring a rough in-house measurement to a rigorous irrelevant one.

The threshold, not the model, is usually the product decision. Enormous energy goes into retraining when the disparity comes from a single operating point chosen for a global alert budget. The tell is a team that can recite the model's AUC but cannot say who set the threshold. The expert treats it as a first-class artefact with an owner, a rationale and a review date — and knows group-specific thresholds are at once the most effective remedy available and, in most Indian enterprise contracts, the likeliest to be read as explicit discrimination.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the currency is exposure and measurement is cheap because traffic is abundant; the difficulty is that users never know what they were not shown, so harm stays invisible until someone aggregates it, as the Coimbatore collective did. In B2B and enterprise the protected attribute is a contract term rather than a constant — a Gulf client may lawfully filter on nationality in ways unlawful in India — so one engine must support per-tenant fairness configuration, and the vendor's obligation is measurement infrastructure rather than a fixed policy. In platforms and marketplaces the defining property is conservation: exposure is zero-sum in a way clinical alerts are not, so every remedy is a redistribution with a named loser. In hardware the constraint is latency of remedy, as Patola's fleet shows; in AI-native products, the absence of a counterfactual baseline. Where the difference is not real: the diagnostic sequence — define group, define outcome, build a comparable pool, measure allocation and error profile, then look upstream at label and missingness — is identical in all five. Teams who believe their domain is special usually mean their data is inconvenient.

Exhibit 3 — what changes with company stage
StageBinding constraintRight first move
Seed to Series ANo sensitive-attribute data; nobody to run an auditProxy correlation scan on existing features; write the intended criterion down while it is cheap to change
Series B to CScale enough to matter, no standing measurement; the first enterprise clause arrivesOne recurring disparity metric beside revenue, with a named owner on the label seam
Late stageBlast radius; several products on one shared modelPer-surface measurement, since a shared embedding's disparity manifests differently in each product on it

8. Three worked examples

Reshmi Circle: exposure re-ranking that worked. Ahmed found two compounding mechanisms — a thirty-day engagement-velocity feature rewarding creators already receiving traffic, and a multilingual caption encoder whose Tamil and Bengali embeddings were compressed relative to English, depressing match scores by a margin small per item and decisive in aggregate. The remedy was an amortised exposure constraint: no language group's exposure-to-relevance ratio may fall below 0.85 in a rolling week, as a post-ranking redistribution that never moves an item more than three positions, so no single feed looks manipulated. Ratios moved from 0.61 and 1.87 to 0.88 and 1.14. Session GMV fell 1.9 percent in week one, 0.7 percent by week four, and was up 0.3 percent by week nine as newly exposed supply built engagement history and the velocity feature stopped starving it. The cost was real and temporary; holding through week four was the actual decision.

Sutradhar: the threshold fix that failed. Covered above; the number to carry is that a seventeen-point catch-rate gain converted into thirty-four escalated patients, because acknowledgement behaviour absorbed the rest. The recovery was to stop treating the disparity as an output problem.

Taanabaana Learning: where the approach failed outright. The Pune company ran scholarship-seat recommendations for a state-subsidised skilling programme serving 2.4 million learners. Under press pressure it imposed a hard parity quota between Tier-1 and Tier-2/3 district cohorts at selection, and the ratio reached 0.99 in one release. Two things followed. Completion among the newly admitted cohort fell from 63 percent to 41, because the quota was filled with learners the model had correctly identified as unlikely to finish — the barrier being shared device access, which the programme did nothing about. And the selection rate for girls in Tier-3 districts, a subgroup cutting across both coarse groups, fell from 19 percent to 14, because the quota was filled by higher-scoring Tier-3 applicants, disproportionately boys. Headline parity improved while the worst-off subgroup got worse. Roughly ₹6.2 crore of programme funding went to seats that did not convert, over fourteen months.

The recovery had three parts, and only the first is what most teams would try. Measurement moved to twelve intersecting cells — district tier by gender by device-access band — with a minimum ratio in each. The label was re-examined: "completion" had meant eighty percent of sessions from a single device identifier, penalising households sharing one phone; recoding it against assessment outcomes raised Tier-3 predicted readiness legitimately, without a quota. And the model change was paired with a programme change, a ₹1,200 device stipend for 4,000 learners, because the model had accurately predicted a real barrier the product refused to remove. The Tier-3 selection ratio settled at 0.91 with completion at 59 percent against Tier-1's 63. The internal lesson is blunt: a quota at the decision layer is what you do when you have decided not to look at the label or at the programme.

9. Failure modes, early warnings, and the cost of catching them late

Exhibit 4 — six failure modes seen across these five companies
Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost if late
Auditing predictions, not the labelTarget is an operational record, not the outcome cared about"If this label were predicted perfectly, would the product be right?"Retrain and re-collect; 14 months, ₹6.2 crore
Threshold hack instead of upstream fixMetric improves, no feature changed"What does the remedy cost whoever reads the output?"Harm transfers as alert fatigue; 17 points, 34 patients
Aggregate-only measurementHeadline ratio hits target in one release"Which intersection got worse while this improved?"Worst-off subgroup regresses behind a passing metric
Fairness owned by the model teamReview chaired by whoever trained the model"Who would recognise this feature as a payer proxy?"Domain proxies survive every technical review
Benchmarks used as deployment evidenceA fairness question answered with a public score"What was the disparity on our own traffic last week?"An attestation signed on evidence about something else
One-time audit treated as permanentNo recurring owner; the metric lives in a deck"What re-ran this quarter, and who read it?"Feedback loop restores the gap in two or three quarters

The pattern is that expensive failures are failures of framing, caught late because the cheap question was never asked. Each question in the third column takes under an hour and none requires retraining. That asymmetry — an hour of asking against quarters of rework — is the whole practical argument for building the habit before a tender demands it.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether group-specific thresholds are the right remedy or an obvious wrong. For: they target the harm directly, they are transparent, and post-processing carries the cleanest theoretical guarantees. Against: treating two people differently on the basis of a protected attribute is what anti-discrimination law exists to forbid, and Ricci v. DeStefano (2009) showed that remedying a disparate impact can itself be actionable. The first fails if transparent group-specific treatment reliably attracts penalties outweighing the harm removed; the second fails if upstream fixes are reliably available, which Patola's fleet suggests they are not.

Whether the work belongs at the model or at the policy layer. The model-side argument is that the model is the only lever a product team controls, and policy change needs capital most teams lack. The policy-side argument, which Taanabaana's stipend exemplifies, is that a model accurately predicting a real barrier is not the problem, and forcing it to predict inaccurately destroys information the organisation needs. Evidence favours policy where the barrier is addressable and the model where it is diffuse; nobody has a test for which case they are in.

Whether measuring requires collecting. One camp holds that refusing to collect sensitive attributes guarantees ignorance — a tension India has not resolved, DPDP pushing toward minimisation while lending norms push toward demonstrable non-discrimination. The other holds that a database of inferred caste or religion is a standing hazard that will eventually be used or leaked, and that Jamdani Money's wall is thinner than it looks. The first fails if proxy-free auditing gets good enough to detect real disparities; the second if secure computation proves durable under organisational pressure.

Whether generative bias evaluation transfers. The optimists hold that stereotype and quality-parity benchmarks correlate well enough with deployed harm to serve as gates. The sceptics, closer to Blodgett, hold that they measure artefacts of their own construction and only in-deployment evidence counts. What would settle it — a published correlation between benchmark movement and measured downstream harm — does not exist at any useful scale.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives with a checklist and a metric. Someone who has internalised it arrives with three questions and will not move until they are answered: fair by which criterion, chosen by whom, measured on which pool. They instrument before they argue, having learned that most fairness disputes concern numbers nobody has computed. They treat the threshold as a product artefact with an owner. When a disparity appears, their first instinct is the label's provenance and the missingness pattern, not the model weights. They write down what their chosen criterion gives up, in a sentence a regulator could read. And they will say aloud that a particular gap is a product policy problem no model can solve — then go and solve it at the policy layer, which is slower, less legible, and the only thing that works in roughly half of real cases.

12. What each of them decides

Rathi signs clause 11.4, but not the version proposed. He attests to a named criterion — catch-rate ratio across admission pathways, measured quarterly on the client's own traffic, floor of 0.90, with a defined escalation if breached — and discloses that the ratio was 0.782 at audit, that the cause was an investigation-count feature acting as a payer proxy, and that the remediated ratio is 0.96. He declines the group-specific threshold and moves the chair of the review from his ML lead to Dr Bose. His reasoning: an attestation to an unstated standard is worthless; one to a measured standard, history included, is the only kind he can honestly renew.

Sridhar ships the exposure constraint at 0.85 with the three-position cap, publishes per-language ratios to creators monthly, and holds the caption tool in guarded mode for the four languages where accept-without-edit rates fall below seventy percent — still generating, but routed through human review rather than published directly. She declines to call the remedy a bias fix, stating it as a distribution policy the platform has chosen and will measure. Her reasoning: the exposure gap lost its justification the moment conversion parity was established, and the generative gap is a quality defect she should not launder as an ethics programme.

For discussion. First: Rathi rejected a remedy that would have detected 340 more deteriorating patients because only 34 more would be acted upon. Was that right, and what evidence would change it? Second: on what basis may a platform change a distribution rule that existing participants built businesses on, and what does it owe them? Third: Jamdani Money kept a feature accounting for six of eleven percentage points of approval-rate disparity because removing it costs 0.9 AUC and eight basis points of default. Build the strongest case for that decision, and name the evidence that would break it.

13. Going deeper

  1. Accountability for what products do to people — the frame this sits inside; bias becomes tractable once you can say who answers for an outcome.
  2. Adding an LLM feature — shipping one makes the generative harm surfaces concrete; you cannot audit a pipeline you have never built.
  3. Responsible AI practices — the machinery around this check: documentation, escalation, cadence, ownership of the seams above.
  4. Engagement-optimised AI and sycophancy — the next-order problem, where a model learns to produce agreeable output that hides the disparity rather than reporting it.
  5. Problem–model fit — most label bias is a fit failure in disguise; asking whether this is a modelling problem at all catches the Taanabaana case early.
  6. The ML lifecycle — checks must attach to named lifecycle stages with owners, or they decay into a launch ritual.
  7. Data strategy and data acquisition — the missingness driving most real disparity is decided years earlier, at acquisition, the cheapest place to fix it.
  8. Labelling and annotation — annotator composition and guidelines are where representational bias enters generative systems, upstream of any model choice.
  9. Model metrics: precision, recall, AUC — the impossibility result is unreadable without fluency here; every fairness criterion is one of these, per group.
  10. What's different when the feature is a model — the trust and feedback dynamics that make the alert-fatigue result the rule, not an anomaly.

The uncomfortable summary: no ranking, recommendation or generation system is fair in every sense at once, and a team claiming otherwise has either equal base rates, which is rare, or an unexamined criterion, which is common. The job is not to eliminate the tradeoff but to choose deliberately, declare the choice, measure it on your own traffic, and stay willing to be argued out of it.

AI & Data Products · AI & ML Product Management

AI Bias and Fairness

Where bias enters ranking, recommendation and generation — and what a product manager can actually check before it ships.

1. A gap on a slide, nine days before the board deck locks

Ritika Sundaram runs AI & Marketplace product at Nyaysetu Works, a Gurugram-headquartered gig-work platform that each month matches roughly 1.3 million worker-partners to shifts in last-mile delivery, warehouse picking and highway logistics across forty-one Indian cities. It is the second week of September 2026, and a fundraising board deck is due to lock in nine days. One slide, built by a data scientist named Naveen for an unrelated efficiency story, contains a number nobody asked for: FitScore, the model that decides which open shifts get pushed to the top of which worker's app first, recommends the premium night highway-logistics shift to 33 percent of the men who apply for it in a given week, but to only 17 percent of the women who apply for the identical shift. The night premium runs about 40 percent over daytime pay — real money for someone earning close to minimum wage. Layered on top of FitScore is a beta generative feature, "Why this shift," which writes each worker a short personalised explanation of a match or non-match; a routine support-ticket review turns up two auto-generated explanations shown to women that cite "shift-consistency history," a phrase no one on the product team approved for external use.

Ritika has ninety-six hours to decide what this means. The deck's growth narrative depends on FitScore's matching efficiency; a false alarm that triggers an unnecessary rebuild costs a fundraising cycle. Understating a genuine gap risks a regulatory letter, a client pulling a contract, or a story later on far worse terms. She needs a way to tell a model behaving badly from a marketplace mirroring a labour pattern that predates FitScore.

2. The idea: bias as accountability applied to a model

In a product context, bias is a systematic, direction-consistent gap between how a model treats members of two groups who are, by the standard the product itself claims to use, equally deserving of an outcome. Fairness is the property of a system that a named authority — a regulator, a company's own written policy, a court, or an enterprise client's compliance team — is prepared to certify does not have that gap, measured against one of several mathematical definitions of "gap" that do not always agree with each other. The idea did not begin in machine learning. It began in US employment law: the 1971 Supreme Court case Griggs v. Duke Power established that a hiring test could be illegal because of its effect on outcomes, regardless of the employer's intent, and in 1978 the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission formalised this into the "four-fifths rule" — a selection rate for any group below 80 percent of the highest group's rate is presumptive evidence of discrimination, triggering a duty to justify it. Machine-learning researchers borrowed and extended this logic from roughly 2012 onward — Cynthia Dwork and colleagues' "fairness through awareness," and Moritz Hardt, Eric Price and Nathan Srebro's 2016 work on equalised odds — because the same question, "is this selection procedure lopsided enough to demand an explanation," applies whether the selector is a supervisor or a ranking model. The single sentence Ritika could say in the board meeting without sounding glib: bias is accountability applied to models — if you'd make a human manager explain why men keep getting the good shifts, you have to make your model explain it too, and "the algorithm decided" is not an explanation.

3. How the check actually works, walked through with FitScore

Practitioners who understand this run the same five steps every time, though most are left implicit in casual talk about "checking for bias." First, define the comparison groups and the outcome precisely — here, applicant gender, and "recommended in the top slice for a specific category in a specific week," not recommended in general. Second, compute the selection rate for each group: the share of that group's applicants who received the outcome, restricted to the same category and window, so the comparison is like against like. Third, compute the impact ratio — the disadvantaged group's rate divided by the advantaged group's. Fourth, compare that ratio to a threshold; the four-fifths rule (0.8) is an inherited convention, not a law of physics, but a defensible default when no stricter internal policy exists. Fifth, the step almost everyone skips: if flagged, do not stop at the number — open the feature list for proxies, features that do not name the protected attribute but correlate with it anyway, often because the world already sorted people unevenly before the model saw the data. Most real bias in shipped ML systems is this kind, "disparate impact," not "disparate treatment" — nobody wrote if gender == 'female' into FitScore; the model learned that "night-shift completion count, last 90 days" predicted a good match, and that feature was a near-perfect stand-in for gender, because women had historically been steered away from night dispatch for reasons — safety concerns, escort logistics, family expectations — unrelated to their ability to do the job.

Exhibit 2 — the five steps applied at Nyaysetu Works
StepApplied to FitScoreWhat teams usually skip
1. Define groups & outcomeGender; "recommended," same shift category, same weekComparing across categories or time windows
2. Selection rate per groupMen 33% vs women 17% (Exhibit 1)Filtering to a genuinely comparable applicant pool first
3. Impact ratio17 ÷ 33 = 0.515—
4. Compare to threshold0.515 < 0.8 → flaggedTreating the threshold as fixed rather than a policy choice
5. Proxy inspection"Night-shift completion count" correlates 0.71 with genderStopping at "we don't use gender as a feature"

4. The worked example, and what changes when one input changes

Naveen's team pulls the raw numbers for the night highway-logistics category, week of 8 September 2026: 8,000 men applied and 2,000 women applied. FitScore placed 2,640 of the men and 340 of the women into the app's top-of-feed slot, the position that drives roughly 70 percent of accepted shifts. The selection rate for men is 2,640 ÷ 8,000 = 0.330, or 33.0 percent. The selection rate for women is 340 ÷ 2,000 = 0.170, or 17.0 percent. The impact ratio is 0.170 ÷ 0.330 = 0.515 — well under the 0.8 threshold, and a large enough gap that "it's just the labour market" is not, by itself, an adequate answer, because the check already restricted the comparison to people who chose to apply for this exact category this exact week.

The team runs a proxy scan and finds that "night-shift completion count, last 90 days" correlates 0.71 with applicant gender in this dataset — almost as informative about gender as it is about anything else — while a substitute feature, "completed shifts of any type, last 90 days," correlates only 0.06 with gender and is nearly as predictive of reliability. They retrain with the substitution, holding every other feature fixed, and re-run the same week's applicant pool: men recommended rises slightly to 2,650 (33.1 percent, essentially unchanged), and women recommended rises to 620 (620 ÷ 2,000 = 0.310, or 31.0 percent). The new impact ratio is 0.310 ÷ 0.331 = 0.937 — comfortably above 0.8. One feature swap, arithmetically, closed most of the gap, which is itself evidence about where the bias had been hiding.

5. Eight things a learner must get straight

Exhibit 4 — the eight nuances at a glance
Impact vs. treatmentIntent vs. outcomeWhose "fair"?Unawareness ≠ fixed
Gap ≠ model's faultThreshold is policyComparable pools onlyText needs its own audit

Disparate impact is not disparate treatment

Treatment discrimination requires a rule that names the protected attribute; impact discrimination needs no such rule, only a lopsided outcome. Most model bias is impact — nobody coded "if female," the pattern arrived through data. This matters because the fix is different: you cannot "remove the rule" that was never written, so the remedy has to live in features or data, not in a line of forbidden logic.

There is no single mathematical definition of fair

Demographic parity (equal selection rates), equalised odds (equal error rates per group) and calibration (a score means the same thing regardless of group) each sound reasonable, and a 2016 result by Jon Kleinberg, Sendhil Mullainathan and Manish Raghavan proved a model cannot satisfy all three at once when base rates genuinely differ across groups. Picking one is a business decision, not a default.

Fairness through unawareness rarely works

Deleting the sensitive attribute feels responsible and accomplishes little, because correlated features — night-shift history, distance from a well-lit metro stop, late-night response times — carry the same signal under a different name. The proxy scan in Section 3 exists because "we don't use gender" is not evidence of anything.

A gap does not prove the model created it

FitScore may simply reflect a labour-market pattern that predates it — fewer women apply for night shifts, for reasons the platform did not cause. That does not make the gap acceptable to ignore, but it changes who owns the fix: correcting a pre-existing societal pattern is a policy choice, not an automatic obligation the check itself settles.

The threshold is a policy choice, not a natural law

The four-fifths rule comes from a specific US employment-testing context; India has no identical statute for algorithmic hiring, though the IT Rules, consumer-protection law and enterprise-client contract terms create parallel exposure. Adopting 0.8, or something stricter, is Nyaysetu Works choosing a standard for itself, worth stating explicitly rather than inheriting by accident.

The comparison pool has to be genuinely comparable

Comparing selection rates across different shift categories, cities or time windows invites a Simpson's-paradox-style illusion, where an aggregate gap reverses or vanishes once you slice correctly. Exhibit 1's category-by-category view exists because a single company-wide number would have hidden that only one category was actually a problem.

Checks decay — a launch audit is not a permanent one

What FitScore recommends this month becomes part of next month's training data: if women are shown fewer night shifts, fewer will accept them, and the model will "learn" that women don't want night shifts, reinforcing the original gap. This feedback loop means the check belongs on a recurring cadence, not a one-time launch gate.

Generative text carries its own, separate bias surface

"Why this shift" can pass every numeric fairness check on the ranking beneath it and still write biased or unauthorised language, as the "shift-consistency history" phrase showed. A model's words are a second product surface that needs its own review — tone, phrase provenance, no invented justifications — independent of whether the underlying score is fair.

6. How this differs by product type and by company stage

In a two-sided marketplace like Nyaysetu Works, bias can appear on either side of the match — workers denied good shifts, or employers shown a narrower candidate pool than they paid for — and checking one side alone is only half the audit. In a consumer product, the analogous check looks at exposure: what share of impressions a group receives, since consumer harm usually shows up as being shown less, not selected less. In a B2B product — Nyaysetu Works licensing FitScore's engine to enterprise logistics clients — the protected attribute becomes a contract term rather than a constant: a Gulf-market client's legitimate nationality filter would be illegal inside India, so "fair according to whom" is configured per client, not assumed universal.

Exhibit 5 — where the check changes by context
ContextWhere bias shows upWho defines "fair"
Consumer feedImpressions/exposure by groupCompany policy, regulator
Marketplace (both sides)Match rate, either sideCompany policy, both sides' regulators
B2B embedded modelWhatever the client's HR/legal rules governThe client's contract, per market

Stage matters as much as product type. An early-stage team often has no labelled sensitive-attribute data at all — many products deliberately skip collecting gender or caste at sign-up — which makes the direct selection-rate check impossible and pushes the burden onto proxy audits alone. A Series C company at Nyaysetu Works's scale has the labelled data and board scrutiny that force a formal cadence, but also a far larger blast radius: the same 16-point gap that touches a few hundred people at a seed-stage pilot now touches roughly 25,000 women applicants a week.

7. Common mistakes

Exhibit 6 — four mistakes and their cheapest diagnostics
MistakeSymptomCheapest diagnostic
"We don't use gender, so we can't be biased"Large gap persists despite the attribute's absenceCorrelate every feature against the held-out attribute; flag anything above ~0.3
One aggregate fairness numberPasses overall, one category or city is still lopsidedAlways slice by category × city × week before reporting a single ratio
Cosmetic override instead of a fixMetric improves, but removing the override reverts it instantlyAsk whether the remedy survives being turned off — if not, it was patched, not fixed
Treating launch audit as the finish lineGap quietly reappears one or two quarters laterPut the impact ratio on the same recurring dashboard as revenue, re-run every quarter
Each shares a family resemblance: the team made the number look right without changing what produced it. The four diagnostics above are cheap enough that skipping them is a statement about priorities, not about cost.

8. What good looks like

The version of this story that ends well has Ritika's team running the same five-step check, finding the same 0.515 ratio, and doing three unglamorous things before the deck locks: swapping the proxy feature for the reliability substitute and confirming 0.937; writing a one-page fairness memo — gap found, remedy applied, layer it was applied at, recheck cadence — attached to FitScore's model documentation; and pausing "Why this shift" from wider rollout until its generated text passes a separate language audit, rather than letting a passing numeric check wave the whole feature through. The board slide, instead of hiding the gap or over-claiming the fix, says plainly: "we found a proxy-driven disparity, corrected it, and will report this ratio every quarter" — the sentence a credible investor and a credible regulator both want to hear, and it costs one engineer-week, not a rebuild.

What Ritika decides: she instructs Naveen's team to ship the reliability-proxy substitution before the deck locks, adds the impact ratio to the standing metrics dashboard the board already sees quarterly, and pulls "Why this shift" back to a smaller pilot pending a text-specific audit — treating the numeric fix and the language fix as two separate problems rather than one.

What to learn next, and why: Responsible AI practices, because this single check is one instrument inside a larger governance system that also covers documentation, escalation and audit ownership; and engagement-optimised AI and sycophancy, because a generative feature tuned to make every user feel good about their match is exactly the kind of feature that will learn to write reassuring language over honest language, quietly hiding the next version of this gap.

Two questions worth sitting with: If you removed every feature correlated above 0.3 with a protected attribute, would your product still work — or does it secretly depend on the proxy? And in your own product, what decides who gets shown the good options first, and have you ever measured whether that gap survives a controlled re-run?

Laghu Credit Services: The Score That Listened Less

A decision case in AI bias and fairness

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 5 October 2026, Lalitha Lingam, Chief Product Officer of Laghu Credit Services, sat in a glass-walled meeting room in Bengaluru with a printout she did not want to be holding. On Friday 2 October the data science team had delivered the result of a fairness audit she had commissioned on 15 September. It said that Laghu's credit score was turning away women who would have repaid, at a markedly higher rate than it turned away men.

The expansion into Lucknow, Indore and Nagpur was set for Monday, 26 October, two weeks before Diwali. The chief executive wanted a yes or no by Friday. Lalitha had to decide what to ship, and on what terms.

2. Company background

Laghu Credit Services was founded in 2021 by Laxman Lamba and two colleagues. It builds "Laghu Line", a small-ticket credit line of ₹10,000 to ₹1,00,000 for people whom bank credit bureaus often know little about: delivery partners, salon owners, kirana shopkeepers and home-based sellers on ONDC-connected apps. Laghu scores applications for a regulated NBFC partner, and operates within the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending framework and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

Paytm and PhonePe also offer small loans inside apps their users open daily. Laghu's bet was that a score built on thin-file signals, such as recharge patterns and app usage, could say yes to people the bureaus could not see.

Each quarter the company receives about 2,00,000 applications and approves 37,000, at an average ticket of ₹40,000: roughly ₹148 crore disbursed per quarter. Its model, "Laghu Score v3", uses about 240 features. Gender is collected at KYC but, by design, is not an input. The team assumed a model that never sees gender cannot discriminate on it.

3. The situation

Lokesh Lakhani built the audit. Lokesh, who heads data science in Pune, took a January to March 2026 cohort whose six-month loans had all matured, and asked a plain question: among applicants who would in fact have repaid, what share did the model approve, separately for women and men? For rejected applicants, "would repay" was inferred from later performance on other credit lines visible through a bureau link.

The audit used four measures. The selection rate is approvals divided by applications. The true positive rate (TPR) is approvals among applicants who would have repaid, divided by all such applicants. The false positive rate (FPR) is approvals among applicants who would not have repaid, divided by all such applicants. The equal-opportunity gap is the difference between the two groups' TPRs. Exhibit 1 sets out the results.

In Exhibit 1, women and men were equally likely to repay, at 70 per cent each, yet the model approved 18.0 per cent of the women who would repay against 26.0 per cent of the men: an equal-opportunity gap of 8.0 percentage points. It was also less accurate on women's files. It also let through more women who would not repay (8.0 per cent against 6.0), and only 84.0 per cent of approved women repaid, against 91.0 per cent of men. The model was not cautious with women; it was noisier about them.

Leena Lobo, head of risk and compliance in Mumbai, noted that the selection-rate ratio of 0.75 fell below the 0.80 "four-fifths" benchmark from United States employment practice, a heuristic and not Indian law.

The cause surfaced in a second cut (Exhibit 2). Lokesh's team found that "shared-device flag", a feature marking phones on which several accounts or users had been seen, was one of the score's strongest negative signals. In Laghu's data, 40 per cent of women applicants carried the flag against 10 per cent of men. Many women customers use a family member's handset. The model never saw gender, but it had found a stand-in.

Within each flag status the gender gap in Exhibit 2 is only two points; across flag status it is ten. A fix aimed at the flag would close most of the gap.

Lucia Lacerda, Laghu's user researcher in Lisbon, four and a half hours behind Indian time that Monday, had interviewed forty applicants. Several women had applied on a family phone because they owned none; two gave up after a second rejection. Lars Lindqvist, an independent fairness advisor in Gothenburg, urged patience: retrained models that look fair in a backtest can drift within a quarter, and he would not sign off on a launch without live monitoring.

Timing compounded the pressure (Figure 1). A full retraining on new features would take ten weeks, ready on 14 December.

Figure 1. The calendar around the decision; spacing indicative.

4. The people

Laxman Lamba, co-founder and chief executive, Gurugram. He has promised investors the three-city launch this quarter and wants to ship on 26 October.

Lokesh Lakhani, head of data science, Pune. He built the audit and the model. He believes the gap is fixable and wants a fix tested on live traffic.

Leena Lobo, head of risk and compliance, Mumbai. She answers to the NBFC partner. She wants a documented test and a written threshold.

Lucia Lacerda, user researcher, Lisbon. She speaks for applicants who never appear in the data.

5. Exhibit 3: what each option does to the women's cohort

Lokesh simulated three options on the same cohort, counting only the 60,000 women applicants. A repaid loan contributes ₹3,200 (8 per cent of the ₹40,000 ticket); a default loses ₹24,000. Figures are quarterly, against the current model.

Exhibit 3. Simulated effect on women applicants, per quarter, versus current model
OptionWomen's TPRWomen's FPRExtra repaid loansExtra defaultsNet contribution (₹ lakh)

Option 2: 2,520 × ₹3,200 = ₹80.64 lakh gained; 162 × ₹24,000 = ₹38.88 lakh lost. Option 3: 3,360 × ₹3,200 = ₹107.52 lakh, an untested target available only after 14 December, before a one-time retraining cost of ₹45 lakh.

6. The options

  1. Launch as is, and monitor. Ship on 26 October. The upside is certain timing. The cost is carrying a known 8.0-point equal-opportunity gap into three new cities, before a partner and regulator who could ask what Laghu knew.
  2. Neutralise the flag, launch on time, and monitor weekly. Set the shared-device flag to "not flagged" in scoring, re-set the cut-off within the partner's loss ceiling, add a manual-review lane for borderline cases, and publish a weekly subgroup dashboard. The upside is a ₹41.76 lakh quarterly gain among women applicants and a gap largely closed. The cost is a higher false positive rate (8.9 per cent) and imperfect labels.
  3. Delay to 14 December and retrain. Rebuild the model with bank-statement data shared through the Account Aggregator framework. The upside is the best modelled outcome. The cost is ₹45 lakh, the loss of Diwali, and an untested target.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. In Exhibit 1, why do the pooled figures differ from a simple average of the two groups, and which column should a PM quote to the board?
  2. Laghu's model never used gender. Using Exhibit 2, explain how bias entered, and what a PM could have checked before the model reached production.
  3. Which measure would you hold the product to: selection-rate ratio, equal-opportunity gap, or repaid share of approved? What does each miss?
  4. Which option do you choose, what conditions would make you stop, and who needs to sign off?

8. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. Bias is accountability applied to models. The PM's job is not to certify that a model is unbiased but to measure performance by subgroup, find where the difference enters, and act on it with evidence and a stop rule. Two habits mark a strong answer: compare rates on the right base (true positive rates among people who would repay, not merely approvals), and trace the mechanism, here a proxy feature, which is why omitting gender protected nothing.

One defensible path: Option 2 now, Option 3 in parallel. The repayment rate is 70 per cent in both groups, so the gap is not explained by underlying risk. Option 1 scales a measured harm; Option 3 alone spends Diwali on an unproven target. Option 2 closes most of the gap, is positive for the business (₹41.76 lakh per quarter among women applicants) and keeps the launch date. Lalitha should launch under three gates: a weekly dashboard of TPR and FPR by gender and flag status; a pause of the new cities if the women's equal-opportunity gap is still above four points after four weeks, or losses breach the partner's ceiling; and retraining started at once, reviewed by Lars Lindqvist, aiming for 14 December. Leena documents the threshold and approval.

Limits to name. The "would repay" label is inferred for rejected applicants, the cohort is one quarter, and a simulation is not a live result; monitoring replaces assumption with evidence.
case40v1-aipm.bias:
Tathya Health Systems: Four Ways to Be Fair

An ambiguous case in AI bias and fairness — AI & Data Products

1. Sunday night, Worli

On Sunday, 11 October 2026, Tanvi Parulekar sat at her dining table in Worli with three printouts in front of her and a fourth turned face down. She was Vice-President, Product at Tathya Health Systems, and at eleven the next morning she had to hand the risk council a written recommendation on the claims-triage model that produced most of the company's revenue.

They disagreed. Bengaluru's data science team said the model flagged women's health-insurance claims for investigation 1.25 times as often as men's, and wrongly flagged them at 12.50 per cent against 7.50 per cent. Claims operations in Kolkata said that once desk reviewers had finished, women's claims were escalated to field investigation less often than men's — 5.55 per cent against 7.13 per cent. The vendor whose sealed engine sat at the centre of the product said the model had passed every fairness test its contract named. The face-down page was an analysis the General Counsel had ordered destroyed in August.

2. How Tathya got here

Tathya Health Systems was founded in February 2021 in Mumbai by Tarun Bhagwat and Tejal Wadekar, who between them had run claims and provider networks for a decade. Its product, Tathya Triage, scores each claim from 0 to 100 for “irregularity likelihood”. Scores below 70 pass to automated approval; at 70 and above the claim is flagged, and a desk reviewer either releases it or escalates it to a field investigator, adding nine to twenty-two days to settlement.

The decision that constrains everything today was made in August 2022. Tvisha Insurance Services, then India's fastest-growing standalone health insurer, wanted a working scorer in twelve weeks; building one in-house was nine months' work. So Tarun licensed a foreign-built engine, Gradient Risk Core v4, from Trinetra Risk Labs, whose modelling team sits in Kraków. The licence bought speed and sold away inspection: Tathya may add features before the core and set thresholds after it, but cannot see its weights, retrain it, or audit it. Clause 11.4 makes reverse-engineering a termination event, and early exit costs ₹12.5 crore.

Tvisha signed in January 2023 on a gain-share of 12 per cent of net savings. Tathya now scores for seven insurers and closed FY26 at ₹214 crore of revenue.

3. The market Tathya sits in

Regulation has tightened around exactly what Tathya sells. The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India has pushed insurers hard on turnaround times and on the Bima Bharosa grievance channel, and its master circular on policyholder protection made cashless authorisation timelines a matter of published record; the National Health Claims Exchange has begun standardising claim data between insurers and hospitals; and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs what Tathya may process and infer.

The exposure is global too. Tvisha administers group health for Taameer Industries, an Abu Dhabi conglomerate covering 41,000 lives, whose procurement policy requires vendors' automated decision systems to carry a non-discrimination statement, and Trevor Fernandes, Tathya's sales head in Chicago, wants the same statement for two United States proposals, a draft of which he has already shared with one prospect.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Between March and May 2026, forty-one grievances reached Tvisha through Bima Bharosa over investigation delays. On 18 May, Tajurba Nagrik Manch, a Delhi policyholder-rights forum, filed a representation citing 1,200 grievances it had collected. Its central allegation was not about women. It was that claims from certain localities — it named districts with large religious-minority populations — were held for investigation at markedly higher rates.

Tathya's first answer, in June, was that the model could not be doing this because it held no field for religion or community. That was believed for about seven weeks, then failed on two fronts.

First, on 3 August, Trishala Menon's team delivered a blind re-audit: 6,000 claims from the April–June quarter, drawn in proportion to the quarter's claimant and district mix and sent to full field investigation regardless of score, investigators blind to it. It gave Tathya a prevalence estimate independent of the model and of past investigation choices (Exhibits 1 and 2).

Second, the team traced the training labels. Gradient Risk Core v4 had been tuned on Tathya's 2022–24 outcomes, where a claim counted as irregular if a field investigation had confirmed it. But panels were unevenly empanelled: metropolitan districts investigated one claim in five, thin-panel tier-3 and rural districts one in twenty, while the confirmation rate among those investigated was 22.0 per cent everywhere. Label rates therefore varied fourfold across district groups while true prevalence barely varied at all (Exhibit 3). The model had not learned who was irregular. It had learned where Tathya used to look.

On 24 July, Tomas Ferreira, a senior data scientist in Melbourne, did something nobody asked for: unable to measure the axis in the complaint, he joined claim PIN codes to Census religious-composition data and compared flag rates across deciles (Exhibit 6). On 14 August, Tharini Iyer, General Counsel and Data Protection Officer, ordered it deleted — inferring religion from a postcode was, in her reading, fresh processing of sensitive data to which no policyholder had consented. On 21 August, Tapan Choudhury presented the operations view, which showed no problem at all. On 9 September, Trinetra updated its model card, again declined to disclose feature weights, and offered an add-on, Fairness Pack v2, at ₹3.4 crore with twenty weeks' delivery. Nine weeks after the re-audit, on 5 October, Tvisha's board asked for a fairness attestation by 30 October.

5. The people

Tanvi Parulekar, VP Product, Mumbai. Owns the attestation; believes the honest version cannot yet be written. Unsaid: she thinks the licence, not the model, is the defect, which puts her against the founder who signed it.

Tarun Bhagwat, co-founder and CEO, Mumbai. Wants a fairness statement that is true and short; his incentive is a Series C round in January. Unsaid: he has told two investors that Tathya's fairness testing is “ahead of the market”, on the strength of the vendor's model card.

Trishala Menon, Head of Data Science, Bengaluru. Built the re-audit and the label trace; wants subgroup error rates published quarterly and a per-group threshold in November. Unsaid: her own team set the 70-point cut-off in 2023 by maximising savings.

Tapan Choudhury, Head of Claims Operations, Kolkata, seconded to Tvisha's hub. Argues desk reviewers absorb the model's noise, so the disparity never reaches a policyholder; his escalation budget is nearly full. Unsaid: his reviewers release 62.5 per cent of women's flags against 40.0 of men's because they have learned the model runs hot on certain files — a correction nobody recorded.

Tharini Iyer, General Counsel and Data Protection Officer, Chennai. Will not permit inference of community or religion, nor sign an attestation citing a metric Tathya cannot reproduce. Unsaid: she is unsure whether refusing to measure protects policyholders or Tathya.

Tejal Wadekar, co-founder and Chief Revenue Officer, Hyderabad. Holds the Tvisha relationship and reads fairness as a renewal question. Unsaid: Tvisha's integrity head has asked whether Tathya's recall is high because it over-flags, and she has not relayed it.

Tomas Ferreira, Senior Data Scientist, Melbourne, five and a half hours ahead. Believes an unmeasured disparity is not an absent one and that the deletion destroyed evidence. Unsaid: his decile analysis is confounded and he knows it.

6. Exhibits

All figures cover 1 April to 30 June 2026 and the 6,00,000 claims Tathya scored for Tvisha. “Irregular” means established so by full field investigation; group prevalence is the re-audit estimate extrapolated.

C. Equalise confirmation rates (Option C). Earns the most and satisfies predictive parity, while pushing 29,850 extra wrongful flags a quarter onto men's claims, cutting women's detection to 45.00 per cent and breaking escalation capacity by 12,000 claims.

F. Stop deciding alone. Tell Tvisha the whole of it, publish subgroup error rates quarterly, and let the insurer choose the criterion, since it owns the claim decision. Tejal believes this loses the account.

She has written the list twice and each time it has bothered her. Every option answers a question about claimant sex, because claimant sex is a field she has. The representation that began this was about something else.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The risk council meets at 11:00 on Monday, 12 October 2026; the board on 16 October; Tvisha's attestation is due 30 October, Taameer's procurement statement 15 November, and Diwali falls on 8 November with volumes about 18 per cent higher around it. Field capacity is 42,000 escalations a quarter and cannot be raised before January. The Tvisha gain-share ran at ₹913.13 lakh last quarter, an annualised ₹36.53 crore, about 17 per cent of FY26 revenue of ₹214 crore. Tharini will not sign an attestation citing a metric Tathya cannot reproduce; Tarun will not send a document that reads as an admission. Nobody has established who decides when those positions conflict.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 2 shows equal detection and unequal false-flag and confirmation rates. Which is “the” fairness number here, and what does that choice commit you to?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 4 describe one quarter and point opposite ways. On which population should harm be measured, and what must you know about desk review to trust Exhibit 4?
  3. Exhibit 3 argues the bias entered through the labels, not the features. If so, what does that imply about Options B and C, which change only thresholds?
  4. The alleged disparity lies on an axis Tathya holds no field for and is advised not to infer. Argue Tharini's position, then against it. What does a PM do with an unmeasurable subgroup?
  5. Option C helps one group by harming another and is the most profitable setting in Exhibit 5. On what basis, if any, may a PM choose it, and who must agree?
  6. It is 11:00 on Monday. What does Tanvi put in front of the risk council, what does she ask of Tvisha, and what does she tell the board on 16 October about what Tathya knew and deleted?

11. Sunday, 23:40

Tanvi turned the fourth page over and read it again. Sixteen point four against eleven point nine: a number she was not allowed to use, about the only question anyone outside the company had asked, got by a colleague who broke policy to get it, and who was right that not knowing was not the same as nothing being there.

Trishala's last message sat unanswered on her phone: whichever criterion we pick, we are choosing who waits at the discharge desk. Below it, Tapan's, six minutes later: we already chose. My reviewers chose, every day, for three years, and nobody wrote it down.

She opened a blank document, typed Recommendation to the Risk Council — 12 October 2026, and looked at the cursor. In Melbourne it was already Monday.
