AI & Data Products — AI & ML Product Management

When the Feature Is a Model

Non-determinism, cost per use, latency and invisible failure, treated as an engineering and economic discipline rather than a caution.

1. Two decisions, ten days apart

On 14 January 2026, Meher Sondhi, Chief Product Officer of Hausla Credit Cloud, spent a morning reading one credit memo. Hausla sells loan-origination software to twenty-three non-banking financial companies and two small finance banks; its customers push about 40,000 memos a month, each condensing bank statements, GST returns and a bureau report into a recommendation an analyst signs. Since September, four lenders had drafted memos with AutoMemo, in which a language model reads the borrower's uploaded documents and writes the memo for the analyst to review and sign.

The memo concerned a Coimbatore textile processor seeking ₹1.8 crore of working capital. It was well organised, internally consistent, and it stated the borrower's turnover as ₹4.2 crore. The GST filings in the same bundle said ₹2.4 crore. Nothing else was wrong; no log recorded anything; the analyst had signed in four minutes. Under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending framework accountability sat with the lender, whose chief risk officer asked a question Sondhi could not answer: how many memos drafted since September contained a number like that one? By 31 March she had to recommend whether AutoMemo went to all twenty-three lenders.

Ten days later Devang Puri, head of product at Safarnama Stays, was looking at different numbers. Safarnama is a Bengaluru travel app with about 12 million monthly actives, competing for leisure bookings against MakeMyTrip, Booking.com and the hotel chains' own apps. Trip Weaver took a free-text wish — "four days in Coorg with my parents, no long drives" — and returned a day-by-day itinerary with bookable stays. In December it reached 4.1 million sessions, raised booking conversion, and generated an inference bill of ₹43.3 lakh growing eleven per cent month on month, at a ninety-fifth-percentile latency of 6.8 seconds. On 19 January a customer in Mysuru complained that the rooftop infinity pool Trip Weaver promised at a Coorg homestay did not exist. Before the summer season opened in March, Puri had to decide whether Trip Weaver became the default entry point to search.

Exhibit 1 — the same four properties, two very different exposures
Hausla (enterprise, regulated)Safarnama (consumer, high volume)
Calls per month40,000 memos13.1 million model calls
Sticker cost per call₹2.80₹0.33
Monthly inference spend₹1.12 lakh₹43.3 lakh
Latency that mattersanalyst waits 9 s, happilyp95 6.8 s, users abandon
One invisible failure costsa mis-sized ₹1.8 crore loan; regulatory exposureone refunded booking; trust at scale

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Conventional software is a deterministic function: given an input and a version of the code it produces one output, and its failures announce themselves as an exception or a status page. A model-based feature replaces that function with a learned conditional distribution — it estimates, for a given input, a distribution over plausible outputs and returns a sample from it. Four consequences follow and none is optional. The output is non-deterministic. Each output carries a real marginal cost, because inference consumes compute a vendor bills for, and takes measurable, variable time. And the system can be wrong without failing, returning a fluent, well-formed answer that is false, with no signal distinguishing it from a correct one.

The history explains why the field's advice is inconsistent. The engineering critique came first: D. Sculley and colleagues at Google published "Machine Learning: The High-Interest Credit Card of Technical Debt" in 2014, arguing that learned components erode the abstraction boundaries software testing depends on — a model has no interface contract, only a statistical one. Martin Zinkevich's "Rules of Machine Learning" supplied the operational folklore. In 2017 Andrej Karpathy reframed the same facts as opportunity in "Software 2.0": the artefact under management is the dataset and the weights, so the lever is data, not specification. Google's PAIR People + AI Guidebook and Microsoft's Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction, both 2019, moved the problem to the interface: you cannot make the model reliable, so make the experience robust to unreliability. The evaluation-first school, visible in work on LLM-as-judge validation by Shreya Shankar and colleagues after ChatGPT's launch in November 2022, holds that shipping a model feature is statistical inference and the eval suite is the product artefact. Against all of them stands the scaling position, anchored in Richard Sutton's 2019 essay "The Bitter Lesson": cost, latency and non-determinism are transient parameters, and scaffolding built around today's limits is depreciating capital.

Exhibit 2 — what each school will and will not sign
SchoolWill signWill not sign
Engineering-debt (Sculley, Zinkevich)"A model must be versioned, monitored and regression-tested like a supplier, not a library.""Product management needs a new epistemology."
Probabilistic UX (PAIR, HAX)"Design for graceful failure and calibrated expectations; the interface carries the uncertainty.""A good enough model removes the need for failure-handling design."
Evaluation-first"No launch without a held-out set, a written bar, and a confidence interval.""Aggregate pass rates on a convenience sample are evidence."
Scaling / Bitter Lesson"Most scaffolding is depreciating capital; buy capability, not workarounds.""Evaluation infrastructure is worth building before the model is good enough."

Each executive could find a school that flattered the decision they wanted. The mechanics below are what let a practitioner referee between them.

3. Mechanics: the arithmetic experts actually run

Start with cost, the property most often mis-measured. Hausla's sticker cost is easy: about 6,000 input tokens of documents and 900 output tokens per memo, at roughly $3 and $15 per million tokens, gives $0.0315, or ₹2.80. That number is nearly meaningless. The unit that matters is cost per accepted outcome, folding in retries, verification and the human rework a rejected output triggers:

C_accepted = ( c_generate × (1 + r) + c_verify ) / p_accept + h × (1 − p_accept)

For AutoMemo in January: generation ₹2.80; retry rate r = 0.06; a verification call at ₹0.55; acceptance p_accept of 0.83; rework h of fourteen analyst-minutes at ₹520 an hour, ₹121. That gives (2.80 × 1.06 + 0.55) / 0.83 + 121 × 0.17 = ₹4.24 + ₹20.57 = ₹24.81 per accepted memo, nine times the sticker price and dominated by human rework, not inference. The consequence is immediate: a model twice as expensive but five points more accurate is cheaper. Against a manual memo at ₹329, AutoMemo still saved over ninety per cent. Sondhi's problem was never the vendor bill.

Second, measurement. The 83 per cent came from a held-out set of 200 memos. The standard error of a proportion is sqrt(p(1−p)/n) = sqrt(0.83 × 0.17 / 200) = 0.0266, so the ninety-five per cent interval runs 77.8 to 88.2 per cent. The lender's contractual gate was 85: the measurement could not distinguish passing from failing. Narrowing to ±2 points requires n = 1.96² × 0.83 × 0.17 / 0.02² ≈ 1,355 labelled cases. Practitioners who have internalised this stop quoting eval scores without an n.

Third, latency, which composes worse than intuition suggests. Trip Weaver makes three sequential calls.

Figure 1. Sequential calls stack medians but not percentiles: the pipeline's p95 of 6.8 seconds sits below the 7.2-second sum of the parts and far above the slowest single call. Were the stages independent, only 0.95³ = 85.7 per cent of sessions would clear all three p95 targets.

At 4.1 million sessions a month, a p99 of 11.4 seconds means roughly 41,000 sessions on a spinner for over eleven seconds. Puri's team had set a two-second target per call and met it on all three. The step usually left implicit is measuring the workflow rather than the component, and separating measured from perceived latency: Trip Weaver streamed its itinerary day by day, and its 0.8-second time-to-first-token was what actually predicted abandonment.

4. When the framing applies, and when it misleads

The four properties are always true of a model; their salience is not. Three testable claims separate the cases where the framing should drive design from those where it is an expensive distraction.

Claim one: per-call cost matters when inference is a material fraction of the contribution margin of the action it enables. False at Hausla: ₹24.81 against a memo that formerly cost ₹329 of labour, on a loan earning lakhs, is noise. True and worsening at Safarnama: ₹43.3 lakh a month against incremental bookings worth ₹1.89 crore is a twenty-three per cent tax on the feature's own gross benefit, scaling with adoption while the benefit does not.

Claim two: non-determinism is a product problem when a user can observe more than one output for the same situation, or someone downstream must reconcile two. Largely false for Safarnama — a traveller sees one itinerary once. Emphatically true for Hausla, where audit will re-run a memo months later and must explain why the second draft differs from the signed one.

Claim three: invisible failure dominates when the output is plausible to its reviewer and consequential downstream. True at Hausla, where an analyst cannot check a turnover figure without opening the GST filing and the memo exists to spare them that. Partly true at Safarnama, where a fabricated amenity is invisible until check-in and costs one refund.

The framing misleads in three situations. Where a model runs as an offline batch feeding a human-adjudicated queue, latency and determinism are not live concerns, and teams that treat them as such build streaming infrastructure nobody needs. Where the output is preference-shaped — image variations, brainstorms, draft copy — variability is the product, and "reduce non-determinism" is a category error. And where the decision was never deterministic: Hausla's audit found two analysts writing the same memo agreed eighty-nine per cent of the time, so AutoMemo's 83 was never being measured against 100.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Multi-product companies hit the seam first. Hausla runs one AutoMemo service for twenty-three lenders whose credit policies differ; a prompt change that improves memos for an unsecured-lending client can degrade them for a loan-against-property client, and no compiler will say so. The mature answer is a per-tenant eval set: nothing ships without running all twenty-three suites, and any suite dropping more than two points blocks release. Most companies say they do this; what they do is run the biggest three and hope.

Two-sided markets add an incentive asymmetry. Nayaab Markets, a Delhi NCR B2B wholesale platform, uses a model to normalise 90,000 supplier listings a week into a common catalogue. Non-determinism there is a fairness issue, not a quality one: two near-identical listings sorted into different categories rank differently, and the disadvantaged supplier has no appeal. Nayaab's control was not a better model but a determinism guarantee at the business layer — results pinned per supplier SKU, re-normalised only on a version bump the supplier can see.

Regulated settings turn logging into a compliance question. RBI's auditability expectations and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's purpose limitation together mean Hausla must retain the full request envelope — prompt version, retrieved documents, model identifier, sampling parameters, output, reviewer action — while not retaining borrower documents beyond the stated purpose. The seam sits between a product team that wants rich logs and a legal team that wants short retention; the resolution is redaction at log time, not a retention argument at incident time.

Hardware inverts the cost picture. Satpura Instruments, a Pune firm, ships vibration sensors that sit on pumps and gearboxes in cement and sugar plants; 4,200 units run an anomaly model on a ₹1,900 microcontroller, once a second, at effectively zero marginal cost. Its problem is the opposite of Safarnama's: updates travel as firmware over patchy connectivity, so the installed base is a distribution over model versions, eleven per cent of it fourteen months stale in March 2026. "Which model is in production" has no single answer, and Satpura's dashboards were built as though it did. AI-native companies face the seam in reverse: with no deterministic fallback, quality ownership dissolves between engineering, research and nobody, which is why the firms that handle it well give one named owner of the eval suite a release veto.

6. Eight things an expert notices that a competent practitioner does not

Temperature zero is not determinism

Temperature zero makes the sampler greedy, not the system reproducible: provider-side batching, non-associative floating-point arithmetic on GPUs and expert routing in mixture-of-experts models all shift outputs between identical calls. The tell-tale sign is a team that says "temperature is zero, so it's deterministic" without having measured it. Hausla sent one request a thousand times and got an exact match 91.4 per cent of the time — and that gap is where a reproducibility claim in an audit collapses.

The distribution over inputs matters more than the distribution over samples

Teams fixate on re-running one prompt and watching answers wobble; that variance is usually small. Real quality is set by variance across traffic — the tail of unusual inputs where the model behaves differently. The tell-tale sign is an eval set built from prompts the team wrote rather than sampled from logs. "Reduce variability" is the wrong reading: this is a sampling problem, not a sampling-parameter one.

Figure 2. Two variances, routinely confused. Re-running one prompt produces a narrow band and reassures everyone; sampling real traffic reveals a left tail that re-running the happy path never surfaces.

Latency budgets belong to workflows, not calls

Per-call objectives certify workflows users experience as slow, because percentiles do not add and sequential calls compound tail risk. The tell-tale sign is three green latency tiles beside a rising abandonment rate. The expert instruments the end-to-end distribution, watches p99 where that is thousands of real people, and separates time-to-first-token from time-to-completion.

Detection capacity is a number, and most teams have never computed theirs

If the true error rate is e and you review n outputs, the chance of catching at least one is 1 − (1−e)^n. Hausla estimated a 1.7 per cent numeric-error rate and reviewed twenty-five memos a week — a 34.8 per cent chance of seeing one error, while shipping about 680 flawed memos a month. The tell-tale sign is "we spot-check a few." The expert states the smallest error rate their review programme can detect and treats it as a design parameter.

Figure 3. Steep, then flat. Going from twenty-five reviews a week to fifty buys a great deal; from two hundred to two hundred and fifty, almost nothing.

Uniform random sampling under-detects segment failure

Errors cluster — in unusual borrower profiles, in one language, in one size band. A uniform sample allocates review effort in proportion to volume, exactly backwards when the failure lives in a nine-per-cent segment. The tell-tale sign is a stable aggregate beside an unexplained rise in complaints from one cohort. The expert stratifies and reports per-segment rates, accepting wider intervals on small strata rather than a precise, misleading average.

Guardrails are models too, with their own error rates

A verification model flagging suspect numeric claims has its own recall and false-positive rate, and at a low base rate its precision is poor. Over 10,000 memos at a 1.7 per cent base rate, 92 per cent recall and a 4 per cent false-positive rate, reviewers see 156 true flags and 393 false ones — 28 per cent precision — while fourteen real errors still pass. The tell-tale sign is a guardrail described by its recall alone. It buys reviewer leverage; it is not a fix, and reviewer fatigue becomes a design constraint.

The vendor is inside your change-management process

Endpoints are updated and deprecated on the provider's schedule, so a feature can change behaviour with no deployment of your own. The tell-tale sign is a team that cannot name the production model version. Pinning only defers the problem, since pinned versions are withdrawn; the practice is to treat the regression suite as a supplier-management instrument and budget for a forced migration nobody asked for.

Self-reported confidence is a writing style, not a measurement

A model's stated confidence comes from the same process that generated the answer and carries no guarantee of calibration. The tell-tale sign is a routing threshold set on it. An expert either calibrates against outcomes — bucketing claimed confidence and measuring realised accuracy per bucket — or uses an independent signal such as agreement between two models, or verification against the source document, which is what Hausla built.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

Across consumer, B2B and enterprise the difference is real and mostly about who absorbs the error. Consumer products face cost and tail latency as binding constraints, because volume is enormous and attention short, while individual invisible failures are cheap. Enterprise faces the inverse: inference cost rounds to zero, latency tolerance is generous, and one invisible failure can be a contractual event. Platforms and marketplaces add fairness — non-determinism between comparable participants reads as arbitrariness, and the answer is usually to make outputs sticky rather than the model steadier. Hardware inverts the cost structure and turns version management into logistics.

Two asserted differences are not real. That AI-native firms need less evaluation discipline because the model is their competence is backwards; they need more, having no deterministic fallback. And that consumer products tolerate lower quality confuses severity with frequency: at 4.1 million sessions a one-per-cent failure rate is 41,000 disappointed users, a larger absolute trust loss than Hausla could generate in a decade.

Stage changes the correct answer more than product type does. A seed-stage team should over-pay per call and under-build evaluation, because its binding risk is that nobody wants the feature; fifty eval cases and a weekly review is proportionate. At Series B, volume makes cost-per-accepted-outcome load-bearing and the eval set is what lets a growing team ship without the founder reading outputs. At enterprise scale the constraint shifts to auditability, tenant-level regression and supplier risk. The common error is applying a later stage's discipline too early, which is expensive, or an earlier stage's too late, which is how a Kashida Apparel happens.

8. Three worked examples

Hausla: buying accuracy with a second call

Between January and April, Sondhi's team added a verification pass: a smaller model extracted every numeric claim from the draft and matched it against the source documents, flagging mismatches for the analyst rather than correcting them. Sticker cost rose from ₹2.80 to ₹3.35 a memo, an increase finance never noticed. Acceptance rose from 83 to 89 per cent and numeric errors reaching a signed memo fell from an estimated 1.7 per cent to 0.3. Cost per accepted memo fell to about ₹17.25, because rework dominates. The eval set grew from 200 to 1,400 memos sampled from traffic and stratified by lender, narrowing the interval on the contractual gate from ±5.2 points to ±1.6.

Satpura: when the fleet is the model

Satpura's anomaly model achieved 94 per cent recall on bearing faults in the lab. Across the installed base it was 81 per cent, and the gap was entirely version skew: the eleven per cent on the fourteen-month-old build scored 46. No call, no cost, no latency — and the same invisible failure, missed faults, with a cement plant's unplanned downtime running to ₹40 lakh a day. The fix was organisational: fleet-version distribution as a first-class product metric, any unit more than two versions behind reported to the customer's maintenance head, and an on-device self-test that phones home a confidence distribution when firmware cannot update.

Kashida Apparel: the failure, and the recovery

Kashida, a Surat ethnic-wear label shipping 1.4 million orders a year, replaced a rules-based size recommender with a model in August 2025. The aggregate return rate improved from 24.1 to 22.6 per cent and the project was declared a success. Nobody looked at segments. Returns in the XXL-and-above band, nine per cent of orders, rose from 27 to 41 per cent, because that band was thin in training data and the model regressed its predictions toward the population mean. The aggregate improved anyway, since the other ninety-one per cent got better. A customer-care escalation surfaced it in January 2026, five months late: roughly 18,000 excess returns at ₹430 of reverse logistics each, about ₹77 lakh. Recovery ran to April in three parts — an eval set stratified by body-measurement decile with a per-segment gate; a rules-based floor for any segment with fewer than 2,000 training examples; and six weeks of shadow-mode comparison before each change went live. The lesson was not about models: they had shipped one number where the business had always had segments.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Exhibit 3 — the recurring failures, the first visible symptom, and the cost of late detection
Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Demo-driven launchEvery review uses the same three examples"What is the pass rate on cases sampled from last week's logs?"Rebuild after launch; lost trust
Segment collapse behind a stable averageAggregate flat, one cohort's complaints rising"Show me this split by our five largest segments."Kashida: ₹77 lakh, five months
Detection capacity too lowIncidents found by customers, not review"What is the smallest error rate our sampling can detect?"Silent error accrual

The sixth deserves emphasis because mature companies misreport it most consistently. Hausla's slides said analysts reviewed AutoMemo drafts. The instrumented reality was that median review time had fallen from four minutes twenty seconds in October to one minute fifty in January, and the edit rate from 31 per cent to 12, while nothing about the memos improved. A human in the loop is a control only while the human is still looking.

10. Where competent experts genuinely disagree

Whether evaluation infrastructure compounds or depreciates. The evaluation-first position holds that a stratified, log-sampled eval set is the most durable asset such a team builds: it outlives prompts, models and vendors, and is the only thing that lets you accept an upgrade with confidence. The scaling position notes that inference prices have fallen roughly an order of magnitude a year and that whole categories of scaffolding — retrieval hacks, chunking heuristics, repair loops — were obsolete within eighteen months. The first rests on incident post-mortems, the second on price curves. Scaling is wrong if tail error rates prove stubborn as average capability rises, which regulated deployments keep observing; evaluation-first is wrong if eval sets rot faster than models improve, which happens whenever traffic shifts.

Whether a model can legitimately grade another model. LLM-as-judge makes large-scale evaluation affordable and, on well-specified rubrics, correlates well with human labels. Critics argue the correlation is measured on the easy middle of the distribution, that judges inherit the generator's blind spots when both come from one family, and that a judge drifts under vendor updates, making the metric a moving ruler. The steelman is pragmatic: a noisy metric on 5,000 cases weekly beats a clean one on 80 quarterly. It is wrong if judge-human agreement collapses on exactly the cases that matter, which audits of numeric verification have found.

Whether to abstract the model or commit to it. One camp builds a routing layer so any model can be swapped in, arguing that vendor risk makes portability essential. The other argues that quality comes from exploiting one model's particular strengths, and that abstraction forces you to the intersection of capabilities — the worst model you could have built. The first is wrong if switching costs prove low anyway; the second the first time a vendor deprecates an endpoint mid-contract.

Whether human review is a control or a comfort. Regulated industries treat sign-off as what makes deployment defensible. A counter-position, grounded in decades of human-factors research — Lisanne Bainbridge's 1983 "Ironies of Automation" and the automation-bias literature after it — holds that review of high-quality automated output degrades predictably into rubber-stamping, that the control is illusory precisely when the model is good, and that full automation with hard verification is safer than an attention process known to decay. Both sides have evidence, and what each concedes is narrower than the public positions suggest: instrumented review is a different thing from review.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this topic can recite the four properties; someone who has internalised them behaves differently in four observable ways. They ask for denominators before numbers: on hearing "the model is 83 per cent accurate," their first question is what n, sampled how, judged by whom. They convert quality arguments into decision thresholds before the meeting, so "good enough" is a written number with an interval. They reason about cost in accepted outcomes and latency in workflows, which routinely reverses the model choice their team arrived with. And they treat detection as an engineered capability with a budget. The subtler mark is temperamental: they are comfortable shipping something they know will be wrong some fraction of the time, because they have quantified the fraction, bounded the consequence and built a route by which the organisation will hear about it. The one who has only studied it oscillates between over-confidence in a demo and paralysis about hallucination, because neither state requires a number.

12. What each of them decided

Sondhi recommended expansion, but not of the feature as built. AutoMemo went to all twenty-three lenders with the numeric verification pass mandatory, per-lender eval suites of at least 400 sampled memos, a contractual gate expressed as a lower confidence bound rather than a point estimate, and — the change her risk counterpart cared about most — instrumented review, with per-analyst edit rates reported monthly to each lender's credit head. Her reasoning: the regulatory exposure lived in the invisible-failure property, cost was immaterial at Hausla's volumes, and the human control had been decaying unnoticed for three months.

Puri decided not to make Trip Weaver the default. His reasoning inverted hers: at 4.1 million sessions cost was binding and would worsen, since defaulting would push volume toward nineteen million sessions and roughly ₹2 crore a month while extending the feature to users with no planning intent, for whom the measured lift — already decaying from 0.62 points in week one to 0.31 by week three — had never been tested. He kept Trip Weaver opt-in, moved itinerary writing to a smaller model with a p95 under three seconds, and made verification against a property's own amenity record a hard gate. He would revisit when price per call halved or the lift held for eight weeks.

Discussion questions

1. Sondhi treated inference cost as immaterial and Puri treated it as decisive, and both were right. What quantity would you compute to decide which case a new feature falls into, before building it?

2. Hausla's human control was degrading measurably while being reported as effective. If instrumented review is the answer, what should trigger an intervention — and what would you do if the intervention is "make the drafts worse"?

3. Kashida's aggregate improved while a segment collapsed. Which metric your own team reports weekly could hide a similar failure, and what would it cost to find out?

13. Going deeper

  1. Adding an LLM feature — the build sequence these four properties constrain.
  2. Quality as a distribution — the sequel: how to sample and report quality so "83 per cent" means something.
  3. Cost, latency and model selection — Section 3's arithmetic as a repeatable method, with routing and cascades.
  4. What a large language model actually is — the mechanism behind non-determinism, and why temperature zero is greedy rather than reproducible.
  5. RLHF and alignment — why models are fluent, agreeable and confidently wrong: the root of invisible failure.
  6. Problem–model fit — whether a model should do this at all, or rules that fail loudly.
  7. The ML lifecycle — the cadence that makes recurring evaluation routine rather than heroic.
  8. Data strategy and data acquisition — Kashida's thin XXL segment was a data problem first.
  9. Labelling and annotation — the cost and reliability of the judgements every eval set rests on.
  10. Model metrics: precision, recall, AUC — needed to reason about guardrails, which are classifiers at low base rates.
  11. What evals are and why PMs own them — where accountability for all of this lands, and why on product.

AI & Data Products — AI & ML Product Management

What's Different When the Feature Is a Model

A reading on non-deterministic output, cost per use, latency, and invisible failure modes.

1. A draft reply, waiting to be sent

On the morning of 3 March 2026, Ananya Rao, VP of Product at Nishaan Support Cloud, a Bengaluru-based platform that runs the customer-support desks of forty direct-to-consumer brands, opened a spreadsheet she had been avoiding for a week. Nishaan's support agents — 620 of them, employed by the brands themselves but working inside Nishaan's software — handled roughly 380,000 tickets a month: refund requests, delivery complaints, sizing questions. For three years, a third of those tickets had been resolved by a rules engine: if the ticket contained the words "where is my order" and the shipment tracking showed "in transit," the system inserted a fixed, pre-approved reply. Same input, same words, every single time.

Ananya's team had spent the past six weeks building something different: Compose, a feature that used a language model to draft a personalised reply for every ticket, which a human agent could edit and send. In the pilot, agents loved it — average handle time fell. But on 27 February, an agent at one of the three pilot brands, a skincare label, sent a Compose-drafted reply promising a refund policy the company didn't offer. Nothing broke. No error appeared in any log. A customer simply received a wrong answer, fluently written, and the company was now honouring a refund it hadn't intended to grant. Ananya had to decide, before an April board review, whether Compose was ready for all forty brands — and the decision turned on a question she hadn't fully answered for herself: what, precisely, is different about a feature whose behaviour comes from a model instead of code she and her engineers wrote line by line?

Exhibit 1 — the two systems Ananya was choosing between
Rules engine (today)Compose draft (proposed)
Same ticket, asked twiceIdentical reply, alwaysSimilar but not identical replies
Cost per ticket handled~₹0 marginal cost₹0.60–₹6 depending on model
Typical response timeunder 50 milliseconds0.9–3.2 seconds
When it's wrongWrong for every matching ticket, loudly, until someone edits the ruleWrong for some tickets, quietly, unless someone checks

2. The idea: a feature that behaves like a distribution, not a function

Traditional software is a deterministic function: given the same input and the same code, it produces the same output, every time, and it fails in ways that are visible — a crash, an exception, a red line in a log. A model-based feature replaces that function with a statistical model: a system trained on data to estimate, for any given input, a distribution over plausible outputs, and to sample from that distribution rather than look an answer up. "What's different when the feature is a model" is the discipline of naming, and designing for, the four properties that follow directly from that shift: the output is non-deterministic (the same input can yield different valid outputs); each output has a real, per-call cost, because inference consumes computation that the provider bills for; each output takes measurable, often variable latency to produce; and the system can be wrong without failing — it returns a confident, fluent, plausible-sounding answer that is simply incorrect, with no error to catch it.

This is not a new observation invented for large language models. Software engineers at Google articulated the underlying problem in a widely cited 2015 paper, "Machine Learning: The High-Interest Credit Card of Technical Debt" (D. Sculley et al.), arguing that machine-learned components violate the abstraction boundaries that let conventional software be tested, versioned, and reasoned about in isolation. What changed between 2020 and 2023 — from OpenAI's GPT-3 research release through the public launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 — is that this property stopped being a concern confined to specialised ML teams and became something any product manager could trigger by calling an API, often without ever training a model themselves. The one sentence Ananya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib: "When the feature is a model, the same input can produce a different output, every output costs us money and time to generate, and the system can fail without ever throwing an error — so I have to design for a range of behaviour, not a single correct answer."

Figure 1. The rules engine maps one ticket to one reply, always. The model samples from a range of plausible replies — usually close together in meaning, occasionally including one, like Reply D, that is fluent and confidently wrong.

3. How it actually works: from ticket to draft

Walking the running example line by line makes the mechanics concrete. First, Nishaan's system assembles a prompt: a fixed system instruction ("you are a support agent for a skincare brand, follow the refund policy below"), the brand's actual refund policy retrieved from a knowledge base, and the customer's message history. Second, that text is broken into tokens — sub-word units, roughly three-quarters of a word each in English — because the model was trained to operate on tokens, not raw characters, and every provider bills and rate-limits by token count. Third comes inference: the model performs a forward pass and, for each token it generates, computes a probability distribution over what could come next and samples from it, a step controlled by a parameter called temperature. At temperature zero the model almost always samples the single highest-probability token, which is why practitioners sometimes call that setting "deterministic" — but it is not perfectly so, because floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware is not strictly associative and providers batch requests together in ways that can shift results by a token here and there.

Fourth, the draft passes a guardrail layer — a moderation filter, a schema check, sometimes a second, smaller model asked to flag policy violations — before reaching the agent's screen. Fifth, the agent reads it, edits or accepts it, and sends it. The step practitioners most often leave implicit is the sixth: logging that exchange, and whether and how much the agent edited it, into a dataset that becomes the only way anyone learns, weeks later, how the feature performs across thousands of tickets rather than the handful anyone happened to glance at.

Figure 2. Six steps, most of them invisible to the agent, each adding tokens, seconds, or risk. The step teams most often skip — logging for evaluation — is the only one that lets anyone find problems after launch.

4. The arithmetic Ananya actually ran

Ananya asked her lead engineer to price two options against the pilot's real ticket data: a frontier-tier model and a smaller, distilled model roughly a fifth the size. Both were fed the same prompt: about 900 input tokens (system instruction, retrieved policy, ticket history) and produced about 180 output tokens per draft.

Exhibit 2 — monthly cost and quality, two model choices, at pilot and full-rollout volume
Model tierPrice per ticketMonthly cost, pilot (52,000 tickets)Monthly cost, all 40 brands (380,000 tickets)p95 latencyAccepted with no edit
Frontier model$0.0072 (~₹0.61)$374 (~₹31,500)$2,736 (~₹2.30 lakh)3.1 s78%
Distilled model$0.0018 (~₹0.15)$94 (~₹7,900)$684 (~₹57,500)1.0 s61%

Input cost was $0.005 per 1,000 tokens and output $0.015 per 1,000 for the frontier model (0.9 × 0.005 + 0.18 × 0.015 = $0.0072 per ticket); the distilled model, at $0.0015 and $0.002 per 1,000, gave $0.0018 per ticket. At full rollout the frontier model cost roughly four times as much — about ₹1.73 lakh a month more — for an acceptance rate seventeen points higher and a latency nearly three seconds slower, multiplied across 620 agents. Neither number alone told Ananya what to do: the extra cost was trivial against Nishaan's revenue, but the latency risked the handle-time gains Compose existed to capture, while the distilled model's lower acceptance rate meant two of every five drafts would need rewriting — and the skincare incident had already shown even 78% left a tail of confidently wrong output no amount of speed or savings could excuse.

5. What a learner has to become alert to

Non-determinism is not the same as randomness

A well-tuned model's outputs cluster around plausible answers; it is not rolling dice. The variation matters for open-ended generation like Compose's drafts, far less for a classification call run at temperature zero to route a ticket, where near-identical inputs should and usually do get near-identical labels.

Cost per use breaks a habit software people don't know they have

Conventional software has near-zero marginal cost: once built, serving the millionth user costs almost nothing extra. A model call has a real variable cost on every use, so unit economics that look fine in a five-person pilot can become a line item finance notices at 380,000 tickets a month.

Latency is a product decision, not an infrastructure footnote

A three-second wait is invisible in a demo and very visible to an agent handling ninety tickets a shift; streaming the reply token by token can make the same latency feel acceptable, which is why perceived and measured latency have to be tracked separately.

Invisible failure breaks the hardest existing habit

Traditional bugs are loud: a crash, a stack trace, a ticket about the app not loading. A wrong-but-fluent reply about a refund policy generates none of those signals; it looks exactly like a correct one until someone with the actual policy checks it — which is why the failure surfaced as a customer complaint, not a log alert.

Quality is a distribution, not a demo

One good-looking output tells a reviewer almost nothing about the other 379,999 tickets a month will produce. The only honest measure is to run the feature against a representative, held-out set of real cases and report the proportion meeting a defined bar — the discipline this topic unlocks next.

The model can change under you without any deploy on your side

Vendors periodically update the model behind an API endpoint, so a feature scoring 78% acceptance in February can shift in March with no change to Nishaan's own code — a one-time evaluation is never a substitute for a recurring one.

Fluency is not evidence of correctness

A model's confident tone and polish are properties of language generation, not proof the claim is true or current; a newcomer should ask what independent source, if any, verified the specific fact, because the model's own phrasing will not tell them.

"Model-based feature" does not require a chat window

These properties apply equally to a model quietly classifying tickets, ranking listings, or scoring fraud risk with no conversational surface at all — non-determinism, per-call cost, latency, and invisible failure are properties of the model doing the work, not of the interface on top of it.

6. Where this looks different by product type and by company size

In a consumer product, users expect sub-second responses and abandon anything slower, so teams lean on smaller models, caching, and pre-computed answers to control both latency and the cost of serving millions of calls; an invisible failure there is usually recoverable — an awkward suggestion, a mildly wrong answer — and shows up as churn rather than liability. In a B2B operations tool like Nishaan, users tolerate a few seconds if the output is useful, so the model can be larger and slower, but an invisible failure inherits the weight of whatever business process it feeds: a wrong refund promise is a contractual event, not just a bad experience. In a marketplace, a feature such as search ranking or listing-quality scoring sits between two sides at once, so cost multiplies by both buyer and seller volume, and an invisible failure erodes trust on both sides simultaneously, while non-determinism raises a fairness question — two similar sellers ranked differently on different days for no visible reason.

Exhibit 3 — the same four properties, different stakes
Latency toleranceDominant cost leverNature of the invisible-failure risk
Consumersub-secondvolume × per-call pricechurn, low severity per incident
B2B operations (Nishaan)a few secondsquality vs. speed trade-offcontractual, brand, compliance
Marketplacevaries by sidevolume on both sidestrust and perceived fairness

Stage matters as much as product type. An early-stage company usually absorbs a high cost per use as the price of proving the feature works at all, and has neither the ticket volume nor the headcount to justify a dedicated evaluation team — it pays for that later, at scale, when the same shortcuts become expensive. A large company has volume that turns even a fraction-of-a-cent difference per call into a meaningful annual number, and has regulatory and brand exposure that turns an invisible failure from a nuisance into something closer to existential, which is why the same underlying properties call for real evaluation infrastructure, model routing, and legal review as a company grows, even though the technology itself hasn't changed.

7. Where teams go wrong

Exhibit 4 — common mistakes, what gives them away, and the cheap test that catches each one
MistakeSymptom from the outsideUnderlying misunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Shipping from one great demoWorks in the review, breaks on real traffic within weeksTreating a single successful run as proof, not a sample from a distributionRun the same twenty prompts five times each; count the distinct outputs
Pricing the feature like softwareFinance flags a surprise bill once volume scalesAssuming near-zero marginal cost still appliesMultiply tokens per call × price × projected monthly volume before greenlighting
No fallback for a slow or failed callThe whole workflow hangs waiting on one responseTreating a model call like a fast local function, not a network-dependent serviceCheck p95/p99 latency, not the average, and design a timeout path
No routine sampling of live outputA customer complaint is the first sign anything was wrongAssuming quiet logs mean the feature is workingManually review a random slice of live outputs weekly, against a written rubric

8. What good looks like

Teams that handle this well treat the launch decision itself as an evaluation problem, not a build problem. Before a feature reaches more than a pilot's worth of users, they assemble a golden set — a few hundred real, representative cases, including the ugly ones — and define, in writing, what "good enough" means: an acceptance rate, a latency ceiling, a small number of hard fails a reviewer would flag by hand. They pick a model tier deliberately against that bar rather than defaulting to the newest or cheapest option, keep a human in the loop wherever output feeds a real customer commitment, and schedule a recurring, not one-time, sample of live output for review, because they have accepted the model can shift under them without a line of their own code changing. None of this eliminates the four properties; it makes each one visible enough to manage on purpose instead of discovering by incident.

9. What Ananya decided

Ananya recommended, and the board approved, a staged path rather than an immediate full rollout. Compose would launch in draft-only mode — never auto-sent — using the distilled model to hold cost down while her team built a golden set of 400 real tickets, including near-copies of the skincare incident, to measure acceptance rate on purpose rather than by anecdote. Full rollout to all forty brands was gated on two written thresholds: acceptance-without-edit at or above 70%, and p95 latency under 2.5 seconds; a compliance reviewer would also manually check a random 1% sample of live drafts every week, specifically for policy accuracy, for as long as Compose ran. What she decided to learn next followed directly from the gate she had just written: how to build an evaluation set that actually represents real traffic — the "quality as a distribution" problem this topic unlocks — and how cost, latency, and model choice trade off once volume, not a demo, is the real test.

Two questions worth sitting with:

If your team cannot state the acceptance rate of a model-based feature on a held-out set of real cases, do you actually know whether it works — or only that it hasn't visibly failed yet?

Which of the "bugs" your team currently tracks are really invisible failures that nobody has yet built a way to see?
case40v1-aipm.what.different:
Darpan Grid Works: Reading the Meter

An ambiguous case on what changes when the feature is a model rather than code

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Thursday, 8 October 2026, Charulata Ambekar was still at her desk in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, with three documents open and no way to reconcile them: a field-audit report from Manila, the February business case her team had written and the board approved, and a draft slide for Monday's board sub-committee on 12 October asking the directors to approve the next phase of Ankan, the computer-vision feature that reads the kWh digits off a photograph of an electricity meter.

Ankan had been live a little over six months. It had cut keying time on a beat by roughly a third and won Darpan two new utilities. It had also, in September alone, produced more than one and a half lakh readings that were silently wrong, cost 1.76 times what February projected, and left the company's oldest contract exposed to an accuracy service level written in 2021 for a process that no longer existed. None of it showed up on a dashboard, because none of it was an error. The system returned a number every time it was asked.

Girish Kaulgi, the chief executive, had sent one line at nine that evening: Board wants a number for the Vaigai migration and a straight answer on Nalanda. Don't give them a distribution. Ambekar replied that a distribution was all she had.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2021

Darpan Grid Works was founded in Hyderabad in 2012 by Kaulgi and a colleague from a metering hardware firm in Jaipur. Its first product was a ruggedised handheld application for meter readers: a beat list, a photograph, a keyed reading, a printed spot bill. By 2026 it had annual recurring revenue of ₹164 crore, some 640 employees and contracts with eleven utilities across nine states. It ran on Android phones costing ₹6,500, in villages where the network dropped out for an hour, operated by readers usually employed by a contract agency paid per beat.

The decision that shapes everything here was taken in March 2021. To win Nalanda Vidyut Vitaran Nigam, then the country's largest manual-reading contract at 38 lakh meters, Darpan accepted three terms its competitors would not: a price of ₹0.90 per contracted meter per month fixed for seven years to 31 March 2028, with no pass-through for infrastructure cost; a reading-accuracy service level of 99.5 per cent, measured by the utility's own quarterly audit, with a penalty of ₹2 lakh for every 0.1 percentage point of quarterly shortfall, capped at ten per cent of that quarter's fees; and deployment inside Nalanda's data centre in Patna, every software change passing a forty-five-day change-advisory process.

In 2021 all three terms were cheap. The pipeline was deterministic: a human read the dial, a human keyed it, a second pass flagged implausible jumps, and the audit returned 99.7 per cent quarter after quarter. Fixed pricing was fine because the thousandth reading cost what the first did, which was nothing. On-premise deployment was fine because the software changed four times a year. All three assumptions have since broken on the same fact: the reading is now produced by a model.

3. The industry

India's distribution utilities are the weakest link in its power sector, and the Ministry of Power's Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme has pushed them hard towards smart prepaid meters. Genus Power Infrastructures, HPL Electric & Power and Secure Meters supply the hardware; Adani Energy Solutions, Tata Power and Larsen & Toubro bid as metering service providers. Every smart meter installed is a meter nobody has to photograph. On a long enough view, Darpan's market is scheduled for demolition.

On a shorter view it is not. Most of the country's service connections were still read by hand in 2026, and in Darpan's states the smart-meter rollout had slipped by eighteen months to four years. Under the Electricity Act, 2003 a consumer can take a disputed bill to a Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum and then to an Electricity Ombudsman, and a utility issuing wrong bills at scale attracts its state regulatory commission long before it attracts a lawsuit. The meter photograph is itself personal data under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; Nalanda's legal cell has raised Darpan's retention policy and its use of those images to retrain Ankan, and neither is settled.

The exposure is not only Indian. Caleb Ondrak, hired in Austin in 2025, had built a Latin American pipeline, and a three-year opportunity with a Mexico City distribution group worth about ₹44 crore was at proposal stage. Ankan had never been evaluated on a Mexican meter face.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The Ankan business case was signed off on 11 February 2026. It projected that by September 52 lakh meters would be read through the model, at one call per reading, at ₹0.26 per call. All three numbers were wrong, and not in the same direction. Exhibit 4 sets the forecast against the telemetry.

Ankan went live at Nalanda on 1 April 2026 across 6.2 lakh meters; Chambal Power Distribution Company began migrating in June, Dakshin Saurashtra Urja Nigam in August. On 1 July the cloud vendor hosting the model gave thirty-one days' notice of a revision effective 1 August: the per-call charge moved from ₹0.26 to ₹0.41, which Darpan could not pass on to Nalanda under the 2021 contract and chose not to pass on to the others.

On Monday, 17 August 2026, Prasanna Udupi's team in Dublin lowered the confidence threshold at which Ankan declines to answer, from 0.82 to 0.74. The reasoning was documented and uncontested: readers were keying manually on about one beat in ten, the field's largest complaint, and a tighter threshold was buying caution they did not want. Readings held for manual keying then fell from 9.4 per cent to 6.2 per cent. Readings that were wrong and confident rose from 2.3 per cent to 3.8 per cent. Nobody saw the second number for thirty-eight days, because a wrong-but-confident reading produces no log line, no retry and no alert. It produces a bill.

On 12 September the Chambal forum admitted forty-one consumer cases alleging inflated bills in two urban divisions. On 24 September, fourteen days before Ambekar's slide was due, Marivic Lacson's team in Manila completed the second field audit wave, the September column of Exhibit 3. On 29 September sales signed Vaigai Power Distribution for 12.5 lakh meters, migrating from January 2027 — celebrated in Austin and Hyderabad on the same day the Manila audit went to eleven people, not including Ondrak. Nalanda's first quarterly accuracy audit of the Ankan period falls on Monday, 16 November 2026.

5. The people

Charulata Ambekar, chief product officer, Hyderabad, owns Ankan's profit and loss and the board slide, and argues the feature should expand only where Darpan can measure it. Her long-term grant vests against recurring revenue, not margin. She is not saying that she approved the 17 August threshold change herself, in two lines on a Sunday evening, without asking what it would do to silent errors.

Girish Kaulgi, co-founder and chief executive, Hyderabad, wants a clean story for a Tokyo strategic investor whose term sheet assumes Ankan on 96 lakh meters by March 2027. Smart meters will eat the category in five years, he argues, so Darpan must grow now. He is not saying that the investor's diligence team has asked for the field-audit reports and he has not sent them.

Sabiha Mankad, vice-president of engineering, Pune, owns the Patna on-premise deployment and is measured on uptime, which the model has never threatened. Any change there takes forty-five days through change advisory, so a fix decided tonight reaches Patna after the audit. She is not saying that her team runs two model versions, one in Patna and one in the cloud for the other two utilities, and that the audit numbers mix them.

Prasanna Udupi, head of applied machine learning, Dublin, four and a half hours behind Hyderabad, built both Exhibit 2's benchmark and the threshold logic, and is measured on an accuracy number his own team controls. He insists the field gap is a data-collection problem. He is not saying that the benchmark was labelled by the same three contractors who assembled the training set, so a meter face labelled wrongly in training is labelled wrongly in the test.

Marivic Lacson, audit and customer-success lead, Manila, two and a half hours ahead of Hyderabad, runs the human re-read and sees failures first. She wants the sample raised tenfold and published to the utilities; a larger audit is also a larger team. She is not saying that her auditors disagreed on 4.1 per cent of sampled photographs, and that the published figure takes the senior auditor's call as truth.

Agnieszka Dudek, design lead, Warsaw, designed the reader's screen and has proposed a redesign for a year. The threshold, she argues, is a design question disguised as a model question: the reader is shown a number in a box and never told the machine is unsure. She is not saying that her usability study covered forty readers, all departmental staff in Lucknow, none from the contract agencies that run most beats.

Caleb Ondrak, senior vice-president of sales, Austin, has Vaigai signed and Mexico City in proposal, wants Ankan as the differentiator in both, and is paid on signature. He is not saying that the Mexico City proposal quotes Exhibit 2's accuracy figure without its footnote.

Bhairavi Kanse, head of regulatory affairs and contracts, Hyderabad, once a deputy general manager at a state utility, reads the 2021 agreement as the binding constraint and wants Ankan's output excluded from the service level by amendment before 16 November. She is not saying that raising it will itself tell Ratnesh Diwakar, Nalanda's chief general manager for information technology, that something is wrong.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Field conditions, September 2026

Exhibit 2. Benchmark accuracy, held-out set

Exhibit 3. Field audit, two waves

Exhibit 4. February forecast against September telemetry

Exhibit 5. Contracted meters against meters actually read, September 2026

Exhibit 6. Two complaint signals, Nalanda and Chambal only

Read together, the exhibits settle nothing. Exhibit 2 says the model is right 93.70 per cent of the time and dangerously wrong 2.05 per cent; Exhibit 3's September wave says 88.60 per cent and 3.80 per cent. The 5.10-point gap is an error in neither. It is the difference between a curated set from two districts, labelled by the people who built the training data, and a random sample of live readings from eleven. Udupi's number is right for judging whether a model change helped; Lacson's, for judging what a utility will experience.

Applied to September's 42.40 lakh readings, Exhibit 3's silent-error rate of 3.80 per cent implies 1,61,120 wrong readings sent to billing in one month; at the full book of 96 lakh meters, 3,64,800. Exhibit 6 then offers two unflattering accounts. The in-app dispute rate falls from 45.0 to 35.0 per lakh readings, which Ondrak has quoted to Vaigai as evidence of improvement. The utilities' own extracts rise from 350.0 to 380.0 per lakh and then appear to collapse to 150.0, almost certainly the two-cycle lag rather than good news. Even at 350 per lakh, column B accounts for 9.2 per cent of the silent errors Exhibit 3 implies, and column A for 1.2 per cent. The rest are invisible to everyone, consumers included: a meter read low gives nobody a reason to complain until it is finally read correctly and a year's arrears arrive at once.

Exhibit 4's columns are not comparable either, and the gap cuts both ways: February over-estimated how fast meters would migrate and under-estimated what each reading would cost. Fewer readings at more than double the modelled unit cost still produced a bill 1.76 times forecast. Against September's billed revenue of ₹75.15 lakh, a serving cost of ₹23.82 lakh leaves ₹51.33 lakh, a margin of 68.3 per cent before audit, support or engineering cost. At the full 96 lakh meters on the same 1.37 calls per reading and ₹0.41 per call, revenue of ₹86.40 lakh a month meets a serving cost of ₹53.92 lakh and the margin falls to ₹32.48 lakh, or 37.6 per cent. Growth in this feature consumes its own margin — a property Darpan's first fourteen years of software never had.

The audit that produces the only trustworthy number is itself a cost. Wave 2 re-read 12,000 of 42.40 lakh readings, 0.28 per cent, at about ₹6.80 each: ₹0.82 lakh. Lacson's one per cent means 42,400 re-reads and ₹2.88 lakh a month now, and 96,000 re-reads and ₹6.53 lakh at the full book — a line no customer is paying for.

7. Voices

"The model has not regressed. Benchmark accuracy went from 93.1 to 93.7 after the threshold change. If the field numbers disagree with the benchmark, the field sampling is wrong, not the model."Prasanna Udupi, Dublin, in the weekly model review, 28 September
"Pras, we re-read the photograph that was actually sent to billing. There is no sampling frame more real than that. You are measuring the exam you set."Marivic Lacson, Manila, same thread, 29 September
"Nobody has told me a single reading is wrong. In six months I have had two P1 incidents and both were network. You are asking my team to rebuild a pipeline that is not broken, forty-five days before an audit we have never failed."Sabiha Mankad, Pune, 2 October
"The screen shows the reader a number in a box. It does not show that the machine is 0.75 confident rather than 0.95. We took the judgement away from the only human in the loop and then measured whether the human was happy."Agnieszka Dudek, Warsaw, design review, 5 October
"Clause 11.4 does not care which of your numbers is correct. It says 99.5 per cent, measured by them, and the audit is on the sixteenth of November. Ten point nine points of shortfall is ₹218 lakh of penalty before the cap and ₹10.26 lakh after it. The cap is not the risk. Clause 19.2 is the risk."Bhairavi Kanse, Hyderabad, note to the executive committee, 6 October
"My readers do not avoid the camera because they distrust it. They avoid it because on a Tier 3 phone in Hardoi it takes twenty-six seconds and they are paid by the beat. Then they key last month's number from memory. You pay for a call and get a guess."Yogesh Fatnani, field operations, Lucknow, 7 October

8. The options as Ambekar sees them

By Thursday night Ambekar had four options on a sheet of paper, in the order they occurred to her, not the order they deserve.

Restore the threshold to 0.82 everywhere and slow the migration. This pushes the silent-error rate back towards the July wave's 2.30 per cent and manual keying towards 9.4 per cent, which Fatnani says the agencies will route around. At Nalanda it cannot happen before late November, after the audit. It also means telling Vaigai migration slips and the Tokyo investor that 96 lakh moves.

Keep the threshold, raise the audit tenfold, publish the results. This costs ₹2.88 lakh a month now and ₹6.53 lakh at full book, and converts an invisible failure into a visible one — exactly what Kanse cannot afford five weeks before an audit against a 99.5 per cent service level.

Negotiate the contract rather than the model. Amend the Nalanda agreement to measure accuracy on readings delivered to billing after human review, under a jointly agreed sampling protocol, and to allow a serving-cost pass-through. This treats the problem as commercial. It also reopens a fixed-price contract Darpan has been glad to keep shut, and signals to Diwakar that something has changed.

Confine Ankan to where it is reliably good. Run the model only on Tier 1 and Tier 2 beats and on the meter faces it reads best, leaving the rest to human keying. Ambekar finds this the most attractive and least defensible option, because nobody can say which faces those are: Exhibit 2's set is not stratified by meter type, and Exhibit 3 is too small to cut by district and face at once.

Writing them down, she saw that all four took the feature as given and argued about its settings. None asked whether a company whose market is scheduled for replacement by smart meters should spend its scarcest engineering capacity reading the meters that remain, nor whether the unit of sale should be a meter rather than a verified reading. Kaulgi's framing — grow now, the category has five years — makes the first three tactics. Mankad's — nothing is broken — makes all four unnecessary. Dudek's makes it a question about a box on a screen.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board sub-committee meets on Monday, 12 October 2026, four days later, and wants a migration number for Vaigai and a position on Nalanda. Nalanda's accuracy audit falls on 16 November, thirty-five days after that meeting. The Nalanda price of ₹0.90 per contracted meter per month is fixed to 31 March 2028 with no infrastructure pass-through, and the 99.5 per cent service level, the ₹2 lakh per 0.1 point penalty, the ten per cent quarterly cap and the persistent-breach termination clause all sit in the same unamended agreement. Any change at Patna takes forty-five days through change advisory. Udupi has four engineers and a hiring freeze; Mankad's team is committed until December to a billing release for Dakshin Saurashtra. The Tokyo term sheet assumes 96 lakh meters on Ankan by 31 March 2027. The Mexico City proposal is due in early November and quotes Exhibit 2. Meter photographs are personal data under the DPDP Act, and Nalanda's legal cell has not agreed they may be used for retraining. Diwali falls on 8 November, emptying the field offices in Bihar for the fortnight before the audit.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibits 2 and 3 report different accuracies for the same model. From the footnotes alone, reconstruct why, and say which decisions each number is fit to support.
  2. The 17 August change improved every metric the team was watching and worsened the one it was not. What property of a model feature, as against conventional code, made that possible, and what instrumentation would have caught it within a week?
  3. Using Exhibits 4, 5 and 6, explain how Darpan's finance view and its product view of Ankan can both be accurate and still support opposite recommendations.
  4. Exhibit 6 shows one complaint signal falling and another rising. If you could commission one additional piece of evidence before Monday, what would it be, and what would each possible result let you conclude?
  5. Ambekar's four options all concern the model's settings. Argue that the binding problem is instead the 2021 contract, the reader's screen, or the unit of pricing — and show what each reframing would cost Darpan.
  6. What should Ambekar do on Monday morning, and what exactly should she tell the board about the accuracy of a feature whose accuracy she cannot state as one number? What would saying it commit the company to?

11. Thursday night

At half past midnight Ambekar opened the February case again. The line she kept returning to was not a number but a sentence in the risk section, written by her own team eight months earlier: Model accuracy will be monitored continuously through the Pratyaksh console and the dispute flag. Both had worked exactly as designed. The dispute flag had fallen every month since July; the console was green. More than one and a half lakh wrong bills had gone out in September, and the only reason anybody at Darpan Grid Works knew it was that fourteen people in Manila had been paid ₹6.80 a time to look at photographs of meters with their own eyes.

She had until Monday. Kaulgi wanted a number, Kanse an amendment, Ondrak a footnote, Lacson a bigger team, Mankad to be left alone until December, Udupi the benchmark believed, Dudek the screen rebuilt, Fatnani phones that worked in Hardoi. Outside, the last of the Gachibowli traffic thinned out. Ambekar wrote one line under the four options, and crossed it out.
case20v1-aipm.what.different:
Ekagra Helpdesk Exchange: The Draft-Reply Decision

A decision case on what changes when a feature is a model rather than code

1. Opening

On the morning of Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Sulochana Pande sat in a glass meeting room on the fourth floor of Ekagra Helpdesk Exchange's Indiranagar office in Bengaluru, with a one-page summary of a four-week pilot and a deadline that would not move. The chief executive, Jaswant Bakshi, had asked her to decide by Friday, 9 October how the company's first AI feature, a tool that drafts replies to customer-support tickets, would go to market. Customers were pressing for it before the mid-October festive sales.

The feature had worked in the demonstration. In the pilot, however, it behaved unlike anything Ekagra had shipped in twelve years: the same ticket could produce different replies on different days, every reply cost real money, some arrived too slowly, and a small share were confidently wrong in ways nobody noticed until a reviewer read them.

2. Company background

Ekagra Helpdesk Exchange was founded in 2014 in Bengaluru by two former call-centre managers. It sells ticketing and live-chat software to Indian consumer brands, chiefly direct-to-consumer companies in beauty, electronics and home goods, whose support queues swell during Diwali, Big Billion Days-style sale events and wedding-season promotions. Its annual recurring revenue stands at ₹86 crore across 410 customers. Product sits in Bengaluru, engineering in Pune, a data scientist in Amsterdam and a customer-success lead in Nairobi.

The competition is crowded. Freshworks and Zoho Desk are the incumbents that most Indian buyers already know, and both have announced AI assistants. Ekagra's edge has been depth in Hindi, Hinglish and regional-language tickets, and in cash-on-delivery and return workflows that global products handle awkwardly. Customers also operate under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and ask where messages go when an AI feature reads them.

Thirty-eight customers have asked for AI drafting. Together they hold about 6,000 agent seats. Ekagra's board plans to price the feature as an add-on at ₹900 per agent seat per month, and the sales plan assumes that half of those seats will take it, which is 3,000 seats. Until now every Ekagra feature cost almost nothing to run: the thousandth use cost no more than the first.

3. The situation

The pilot ran from 1 September through 28 September with 12 customers. For each ticket, a large hosted language model read the customer message, the order history and the customer's policy documents, then proposed a reply for the agent to send, edit or discard. At the end, a panel of three senior support reviewers scored a random sample of 1,000 tickets against each customer's written policy. Exhibit 1 sets out what they found.

Most of the news was good: more than three-quarters of drafts were correct. The troubling row was the last. On 22 of the 1,000 tickets, a draft promised something the policy did not allow, and the agent sent it without noticing. No alert flagged these; the dashboard showed a healthy acceptance rate while 2.2 per cent of replies were quietly wrong. At the 24 lakh drafts a month of a full rollout (3,000 seats at 800 drafts each), that means 52,800 wrong replies reaching customers every month.

The second discovery was cost. Each draft on the large model cost ₹1.60, because every call carried the message, order history and policy text. Exhibit 2 compares three ways of serving the feature, using replays of the same pilot tickets.

Exhibit 3 turns those unit costs into monthly economics at the planned scale of 24 lakh drafts and 3,000 seats paying ₹900 each.

The most accurate option lost ₹11.40 lakh every month at the proposed price, and the cheapest was less accurate and more often wrong. A conventional feature presents no such trade-off.

Pieter Smit in Amsterdam, three and a half hours behind Bengaluru, noted that the pilot showed a distribution of outcomes, not a pass or fail. Achieng Odhiambo in Nairobi, two and a half hours behind, reported that two pilot customers had complained about wrong refund promises before anyone at Ekagra spotted the pattern.

4. The people

Sulochana Pande, chief product officer in Bengaluru, owns the launch decision and the add-on's profit and loss. She wants to win the festive season without damaging Ekagra's reputation for reliability.

Dattatray Kale, engineering head in Pune, leads the team that built the integration. He wants a design that lets his team swap models later and worries about the freeze date.

Pieter Smit, data scientist in Amsterdam, built the replay harness behind Exhibit 2. He would rather launch late than launch blind.

Achieng Odhiambo, customer-success lead in Nairobi, hears the complaints first. She wants agents able to flag a wrong draft, and customers told plainly what the feature can and cannot do.

5. The timeline

6. The options

Option A: ship the large model to everyone before the freeze. This gives the best measured quality and the strongest story against Freshworks and Zoho Desk. The cost is Exhibit 3's first row: a loss of ₹11.40 lakh a month at the proposed price, a 95th-percentile wait of 7.5 seconds that agents will not tolerate, and 52,800 silently wrong replies a month at scale.

Option B: ship the small model to everyone. This is fast, at 0.9 seconds median, and it earns a 60.0 per cent margin. Its price is quality. Only 69.0 per cent of drafts are usable and correct, and the wrong-policy rate rises to 10.5 per cent, higher than in the pilot. Ekagra would sell a faster feature that is wrong more often.

Option C: a staged hybrid. Route policy-sensitive tickets, such as refunds, cash-on-delivery disputes and warranty claims, to the large model with the policy text attached, and send everything else to the small model. Release it to the 12 pilot customers and a handful of others before the sale season, with a written test set, a one-click wrong-draft flag and weekly review of sampled drafts. Open general availability once the wrong-policy rate is stable. The gains are a 29.3 per cent margin, a 6.8-second 95th-percentile wait confined to the large-model path, and a wrong-policy rate of 7.5 per cent. The cost is a smaller launch, a more complex system for Pune to run, and the risk that rivals announce wider availability first.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, why does a healthy acceptance rate fail to tell Pande how good the feature is, and what would she need to measure instead?

2. Using Exhibits 2 and 3, why can no single row be called best, and what does it mean that cost is incurred on every use?

3. Which of Achieng Odhiambo's and Pieter Smit's concerns is addressed by each option, and which can be deferred until after Diwali?

4. Which option would you choose by Friday, and which single number would tell you, within a month of launch, that you had chosen wrongly?

8. A note for the learner

This case contrasts a model with conventional code on four counts. Output is non-deterministic, so quality is a distribution measured on samples, as Exhibit 1 does, and never a pass or fail. Every use has a cost, so unit economics decide whether a feature is viable at all, as Exhibit 3 shows. Latency is a product constraint, because the agent's three-second patience sets a boundary no engineering heroics can extend. And the failure that matters is invisible: the 2.2 per cent of wrong replies sent to customers produced no error signal.

A defensible path is Option C, with discipline. Its economics are positive, its measured error rate is close to the best available, and a staged release lets Ekagra learn from real tickets while exposure is small. Before launch, Pande should ask Smit to freeze a written test set, set a launch gate on the wrong-policy rate (for example, no worse than the pilot's 7.2 per cent on the sampled review), and require Odhiambo's flag-a-draft control in the agent screen. She should also leave general availability open until January and give Kale a model-swap interface so that cost and quality can be re-measured as vendors change their prices. Choosing Option A would sacrifice margin for quality that the hybrid nearly matches; choosing Option B would accept more wrong promises to save money.
