AI & Data Products · AI & ML Product Management · Near-expert reading

Quality as a Distribution

A model has no specification; it has an output distribution and an operating point chosen on it. Choosing that point is the most consequential decision in AI product management.

1. Two operating points, three weeks apart

On Thursday 5 February 2026, Sharanya Pillai spent the morning in a portable-X-ray van outside a municipal health post in Kalyan, watching a radiographer photograph forty-one people in three hours. Sharanya ran product for Aks Imaging Systems, a Bengaluru company whose software read chest radiographs and flagged patterns consistent with pulmonary tuberculosis. Aks did not diagnose; it triaged. A film it called negative meant the person went home without a molecular confirmatory test; a film it called positive meant a sputum sample and a Truenat or CBNAAT cartridge, at roughly ₹900 of programme money and a return visit. Aks read about 60,000 films a month across 180 vans and screening centres in Maharashtra and Odisha, under a contract tied to the National TB Elimination Programme. Before the state's technical review on 20 February she had to name one number: the score above which a film was called presumptive-positive. Every candidate traded people missed against cartridges burned.

Three weeks later and 1,800 kilometres north, Aditya Barve was reading an escalation he could not dismiss. Khabardaar, the call-screening app he built product for in Gurugram, screened about 220 million calls a month for 41 million users, scoring each for the likelihood of fraud and silently blocking the worst. On 24 February a Bengaluru hospital's outbound line — used to tell patients their reports were ready — had been auto-blocked for nine hours across an estimated 3,400 users. Growth wanted the threshold loosened; trust and safety, facing a quarter of rising reported fraud losses, wanted it tightened. Both cited the same model and the same headline: 94.6% accuracy. Neither number told Aditya anything he could act on, because accuracy is a property of a sample and a threshold is a property of a business.

Sharanya and Aditya were making the same decision in different currencies. Neither had a bug to fix; both had a distribution to cut.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

State it precisely. A trained model maps each input to a score, and over any population those scores form a distribution that overlaps between the cases where the model is right and where it is wrong. Because the overlap is irreducible for a given model and population, there is no single behaviour to specify; there is a family of behaviours, one per cut point, each with its own error rates and coverage. Quality as a distribution treats the choice among that family — the operating point — as the product decision, and expresses quality as conditional rates attached to named populations rather than one scalar attached to the model.

The lineage is older than machine learning. Walter Shewhart's control chart at Bell Labs in 1924, carried into post-war manufacturing by W. Edwards Deming, established that management's job is to bound a process's variation rather than demand identical units. Neyman and Pearson's 1933 paper named the two error types and showed you cannot minimise both at once. Signal detection theory, developed on radar operators and codified by Green and Swets in 1966, contributed the ROC curve and the separation between a detector's discriminability and the observer's criterion: two operators with identical eyesight produce very different hit and false-alarm rates purely by where they set their willingness to say yes. C. K. Chow's 1970 result on the optimal reject option added a third action — decline to decide. Software borrowed all of it late, through Musa's reliability growth models and then site-reliability error budgets; disaggregated evaluation later still, via Buolamwini and Gebru's 2018 subgroup audit of face classifiers, and now sits inside the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act.

Four schools now argue over this inheritance, and a manager refereeing a disagreement should be able to name which one each side speaks from.

The decision-theoretic school, from Neyman–Pearson through Wald, will sign: the acceptable failure rate is whatever the loss function implies, and a team that refuses to price its errors has only delegated the price to whoever last shouted. It will not sign: a failure rate can be unacceptable independent of what the failure costs. The reliability-and-assurance school, from IEC 61508 into medical-device regulation, will sign: certain named hazards get a budget of zero and are engineered out of the causal path, not priced into an expected value. It will not sign: a severe harm can be traded against an operational saving at the margin. The disaggregation school will sign: an aggregate rate is a weighted average over populations whose weights nobody chose on purpose. The recoverability school will sign: what governs perceived quality is the cost of recovering from an error, not its frequency — and will not accept an operating point chosen from the confusion matrix alone.

Aks's regulator speaks the second language; Khabardaar's growth team the first. Both of Aditya's teams quoted 94.6% because neither had been asked which population, which direction of error, and at what cut.

3. Mechanics: what an expert actually computes

The procedure has six steps, of which practitioners routinely perform four and skip the two that matter.

Step one is a stratified audit sample with independent ground truth. Khabardaar's data lead pulled 20,000 calls from the previous quarter and had them adjudicated using call-recording metadata, subscriber complaints and telecom-registry lookups — evidence the model did not see. The sample was stratified by score band: at a fraud prevalence near 1%, a uniform draw of 20,000 would hold perhaps 200 scams and produce useless per-band estimates. Within-band rates are then unbiased, but any production figure must be re-weighted by each band's share of real traffic, which is the step everyone forgets.

Step two is the per-band table, not the aggregate.

Table 1. Khabardaar scam-score bands. Within-band precision from the 20,000-call stratified audit; volumes re-weighted to 220 million calls a month at 1.0% fraud prevalence.

Step three is the marginal rule, the first commonly skipped step. Teams choose a cut by asking whether the average error rate above it looks acceptable. That is the wrong question: blocking is applied band by band, so the question at each band is whether blocking it beats not blocking it. Let p be the band's precision, Cfp the cost of wrongly blocking a legitimate call and Cfn the expected cost of letting a scam through. Block while (1 − p) × Cfp stays below p × Cfn, which rearranges to the formal content of this whole topic: p* = Cfp / (Cfp + Cfn). The optimal cut is the band where local precision crosses the cost ratio. Above a cut at 70, Khabardaar's average precision is 75.4%; the precision of the band that cut newly adds is 41%. The last slice is majority-wrong while the blend looks healthy.

Step four is pricing the two directions honestly. Khabardaar estimated that one scam call in 900 reaching a user ends in a completed fraud averaging ₹38,000 — an expected ₹42 per scam call allowed — and costed a wrong block at ₹18, blending support contacts and a modelled churn hazard. That gives p* = 18 / (18 + 42) = 30%, which says block down to band 70–79 and accept 623,700 wrong blocks a month. Aditya's instinct that this was wrong was correct: ₹18 is a mean over a false-positive population whose tail contains hospital callbacks and a bank's fraud-alert desk. Expected-value logic holds only when loss is linear in count.

Step five is the confidence interval on the error rate itself, which almost nobody computes. Aks's validation set held 500 films in its highest-confidence negative band with two subsequently confirmed TB cases: an observed miss rate of 0.4%, whose Wilson 95% interval runs from about 0.11% to 1.45%. A team that writes 0.4% into a tender has promised a point estimate whose upper bound is three times worse. The companion rule of thumb: zero errors in 300 audited cases puts the 95% upper bound near 1%, not at zero.

Step six separates practitioners who last three years from those who last three quarters: deciding how you will keep observing errors once the threshold hides them. Auto-actioned cases stop generating ground truth. Khabardaar's blocked calls are never answered, so nobody reports that a blocked call was legitimate. The rate above the line becomes structurally unobservable and the dashboard settles into a flat line that measures nothing. The only remedy is to buy labels: a permanent randomised sample of auto-actioned cases routed for human adjudication, funded as a standing cost.

4. When the framing applies, and when it misleads

Five conditions make the distributional framing the right tool, and each fails somewhere for one of our protagonists. Ground truth is obtainable independently of the model. Aks passes cleanly — a Truenat result is an answer the model did not produce; Khabardaar passes only partly, because its adjudicators use complaints, and complaints are shaped by whether the call was blocked. Errors become visible within a horizon short enough to steer by. Aks's misses surface in weeks; Khabardaar's may surface months later or never, since a defrauded user rarely blames a screening app that stayed silent. The population is stable enough that last quarter's curve predicts next quarter's. Aks is reasonably stable; Khabardaar fails hardest, because fraud is adversarial and a published threshold is an invitation to sit just underneath it. Errors are approximately independent. A 1% rate of scattered singletons differs from the same 1% arriving as three bad days on one scanner model. Loss is roughly linear in count. This is where Khabardaar's ₹18 breaks.

Where the framing actively misleads is worth naming. It misleads for one-shot decisions with no repeated play, because a rate describes a long run that will not occur. It misleads where a single instance constitutes a violation regardless of frequency, which is how data-protection and medical-device regimes are written: under the DPDP Act a breach is a breach, not a rate. It misleads for first impressions, where one bad output in a new user's first three interactions destroys a relationship a thousand good ones cannot rebuild. And it misleads for open-ended generative outputs, where the distribution being cut is one of graded quality rather than of right and wrong.

5. Hard edge cases, and what the seams do

The clean version of this decision assumes one model, one surface, one owner; reality supplies none. In multi-product companies a single model serves several surfaces at different operating points, and one incident on the lowest-stakes surface is reported as a fact about the model, tightening every other threshold within a week. In two-sided marketplaces the budget must be allocated between sides and never is: a moderation model tuned to protect buyers spends its false positives on sellers, disproportionately new ones, which the growth team experiences as an unexplained cohort drop. In regulated settings the operating point is an evidenced claim, not a choice — Aks's threshold enters a technical file and moving it triggers revalidation, so Sharanya is choosing the point she can defend for eighteen months. In hardware-plus-software deployments the hidden slice is the device: Aks's error rate differs between two van-mounted detector models, and a fleet-wide figure averages over a composition procurement changes without telling product. In AI-native products the evaluator is itself a model, so a grader with 8% disagreement against human raters cannot certify a 2% product error rate.

At the seam, what mature companies say is that a model risk committee owns the operating point quarterly. What happens is that a data scientist picks the number in a notebook, it is ratified in a slide nobody re-reads, and it moves when a large customer escalates. The mature pattern is identifiable: one named owner, a dated change log, a randomised-audit budget that survives cost-cutting, and a re-baselining schedule that runs whether or not anyone is worried.

6. Eight things experts see that competent practitioners miss

Set the cut on the marginal band, not the average above it. The tell-tale is a review deck quoting one precision figure "above threshold", read as a 75% blend sitting safely above a 30% bar. It is wrong because nobody is choosing to block the whole blend; they are choosing whether to add one more band, and that band's own precision is the only number the choice depends on. Experts ask for the per-band table first and refuse to discuss the aggregate before it.

Calibration and discrimination are different goods, and fixing one is routinely mistaken for improving the other. The tell-tale is a release note claiming a calibration fix improved quality alongside an unchanged ROC curve. Any strictly monotone recalibration — Platt scaling, isotonic regression — relabels scores without changing which cases outrank which, so it moves the threshold number and leaves the achievable frontier where it was. Calibration buys interpretability, not capability; treating it as capability is how a quarter disappears.

Prevalence, not the model, usually decides whether precision is acceptable. The tell-tale is a pilot whose precision does not reproduce in the second city. At Khabardaar's 1% prevalence a detector with 95% sensitivity and 98% specificity yields precision near 32%; the same detector in a high-risk segment at 6% prevalence exceeds 75% with nothing changed. Experts refuse to quote precision without the base rate attached, and know that the way to make precision acceptable is often to narrow the population rather than improve the model.

Count-weighted and value-weighted error are different numbers, and the second shows up in the accounts. The tell-tale is an error budget expressed as a percentage of cases. Because exposure is heavy-tailed — a handful of very large invoices, very sick patients, very high-value claims — a rate comfortable per case can be ruinous per rupee. Experts report both and set the budget on whichever binds, which is almost always value.

The error rate you quote has its own error bar. The tell-tale is a commitment written at a point estimate: false-approval rate below 0.5%. With a few hundred audited cases the confidence interval routinely spans a factor of three, and the contractual promise sits at its optimistic end. Experts commit to the upper bound, or buy labels until the interval narrows enough to commit safely, and can say how many audited cases their number rests on.

The failure rate belongs to the workflow, not to the model. The tell-tale is a model target set stricter than any measured human baseline — a 1% target in a process whose human reviewers were never audited, and where document capture and retrieval each contribute their own errors. End to end, the rate that reaches the customer is the composition of every stage. Experts insist on measuring the incumbent human process first, because the comparison that decides whether to ship is almost never model-versus-perfect; it is model-plus-workflow versus human-plus-workflow.

Asymmetry is rarely two numbers; it is a distribution over harm types. The tell-tale is a cost matrix with exactly four cells. Collapsing every false positive into one price is what produced Khabardaar's ₹18 and the blocked hospital line. Experts tier the harms — recoverable in seconds, recoverable with effort, irrecoverable, reportable to a regulator — and bound each tier separately, accepting that the top tier's bound may be an absolute count rather than a rate.

A published threshold is a behavioural incentive, and incentives get exploited. The tell-tale is bunching: a histogram of scores or case values with an unnatural pile just on the favourable side of the cut. The obvious reading is seasonality; the correct one is that someone — a fraud ring, a partner, occasionally an internal sales team — has learned where the line is. Experts watch the shape of the distribution near the cut, not just the rate on either side.

7. How the decision changes by product type and stage

The arithmetic is the same everywhere; what varies is who pays for an error, how fast it becomes visible, and how freely the number can move afterwards. In consumer products errors are individually cheap and enormously numerous, feedback is weak and selection-biased because unhappy users leave rather than complain, and the binding constraint is support load or a viral incident rather than per-case cost. In B2B and enterprise volume collapses and loudness rises: one wrong output reaches a named account, so buyers negotiate an explicit error commitment and the operating point acquires legal review. In platforms and marketplaces the two sides do not share the budget, and the side absorbing false positives usually has less power and less voice. In hardware a threshold shipped to a fleet is hard to walk back, so teams choose conservatively and pay in coverage. In AI-native products the scoring function is itself learned and drifting, so the operating point must be re-derived after every model swap.

By stage the differences are smaller than people assume. An early-stage team has fewer labels and a wider confidence interval, which argues for a conservative point and a faster re-baselining cadence — not for skipping the analysis. A scaled company can slice finely and monitor continuously, but faces larger absolute losses from the same percentage and more process before the number can move, so precision arrives later than the ability to act on it. What does not differ by stage is the obligation to name the population, the direction and the cost.

8. Three worked cases, including one that went wrong

Aks Imaging Systems: the currency is cost per additional case found. At 60,000 films a month and 2.5% prevalence, Sharanya's candidate points produced the table below; the revealing calculation is not the error rate but the ratio between adjacent points.

Table 2. Aks operating points at 60,000 films a month, 2.5% TB prevalence, confirmatory test ₹900.
Operating pointSensitivitySpecificityCases missed / monthConfirmatory tests / monthTest cost / month
A — sensitivity-first92%72%12017,760₹1.60 crore
C — balanced89%83%16511,280₹1.02 crore
B — specificity-first85%86%2259,465₹85.2 lakh

Moving from B to A costs an extra ₹74.6 lakh a month and finds 105 more cases: about ₹71,000 per additional case detected. Against a disease where an untreated infectious case transmits to roughly ten contacts a year and drug-resistant treatment runs into several lakh rupees, ₹71,000 is plainly worth paying, and the decision-theoretic answer is A. A second-order effect decided otherwise. District laboratories could run about 11,500 confirmatory tests a month for this programme; point A's 17,760 would create a queue, and a queued confirmatory test is a person who does not return. The binding constraint was cartridge capacity, not money, which is why Sharanya's shortlist converged on C.

Khabardaar: replace one threshold with an action ladder. Aditya's team stopped asking where to cut and asked how many actions they had. Blocking below band 90 was unacceptable because of the false-positive tail; allowing 70–89 through untouched forfeited 745,000 scam calls a month. The third action — Chow's reject option, dressed as product — was a warning banner that let the user answer anyway. Blocking above 90, warning at 70–89, allowing below 70 and exempting the DoT-approved caller-name registry cut wrong blocks by roughly 92% against the expected-value optimum while keeping 88% of scam-call coverage.

Zamaanat General Insurance: where the approach failed. Zamaanat's motor own-damage team auto-approved fast-track claims below ₹40,000 against a leakage budget of 1.5% of auto-approved value — about ₹55 lakh a quarter on 22,080 claims averaging ₹16,500. The count-weighted error rate stayed inside budget at 1.4% for five straight months; realised leakage over two quarters was ₹3.7 crore against a budgeted ₹1.1 crore. Two things had gone wrong at once. Errors had migrated to the top of the value range, so the value-weighted error rate was 10.2%; and the share of auto-approved claims in the ₹36,000–₹39,999 bucket had risen from 7% to 23% of volume, the signature of garages that had worked out where the cap sat. Nobody saw it for five months because auto-approved claims generated no ground truth. Recovery took nine months: a permanent 2% randomised re-audit at about ₹19 lakh a year, a value-weighted budget, per-segment thresholds, and a temporary ₹25,000 cap that cut fast-track coverage from 46% to 29% before segment thresholds restored it to 41%.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

The universal bar. A launch gate of "99% accuracy" applied to every AI feature regardless of what failures cost. The warning sign is a quality standard stated without a population or a direction. The diagnostic: what does this rate mean in wrong outcomes per month, and what does one cost? Caught late it yields either a feature that never ships or one whose bar is far too loose for its exposure.

The frozen threshold. A number chosen at launch and never revisited. The warning sign is complaints rising months later with no model change to explain them. The diagnostic: when was the audit sample last refreshed, and has the curve itself moved? Zamaanat's five silent months are the cost of catching it late.

Confidence mistaken for probability. Treating a model's score as a calibrated chance of correctness. The warning sign is a threshold chosen with no audited band table behind it. The diagnostic: at a score of 0.9, what fraction of cases were actually correct in the last audit? Caught late, every downstream commitment built on the score is mis-specified by an unknown factor.

Aggregate blindness. A healthy blended metric concealing one badly served segment. The warning sign is a loud complaint from one customer type shortly after a good launch review. The diagnostic: show me this rate sliced by device, region, tenure and value band. Late, it surfaces as a contractual dispute rather than an engineering ticket.

Capacity ignored. A threshold chosen on cost alone, generating a queue nobody can staff. The warning sign is a backlog growing steadily in week two. The diagnostic: what queue does this cut create per month, and what is our throughput? Caught late, the queue is cleared by quiet rubber-stamping, which destroys the ground truth the system depends on.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first live disagreement is whether every error should be priced. The decision-theoretic position, at its strongest, is that refusing to name a price protects nobody: an unpriced error still gets traded, by escalation and seniority rather than arithmetic, and the record of error budgets in reliability engineering suggests that naming the number makes the trade auditable and usually more conservative. It would be wrong if the loss distribution were heavy enough that expected value is the wrong functional, or if some harms are genuinely non-fungible. The assurance position, at its strongest, is precisely that: certain hazards should carry a zero budget and be removed by design, because expected-value thresholds erode predictably under commercial pressure until the erosion is large. It would be wrong if the hazard cannot be isolated, or if the zero-budget control has its own failure mode — mandatory confirmation produces alarm fatigue and automation complacency, both measurable and both able to end up worse.

The second disagreement is over disaggregation. The maximalist position holds that an aggregate rate is not a quality claim at all and that per-segment budgets are mandatory. The statistical objection is real and rarely answered well: slice finely enough and multiplicity guarantees a bad slice, so a rule requiring every slice to clear a bar can never be satisfied and will be applied selectively. Serious practitioners converge on pre-registering a small number of segments that matter for policy or contract reasons and treating the rest as monitoring rather than gating — but they disagree sharply about who chooses the list.

The third disagreement is how much to invest in the curve at all. One camp argues that capability has improved fast enough that elaborate threshold engineering is depreciating capital, and that the durable investment is recoverability and the ability to swap models. The other points out that the tail is where the last two percentage points never arrive, and that regulated deployments like Sharanya's need a fixed, evidenced operating point regardless of what ships next quarter. Both describe real experiences of the same decade.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this can recite that a model has a failure rate rather than a specification. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently. They ask for the per-band table before the headline metric, and ask how many audited cases sit in the band under discussion. They state quality as a sentence with four slots filled — which error direction, for which population, at what rate, measured when — and notice when a colleague's is missing one. They budget permanently for labels they do not strictly need, because automation buys coverage by destroying the evidence that justified it. The clearest tell: asked how good their model is, they ask what it is for before answering.

12. What each of them did

Sharanya took operating point C to the 20 February review, not because it minimised cost or misses but because it was the most sensitive point the district laboratories could actually serve, and because a queued confirmatory test is a missed case under another name. She wrote the commitment as an interval — a miss rate defensible at the upper bound of the Wilson interval on 1,400 audited films — and attached a revalidation trigger for any change in detector model.

Aditya stopped defending a threshold and changed the action set. Blocking stayed above band 90, a warning banner covered 70–89, the caller-name registry supplied an exemption list, and a randomly sampled 0.5% of blocked calls went to a human adjudication queue funded as a permanent line rather than a project. He kept one number on the wall: wrong blocks per million calls, sliced by whether the calling number belonged to a registered institution.

  1. Sharanya's binding constraint was laboratory capacity, not money. If the state funded 8,000 extra cartridges a month, should she move to point A, and what would she measure first to know whether that money bought detected cases or queue?
  2. Khabardaar's ladder cut wrong blocks by 92% but shifted many decisions onto users through a banner. When is transferring the decision to the user a real improvement in quality rather than a transfer of liability?
  3. Zamaanat's count-weighted rate stayed in budget for five months while leakage tripled. Inheriting that portfolio in month three, which single monitoring change would most likely have surfaced it, and why would tightening the threshold have failed?

case40v1-aipm.quality.dist:
Nikhaar Grading Network: Seventy-Seven Per Cent of What?

A case on deciding what failure rate is acceptable, for which job, when the ruler itself is uncertain

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Thursday 15 October 2026, Enakshi Raiturkar sat at her dining table in Baner, Pune, with two documents open. The first was the slide she would take to the board of Nikhaar Grading Network at seven the next evening, timed so Austin could join at half past eight in the morning and Dublin at half past two. The second was a spreadsheet she had been told not to circulate.

The slide said that Netra, the company's machine-vision fruit grader, agreed with the on-site grader 94.6 per cent of the time, and recommended that from Monday 7 December the machine's grade become binding at all thirty-four centres: the farmer paid on the machine's call, the grader's post gone at twenty-six of them. The spreadsheet said that when three independent experts re-graded 1,200 lots the machine had already been paid on, it reached the same grade 77.0 per cent of the time.

Both numbers were correct. What Enakshi could not work out was which described the product she was selling, or whether what she was approving had a nameable failure rate. Nilay Vaishampayan, the chief executive, wanted a date; Neeraja Kandaswamy, the chief financial officer, wanted a cost line out of the FY2028 plan; a farmers' collective in Sangola wanted an explanation in Marathi for why a machine had called its fruit second grade. In a hundred and two days the first export container loaded for Dublin.

2. How Nikhaar got here

Nikhaar Grading Network Private Limited was founded in Nashik in 2017 by Nilay, then a cold-chain engineer. Its proposition was unusual in Indian fruit procurement: a farmer could bring pomegranate, table grapes or banana to a collection centre, have it graded on a published ladder and be paid by UPI before leaving. By FY2026 it ran 212 centres across seven states, handled 94,000 tonnes and turned over ₹486 crore (Exhibit 1), selling to modern trade — Reliance Retail, BigBasket, Zepto — to processors, and at the premium end to EU importers.

Two past decisions shaped what was possible in October 2026. In February 2022, to win its first national modern-trade contract, Nikhaar committed to paying the farmer within four hours of delivery. That promise was why farmers drove past APMC mandis and eNAM screens to a Nikhaar gate. It also meant there was no clawback: by the time a buyer's inward check disagreed, the money had left the company's account, usually before the truck had. In 2023, after disputes at three centres, Nikhaar simplified its ladder to four steps — A export, B premium domestic, C standard domestic, R processing — and printed each price on every receipt and in the Nikhaar Patti app. The ladder was built to be explainable to a farmer at a weighbridge, not to match a buyer's specification; no buyer bought on it, and packhouse staff mapped the specs by hand.

Netra was funded out of a ₹214 crore round raised in November 2024: a steel tunnel with four cameras, through which three crates from each lot passed. Roughly ninety fruit were scored for calibre, blemish, crack, sunburn and colour, and those scores were collapsed into one lot grade by a rule Enakshi wrote into the spec in December 2024 — a lot was A if at least 85 per cent of the sampled fruit met export specification, B if at least 85 per cent met premium, and so on.

3. The industry

Indian fruit aggregation is a thin-margin business in which the grading decision is the business. Nikhaar's FY2026 gross margin was ₹4.10 a kilogram on an average realisation of ₹51.70, or 7.9 per cent (Exhibit 1), while one one-step grading error on a 240-kilogram lot moved ₹3,360 to ₹9,120 of cash. Ninjacart, DeHaat, WayCool and Samunnati competed for the same arrivals, and the commission agent who had financed the farmer's inputs competed hardest. A farmer who felt cheated on Tuesday delivered to the mandi on Wednesday.

Regulation touched the product at three points: APEDA registration and European Union residue limits on exports, FSSAI rules and Agmark designations behind the domestic ladder, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 on Netra itself. Every fruit image was captured against a farmer identity in the Patti app, making the corpus personal data: Lipika Bhattacharyya's team had waited since July for a consent flow before it could label images from thirty-one further centres.

Export exposure ran through one account. Northquay Produce, a Dublin importer supplying EU retailers, had contracted for 160 containers between January and April 2027, each 58 lots and 13,920 kilograms, at ₹118 a kilogram — ₹26.28 crore of revenue and, at ₹14 a kilogram, ₹3.12 crore of gross margin, a twelfth of the company's. Last season four of 96 containers were claimed on grade: realisation fell to ₹76 a kilogram, costing ₹5,84,640 of lost value and ₹1,23,360 of re-handling, ₹7,08,000 a container.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Netra went live in advisory mode on Monday 1 June 2026 at thirty-four centres — twenty-one in the Nashik belt, thirteen in the Deccan cluster of Vijayapura, Bagalkot and Solapur. The machine proposed a grade, the grader accepted or overrode it, and the farmer was paid on what was entered (Figure A).

The dashboard improved through the monsoon. The headline metric, labelled "model agreement", rose from 89.1 per cent in June to 94.6 in September (Exhibit 5), and voided scans — lots the rig could not read for rain, dust or a camera fault — fell from 420 to 274. On Friday 14 August, Nilay told the board that binding grading at 180 centres by March 2027 would take ₹4.80 crore of annual cost out of the network. The figure went into the FY2028 breakeven plan.

Two things then happened that the curve had not predicted. On Wednesday 2 September a delegation from an FPO at Sangola declined to unload. Its chairman, Namdev Shelar, wrote that his members' fruit had been called C by a machine that could not be asked why, in a season when the same fruit fetched B at the mandi. Nithin Varkey, who ran centre operations from Kochi, forwarded it with one line: this is the fourth one.

Second, Enakshi commissioned an independent re-grade. Between Monday 7 and Tuesday 22 September a panel of three — a retired APMC grader, a Krishi Vigyan Kendra agronomist, a packhouse quality head — re-graded 1,200 lots drawn at random from the 25,184 accepted at the Netra grade between 1 June and 31 August. Results circulated on 30 September. Exhibit 2 is what Enakshi could not unsee: exact agreement on 924 lots, 77.0 per cent; 144, or 12.0 per cent, graded better than the panel thought right; 132, or 11.0 per cent, worse.

Three further facts emerged after. Only 180 of the 1,200 lots had been re-graded in triplicate; the other 1,020 were seen by one expert each. On those 180 all three agreed on 122 lots (67.8 per cent), two of three on 49, and all three differed on 9, settled by the senior member alone. A ruler with 67.8 per cent unanimity, Lipika said, could not certify a machine at 95 per cent, and 77.0 per cent might be near the ceiling of what such a panel could record.

Next, Nithin conceded on Monday 12 October that at nine centres his graders had been overriding Netra to protect high-volume suppliers: overrides were not a record of the machine's hard cases but partly of which farmers mattered. And because the audit sampled only accepted lots, nothing in Exhibit 2 described the 612 lots overridden in September.

Finally, Figure B showed where the errors lived. Of the 1,200 lots, 268 fell in the 80 to 89 per cent band of sampled fruit meeting the next specification up — astride the 85 per cent rule — and carried 142 of the 276 errors, a rate of 53.0 per cent against 14.4 per cent across the other 932. The machine was not uniformly unreliable: it failed where a continuous distribution of fruit had been forced across a line drawn in a hurry.

5. The people

Enakshi Raiturkar, 38, vice-president of product, Pune. Joined 2024; wrote the Netra business case and the 85 per cent rule. She argues for a decision per cluster and per grade, not per network. Her vesting rides on the FY2028 plan she is now contradicting. She has not said that she never revisited the threshold.

Nilay Vaishampayan, 46, co-founder and chief executive, Nashik. Binding at the thirty-four from 7 December, 180 centres by March: advisory, he says, pays for a machine and a grader and learns nothing. He is in early talks with a larger agri-platform, and automated grading is the asset being valued. Enakshi does not know.

Lipika Bhattacharyya, 41, head of data science, Austin. Three people, ₹1.94 crore a year — ₹16.17 lakh a month, more than the thirty-four graders together. She argues 77.0 per cent understates the model: the labels are noisy, the Deccan gap a sampling artefact. She knows, and has written where nobody read it, that the corpus was labelled at eleven Nashik-belt centres.

Nithin Varkey, 44, head of centre operations, Kochi. Keep the grader everywhere: they catch what the machine misses. His function is 212 centres and 340 people, and headcount is how it is measured. Eleven grader contracts expire on 31 December, unrenewed — a deadline nobody has acknowledged.

Elango Shanmugam, 50, head of exports and key accounts, Chennai. Binding is fine for domestic grades, unthinkable for A; his commission is on export realisation. He circulated last season's four claims in 96 containers, 4.2 per cent, as evidence that grading was under control, without saying that two came from a cold-chain delay at Jawaharlal Nehru Port, or that Netra was not live then.

Neeraja Kandaswamy, 48, chief financial officer, Bengaluru. ₹68 crore of cash against ₹3.4 crore a month: twenty months. The net payout error is ₹13.37 lakh a month against ₹12.92 lakh of grader cost, and the board has seen a plan in which grader cost falls from the fourth quarter of FY2027. She has run no scenario in which the rate is worse than measured.

Lydia Noonan, Dublin, quality director at Northquay Produce. On 9 October she asked for a grade certificate per container and a 2 per cent claim ceiling, and mentioned that her team was evaluating Peruvian supply for February. Her retailers penalise her. She has not said that Northquay's own inward check samples two crates a container.

Namdev Shelar, 57, chairman of the 1,420-member FPO at Sangola. A machine that cannot be argued with, his letter says, is worse than a grader who can be wrong and admit it. His standing rests on beating the mandi price, and a rival aggregator has offered his members ₹1.50 a kilogram, so the dispute is leverage.

6. Exhibits

Exhibits 2 and 5 were not in conflict so much as unrelated: one measured whether a grader pressed accept, the other whether he should have. Exhibit 6 was worse, because it looked decisive. The ₹4.80 crore a year promised to the board came out, on the same arithmetic scaled from thirty-four centres to 180, at ₹19.04 lakh a month — ₹2.28 crore a year, less than half. And the churn line left out of every column had a sharper edge: the net was small because over- and under-payments offset, but no farmer experiences a net. September's accepted lots carried ₹59.74 lakh of under-payment and ₹73.11 lakh of over-payment, and the farmers in the first group were not those in the second.

7. Voices

"Seventy-seven is not the model's number, it is the panel's. Three graders agreed with each other on sixty-eight per cent of the lots they all saw. Tell me what the machine is supposed to beat and I will tell you whether it beats it."

Lipika Bhattacharyya, product review call, 1 October 2026, 9.00 pm IST

"Every month we argue, we pay for a camera and a grader to do one job and learn nothing, because the grader covers for the camera. Put it live and we will have a failure rate instead of an opinion."

Nilay Vaishampayan, same call

"My members do not read percentages, they read the slip. Last year the grader told Sakharam his fruit was B and showed him the crates. This year the screen said C and the boy at the counter said the machine had decided. I cannot take that back to fourteen hundred and twenty families."

Namdev Shelar, letter to Nashik, 2 September 2026, translated from Marathi

"Domestic, do what you like. On export, one over-graded lot in fifty-eight contaminates a container, and twenty-six per cent of your A calls are not A. I am not putting my name on that in January."

Elango Shanmugam, email to Enakshi and Nilay, 9 October 2026

"Nithin bhai, if we void it shows red on the scorecard, so we wipe the lens and shoot again. The second shot usually comes out a grade better."

Centre manager, Bagalkot, operations WhatsApp group, 18 September 2026

8. The options, as Enakshi now frames them

Option 1: binding at all thirty-four centres from 7 December. Graders go from twenty-six centres, the eight export-feeding centres keep theirs, and six roving auditors arrive with a doubled audit sample. It saves ₹3.60 lakh a month on Lipika's assumption and ₹2.07 lakh on Nithin's, and gives a measured failure rate for the first time, because nobody will be patching the machine. It also makes the machine's word final through the peak in the Deccan, where A precision is 59.0 per cent.

Option 2: binding only where measured error clears a written threshold. The Nashik belt, at 80.8 per cent match and 80.6 per cent A precision, goes binding; the Deccan cluster stays advisory until a fresh sample clears the same bar. This is the option Enakshi believes she can defend, and the one that makes her set a number — what match rate, at what sample size, for which grade — that nobody has set.

Option 3: hold advisory through the export season. Retrain on Deccan-labelled images once the consent flow ships, re-audit in April 2027. It protects the Northquay window and Namdev's members, costs the ₹4.80 crore line its credibility, keeps eleven grader contracts alive, and leaves Nilay negotiating over automation he does not have.

Three things sat outside that frame. Every option measured Netra against a panel that agreed with itself 67.8 per cent of the time, on a single opinion for 1,020 of 1,200 lots. Figure B suggested the defect might be in the ladder, not the model: Nikhaar could pay a blended per-kilogram price off the measured fruit distribution and have no boundary to be wrong about — except that the slab was printed on every receipt and promised in two contracts. And there was Namdev's point, which no exhibit addressed: whether what farmers bought was accuracy at all, or the ability to argue.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board votes on Friday 16 October. Mrig Bahar arrivals peak from 7 December, the heaviest ten weeks of the pomegranate year. The first Northquay container must load on 25 January 2027, and the renewal, with or without a 2 per cent claim ceiling, is signed before that. Eleven grader contracts lapse on 31 December. The senior panellist is available only to 31 January. Cash is ₹68 crore against ₹3.4 crore a month, and the board's standing resolution is EBITDA breakeven in the fourth quarter of FY2028. The four-hour payment promise cannot be reopened — it is in the modern-trade contract and on the farmer's receipt — so every grading decision is final when it is made. The consent flow is with legal, with no date.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Which number — 94.6, 77.0, 80.6, 59.0 — should a product manager be managing, and what must be true for each to be the right one?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 5 are both accurate and point opposite ways. Which would you take to the board, and what would you say about the other?
  3. Using Exhibits 4 and 6, what failure rate would you accept for grade A, and for R? Should the rate differ by grade, by cluster, by season, by farmer?
  4. The net payout error is ₹124.80 a lot and the gross is ₹1,240.00. Which belongs in the business case, and whose interests does each serve?
  5. If the panel agrees with itself 67.8 per cent of the time, what would you build before claiming any accuracy figure — and can it be built before 7 December?
  6. Is this a decision about automation level, about the ladder, or about what Nikhaar sold farmers in 2022? What should Enakshi do on Monday morning, and what should she say to the board on Friday evening?

At ten past midnight Enakshi opened the Patti app as a farmer would see it. One line, one grade, one amount, a green tick. No confidence band, no second opinion, no way to ask. She closed the laptop with the slide unchanged and the spreadsheet open, unable to decide whether the honest thing to carry into Friday's call was a number, a range, or an admission that after nineteen weeks she did not know what the 1,200 lots had answered.

All figures are fictional teaching data. Exhibit totals are computed from the rows shown, and rates within the denominators stated. Real companies and regulations appear only as market context.
exp20v2-aipm.quality.dist:
AI & Data Products · AI & ML Product Management

Quality as a Distribution

A model has no spec, it has a failure rate — the product decision is choosing which rate a given job can absorb, not chasing zero.

A threshold due Friday

Ananya Rao got the email at 7:40 on the morning of Tuesday, 15 September 2026: the head of finance operations at Ratlam Steel Works wanted to know, in writing, what would happen the first time Chalan Systems' invoice-matching model approved a payment to the wrong vendor. Ananya led product for Auto-Match, the feature that read a supplier's invoice, compared it against the matching purchase order and goods-receipt note, and decided whether the two matched closely enough to release payment without anyone looking at it. For eight months Auto-Match had run in shadow mode: it scored every invoice a confident match or a case needing review, but a human always made the actual approve-or-hold call, so a wrong score cost nothing. On Friday that changed. Chalan's board had approved switching Auto-Match to live mode for the first cohort of clients — Ratlam Steel among them — meaning invoices above a chosen confidence score would be paid automatically, with no person in the loop.

The number Ananya had to bring to Friday's steering meeting was a single threshold: the confidence score above which the model's judgment would be trusted unsupervised. Chalan processed roughly 40,000 invoices a month across twenty-six client accounts, with a twelve-person review team currently checking every one by hand. Move that threshold down and more invoices flow through untouched — faster payment, better vendor terms, fewer reviewer hours, the entire pitch to clients. Move it down further and more wrong matches slip through unchecked, each one a real payment to a real bank account somebody would later have to claw back. No line of code would tell her the right number. What she had was eight months of scores and outcomes, and the discipline to read them as a distribution rather than a verdict.

The idea

The habit Ananya needed is one product teams reach for once a feature stops behaving like ordinary software. Traditional software either works or it has a bug — something to be found and fixed until the defect count reaches zero. A machine-learning model is different in kind. Trained on examples rather than written as rules, it will be wrong on some share of the cases it meets, by design, permanently, and no amount of further engineering drives that share to exactly zero. The model does not have a specification it either meets or fails; it has a failure rate, a share of outputs that are wrong, spread unevenly across the situations it encounters. The job of the person shipping it is not to eliminate that rate but to decide which one is acceptable for the particular job the feature does.

The framing borrows from statistical quality control, the discipline Walter Shewhart built at Bell Labs in the 1920s and Edwards Deming carried into manufacturing after the Second World War: no physical process turns out identical units, so instead of demanding perfection you measure the distribution of output and set limits around what you will tolerate. Machine-learning product teams inherited the same logic once models moved from research demos into things people depended on, as evaluation practice matured alongside the models themselves through the early 2020s. The sentence Ananya could say on Friday without sounding glib was plain: a model doesn't have a spec, it has a failure rate, and this week's job is deciding which failure rate this job can absorb — not chasing zero.

How it actually works

Turning that principle into an actual number takes a specific sequence of steps, and teams routinely skip one without noticing. The first is building an audit sample: past cases where the model's decision can be checked against ground truth established some other way — for Auto-Match, invoices a senior reconciler had already checked by hand, independent of what the model had scored them. Skipping this and trusting the model's own confidence score as if it were the truth is the most common shortcut, and the most expensive one, because a model's stated confidence and its actual correctness are two different numbers that happen to be correlated, not identical.

The second step is sorting the audited sample by the model's score and measuring the true error rate inside each band — not one aggregate accuracy figure, but a curve. Chalan's data science lead, Farhan Mistry, pulled two thousand invoice-PO pairs the review team had already checked over the prior quarter, grouped them into six confidence bands, and counted how many "matches" in each band were, on inspection, actually wrong. As the model's stated confidence rose, the true error rate fell — but never to zero, and not smoothly: it plateaued through the middle bands before dropping sharply above 90.

The third step, where this page spends the most time, is choosing where along that curve to draw the line, because every point on it trades how much the model does unsupervised against how often it is wrong when it does. Only once the curve exists does a threshold mean anything; a number chosen before it, or without it, is a guess dressed as a decision.

The arithmetic behind Friday's number

Farhan and Ananya tested three thresholds against the table below, each one asking the same question at Chalan's real volume of 40,000 invoices a month: if everything at or above this score auto-approves, what happens?

Table 1. Audit sample by confidence band, and what each threshold implies at 40,000 invoices/month, average error value ₹20,000.
Threshold (auto-approve ≥)Sample auto-approvedError rate above cutWrong payments/monthCost/monthReview queue/month
95500/2,000 = 25%0.4%≈40≈₹8 lakh30,000
90800/2,000 = 40%0.625%≈100≈₹20 lakh24,000
801,200/2,000 = 60%1.42%≈341≈₹68 lakh16,000

Reviewer capacity set the other side of the trade: twelve reviewers, fifty invoices a day each, twenty-two working days a month, gives 13,200 invoices a month of manual capacity. At a threshold of 95 the review queue of 30,000 outgrows capacity by nearly 17,000 a month, an unworkable backlog inside a quarter, even though it is the cheapest option in mispayments. At 80 the queue of 16,000 sits close to capacity, needing only a handful of additional hires, but produces roughly ₹68 lakh a month in wrong payments — eight and a half times the cost of the strict cut. Ninety sits between the two: a 24,000 queue still above capacity, but by a gap hiring could close rather than one that would require tripling the team.

The ₹20,000 average error value was itself worth stress-testing, because it was an average across very different clients. Ratlam Steel's purchase orders ran far larger than Chalan's typical account — roughly ₹85,000 per invoice rather than ₹20,000 — and Ratlam was exactly the client asking the hard question that morning. Rerun the threshold-90 arithmetic on Ratlam's numbers alone and the same 100 monthly errors become roughly ₹85 lakh in mispayments, not ₹20 lakh: more than four times higher, with nothing about the model changed — only whose invoices were flowing through it. The acceptable failure rate was not one number for Chalan. It depended on whose invoices were being scored.

What a learner has to notice

The error rate is conditional, not fixed

The 10.5% overall error rate in Farhan's unfiltered sample described the sample, not the business, because the business was several distributions layered together — routine repeat vendors, new vendors, small invoices, outsized ones like Ratlam's. A launch-deck headline of "96% accurate" hides which 4% is wrong and for whom; any threshold set from the aggregate alone is really set by whichever segment dominates the sample, then applied silently to every segment that doesn't.

A failure rate is a symptom, not a diagnosis

The curve tells Ananya how often the model is wrong at each score; it says nothing about what kind of mismatch is common in the wrong 3% at band 80–89 — a rounding difference, a wrong purchase order entirely, or a vendor-name variant the model had not met. Two features can share an identical curve and deserve opposite responses, because one failure type is a five-minute reviewer fix and the other routes money to the wrong company. Setting a threshold without ever opening the wrong cases mistakes the diagnostic for the diagnosis.

The two error directions rarely cost the same

Auto-Match's errors were not symmetric: approving a bad match paid the wrong account, a loss that might not be recoverable; holding a good match for review only delayed a correct payment by a day. Because the costs differ, "acceptable" is really two rates, one per direction, and a single threshold necessarily trades one against the other whether the team names that trade-off or not.

The distribution moves even when the model doesn't

Farhan's sample was eight months of history; Chalan kept signing client types like Ratlam's outsized orders that the model had barely trained on. September's curve would not describe December's invoices, not because the model changed, but because who was sending them had. A threshold set once and left alone drifts quietly out of calibration with the business underneath it.

Confidence scores are not audited probabilities

Reading the model's own score as "percent chance correct" is the shortcut that makes thresholds meaningless: a score of 90 carrying an actual 3% error rate rather than 10% is common, and only an audited sample against ground truth reveals the gap. Confidence and correctness correlate, which is why the curve slopes the right way, but its exact shape has to be measured, never assumed from what the model reports about itself.

Severity deserves weight alongside probability

A wrong ₹4,000 stationery invoice and a wrong ₹40 lakh capital-equipment invoice can carry an identical confidence score, yet one is a rounding note and the other is a call to the CFO. An error rate averaged across amounts hides the tail: a policy that looks safe on the sample can still be ruinous on the one invoice, out of ten thousand, that happens to be enormous.

An acceptable average can still be an unfair distribution

A low blended error rate can sit almost entirely on one type of vendor — smaller, newer suppliers the model had fewer examples of — meaning the acceptable rate for the business is quietly a much higher, unacceptable rate for that group. Slicing the audit sample by vendor segment, not only by confidence band, is the only way this surfaces before a client notices it first.

Where the shape of the problem changes

The same distribution shows up differently depending on who is on the other end of it. In a consumer product, individual failures are usually cheap and reversible — a wrong autocomplete, a mistranslated line — so quality management tends to run off aggregate metrics at huge volume, and unhappy users mostly leave quietly rather than escalate; a 2% error rate across ten million monthly interactions is two hundred thousand bad experiences a team may never directly hear about. In B2B, volumes are far smaller and each failure is far louder: a wrongly auto-approved invoice reaches a named account manager and sometimes a CFO's inbox, which is why B2B buyers increasingly ask for an explicit error-rate commitment rather than a marketing claim, and why human review stays economically sensible long after it would be automated away in a consumer product. In a marketplace, the distribution has two sides at once, and an error rate that looks fine in aggregate can still be systematically unfair to one side — a ranking model that mismatches new sellers' listings more often than established ones is not just less accurate, it tilts the marketplace, turning a quality question into a trust question.

Company stage changes the decision too. An early-stage team rarely has Farhan's two thousand labelled pairs to draw on, and has to accept a rougher estimate, correcting the threshold as real outcomes accumulate. A larger company has the volume to monitor the curve continuously and slice it finely by segment, but also faces bigger absolute losses from the same percentage error, and more process before a threshold can be moved — precision arrives later, but so does the freedom to act quickly on what precision reveals.

Where this goes wrong

Treating one round number as a universal bar. The symptom is a launch gate of "99% accuracy" applied to every AI feature regardless of what a failure costs. The misunderstanding is treating accuracy as a general-purpose certificate rather than something that only means anything once translated into costed outcomes at real volume. The cheapest diagnostic: ask what 99% means in absolute wrong outcomes per month, and what each one costs — if nobody can answer, the number is decoration.

Reading the aggregate and missing the tail. The symptom is a healthy launch metric followed by one segment complaining loudly within weeks. The misunderstanding is assuming the input population is uniform, when a mean can be built from one clean majority and one badly served minority. The diagnostic is re-slicing the same audit sample by every attribute available — vendor size, invoice type, account age — before shipping, not after a complaint arrives.

Setting the threshold once and never returning to it. The symptom is complaints creeping upward months after launch though nobody touched the model. The misunderstanding is treating the decision as a one-time launch gate rather than a number tied to a population that keeps shifting underneath it. The diagnostic is a standing schedule to refresh the audit sample and re-plot the curve, watching the curve itself move, not just the headline rate.

What good looks like

Contrast Ananya's Friday with a comparable decision a fraud-screening team at a payments company had made a year earlier, facing the identical shape of problem. Rather than pick one global score, they built the audit-sample habit into the roadmap itself: every model change regenerated the error curve against a continuously refreshed held-out sample, sliced by transaction size and customer tenure, before any threshold moved. The team could state, in one sentence, the current false-approval rate for new customers above ₹50,000, the capacity available to absorb the resulting review queue, and the date the curve was last checked. Nobody there could recite the model's overall accuracy from memory, and nobody needed to — they could name the one number the business actually depended on, for the segment that mattered, current as of last week.

Friday, and after

Ananya walked into the steering meeting with a segmented answer rather than a single number. Invoices from established vendors under ₹5 lakh would auto-approve at a 90 cut, the band Farhan's curve showed clearing a 0.625% error rate. Invoices from new or unverified vendors, and anything above ₹5 lakh — Ratlam Steel's account included — would sit at 95, trading automation for safety on exactly the cases where a wrong match cost the most. She paired the decision with a number the CFO could hold her to: no more than ₹15 lakh a month in false-approval losses, checked against the next audit sample rather than assumed, revisited the moment the curve moved. She also asked finance for three more reviewers to absorb the resulting queue, rather than pretending the automation was free.

What Ananya still needed to learn, and what this topic unlocks, is how to build and read the evaluation systems that produce curves like Farhan's on an ongoing basis, how to talk about the resulting error rate honestly with people who will use it, and how to design an interface where a held-for-review invoice reads as normal, expected behaviour rather than a broken product. Two questions worth sitting with: what failure rate would you have accepted in Ananya's place, and for whom — and how would you know, a year from now, if the answer had quietly stopped being true?

Kavach Systems: Four Point One Out of Five

A teaching case on deciding what failure rate is acceptable for which job

1. Opening

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, Yamini Nadkarni, head of product at Kavach Systems, sat in a glass-walled room in the company's Indiranagar office in Bengaluru with a single number on the screen: 4.07. It was the mean score, out of five, that three human reviewers had given to 400 customer-support replies drafted by Kavach's model during a three-week pilot. Her largest prospective client wanted the model switched from "draft for an agent" to "send automatically" by Friday 16 October, so that it could carry the ticket surge before Diwali on 8 November. The client's head of customer experience had called 4.07 "a very good number." Yamini was not sure it was the right number to be looking at.

2. Company background

Kavach Systems was founded in 2019 by two former product engineers and grew to about 140 people, with annual recurring revenue of roughly ₹46 crore. It sells customer-support software to Indian lenders, payments firms and online retailers. Its product, Kavach Reply, drafts responses in English or Hinglish from the customer's record; until now a human agent read, edited and sent every one.

The market is crowded. Freshworks sells Freshdesk with its own AI assistant, Zoho Desk has Zia, and Jio Haptik and Gupshup are strong in conversational channels. Kavach competes on depth in regulated finance, where replies must respect the Reserve Bank of India's expectations on grievance redressal, and where customer data falls under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. A reply that wrongly tells a borrower a charge is waived, or quotes the wrong amount, is not merely unhelpful. It can become a formal complaint.

The prospective client, a Mumbai-headquartered consumer lending and payments company, handled 1,20,000 tickets a month and expected more in the festive weeks. Its agents cost ₹38 per ticket handled, fully loaded, and it wanted that figure down.

3. The situation

The pilot ran from 1 to 21 September 2026. Kavach Reply drafted replies to live tickets, agents sent them, and a random sample of 400 drafts, taken in proportion to the ticket mix, was scored afterwards. Reviewers used a five-point rubric. A score of 5 meant the draft could be sent as written; 4 meant a light edit; 3 meant a real rewrite; 2 meant wrong in substance; and 1 meant harmful, for example a false promise, a leaked detail or a policy breach. Review finished on 30 September.

Chinmay Rege, the machine-learning lead in Pune, argued that the headline was strong. Exhibit 1 shows the 400 scores: 188 fives, 112 fours, 56 threes, 28 twos and 16 ones. The mean is 4.07, the median is 4, and 300 of 400 drafts, or 75.0 per cent, scored 4 or better.

Not everyone saw the chart the same way. Ivo Marques, who designed the reviewer rubric from Lisbon, pointed out that a mean of 4.07 was compatible with very different realities, and that the 44 drafts at 2 or below were the ones a regulator or a newspaper would notice. Kritika Mathur, Kavach's customer-success lead in Melbourne, warned that the client's board expected a decision in writing before the festive freeze and read hesitation as weakness. Sandeep Khatri, the client's head of customer experience in Mumbai, wanted full automation: more than three-quarters of replies were already good, he said, and agents were exhausted.

Yamini asked Ivo to split the sample by ticket type. The result is Exhibit 2.

The aggregate was hiding a gradient. Order-status tickets, simple lookups, scored 4.52 with only 2.5 per cent at 2 or below. Fee disputes, where the model had to interpret policy and tone, scored 3.38, and 10 of the 80 drafts, or 12.5 per cent, were rated harmful. Together, fee disputes and refunds supplied 14 of the 16 harmful drafts. The fee-dispute sample was only 80 drafts, so its true failure rate could plausibly lie anywhere from roughly 18 to 37 per cent. The model had no specification, only a rate at which it went wrong, and that rate differed sharply by job.

4. The people

Yamini Nadkarni (Bengaluru) owns the decision. Her concern is that Kavach's reputation with lenders rests on never being the reason a customer complaint reaches the RBI ombudsman. Chinmay Rege (Pune) wants a launch that proves the model in production, where real traffic will teach it faster than any pilot. Ivo Marques (Lisbon) wants decisions made per ticket type, with a written threshold for each. Kritika Mathur (Melbourne) wants the client relationship protected and a clear, dated commitment she can carry into her next call. Sandeep Khatri (Mumbai), the client, wants lower cost per ticket and a visible festive-season plan.

5. Exhibits on cost

To turn the scores into money, Yamini's analyst built Exhibit 3 for the client's 1,20,000 tickets a month. The assumptions were these. The model costs ₹6 per ticket, whether the draft is sent automatically or reviewed. A human reviewing a draft costs ₹24 per ticket, against ₹38 for writing from scratch. Each bad reply, defined as a score of 2 or below, costs ₹210 in escalation, re-handling and goodwill. Traffic splits 48,000, 36,000, 24,000 and 12,000 tickets across the four types, and failure rates follow Exhibit 2. Agents are assumed to catch errors in the drafts they review.

The table cut against intuition. Option A, the fully automatic route, saved ₹10.68 lakh a month, but the bad-reply bill of ₹27.72 lakh consumed most of the gain. Option B saved ₹18.60 lakh, more than A, because it automated only the work the model did well. It also left agents reviewing 72,000 drafts, less relief than Sandeep wanted. Option C cost nothing in risk but delivered no saving and would miss the festive peak entirely.

6. The options

Option A: auto-send every ticket type from 16 October. The upside is the clean story Sandeep wants and a signal of Kavach's confidence. The cost is 13,200 bad replies a month, including roughly 4,800 rated harmful, concentrated among borrowers disputing charges, at precisely the time the client's brand is most exposed.

Option B: auto-send order and payment status only, keep agent review for everything else. The upside is the lowest total cost in Exhibit 3, a failure rate of 2.5 per cent on the automated slice, and a staged expansion plan. The cost is a smaller visible change for the client and continued agent workload.

Option C: hold the launch for three months. The upside is a larger sample, a better model and no festive-season risk. The cost is the ₹18.00 lakh tuning bill, no savings through Diwali, and a client who may turn to Freshworks or Zoho.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does the mean of 4.07 tell you about the product, and what does it conceal? Which rows of Exhibit 2 would you show the client?
  2. For each ticket type, what failure rate would you accept, and what would you need to know about the cost of a failure to defend it?
  3. Using the assumptions in Exhibit 3, at what bad-reply rate does auto-sending a ticket type stop paying for itself? Which types are above or below it?
  4. Which option would you recommend by 16 October, and what evidence would make you change it later?

8. A note for the learner

This case frames a model as something with a failure rate rather than a specification. A model produces a spread of outcomes, and the product manager's job is to read the whole distribution, decide which tail is tolerable for which job, and design the product around the rest. A single mean averages away exactly the information a decision needs.

A well-reasoned answer sets the acceptable rate from the economics and the harm of a failure, not from the model's average. In Exhibit 3's assumptions, replacing a ₹24 agent review with automation saves ₹24 per ticket and risks ₹210 per failure, so the break-even bad-reply rate is 24 divided by 210, about 11.4 per cent. Order status, at 2.5 per cent, is far below it. Fee disputes, at 27.5 per cent, are far above it, and carry harm that ₹210 does not capture. Refunds are the interesting middle: 10.0 per cent is just under break-even. Automating the 36,000 refund tickets would save ₹8.64 lakh in handling and cost ₹7.56 lakh in bad replies, a net ₹1.08 lakh, thin enough that a small shift in failure rate removes it. The sample of 120 also allows a true rate of roughly 5 to 15 per cent, which straddles the break-even.

One defensible path is Option B on 16 October, presented to the client as phase one with a written expansion rule. Fee disputes and KYC stay with agents. Refunds move to auto-send only after a fresh sample shows a bad-reply rate comfortably below 11.4 per cent, with a larger sample to narrow the range, and with a tripwire that returns a type to review if its measured rate rises above the threshold. Kritika gets a dated commitment, Ivo's per-type thresholds become the contract, and Chinmay gets production learning on the slice where it is safe.

All figures are fictional teaching data. Review counts, rates and costs in the exhibits are internally consistent as shown; rounded means are given to two decimals.
