6. The options

Option A: launch to every intent on 26 October. The upside is speed and the lowest monthly cost, ₹36.0 lakh against ₹228.0 lakh for agents alone, a saving of ₹192.0 lakh a month. The cost, from Exhibit 2, is about 62,550 wrong answers a month, of which 27,000 fall on borrowers who are already complaining and 18,900 on borrowers asking for a figure they will pay.

Option B: stay with agents until the model passes 95 per cent overall. Nothing wrong would reach a borrower, and the model could improve meanwhile. But each month of waiting costs ₹228.0 lakh rather than ₹73.2 lakh under Option C, a difference of ₹154.8 lakh. The 95 per cent target was also arbitrary: complaints might never reach it, and two routine intents already had.

Option C: launch on the behavioural specification in Exhibit 3. The assistant acts alone on the three intents that clear the quality floor, drafts for agents on foreclosure quotes, and passes every complaint to a person. Cost is ₹73.2 lakh a month, about 32.1 per cent of Option B, and the autonomous error exposure falls to 16,650. The cost is operational: Agents must approve about 1,05,000 drafts and take 90,000 complaints, so staffing must change, and the specification needs an owner and weekly measurement.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Why did the overall rate of 89.6 per cent tell Jayanti so little? Which intents would you have looked at first, and why?
  2. Jomo's specification sets a quality floor, a confidence floor and a latency limit. What does each protect, and what failure would each miss?
  3. Compare the three options using Exhibit 2. Which costs are certain and which are exposures? How would Jorawar and Jyotsna each weigh them?
  4. What must be true on 26 October for Option C to be safe, and what evidence would make Jayanti pause the launch?

8. A note for the learner

A probabilistic feature cannot be specified by listing what it does. It must be specified by stating the distribution of behaviour the company will accept, with the boundary cases defined and a human standing behind the boundary. That is the behavioural specification: acceptable outputs, failure modes, confidence, latency, cost, escalation and fallback.

One defensible path: Option C. Jayanti should recommend launching on 26 October under Exhibit 3, for four reasons. First, the evidence in Exhibit 1 is about intents, not averages; three of five clear 93 per cent, and two do not. Second, Exhibit 2 shows that the specification captures ₹154.8 lakh a month of saving relative to agents while cutting autonomous exposure from 62,550 to 16,650 wrong answers. Third, it gives Jorawar a rule he can audit, including ledger-only rupee amounts. Fourth, it is reversible: weekly labelled samples, and an intent falling below its floor reverts to agents within a day.

She should attach conditions: Jyotsna's staffing agreed before launch; Joana's handover tested with Hindi and Marathi transcripts; and the complaint and foreclosure rules treated as permanent until evidence, not enthusiasm, earns the assistant more autonomy. The strong answer specifies behaviour, prices it, and says when a person takes over.
exp20v2-aipm.behavioural.spec:
Behavioural specification for AI products

1. A Tuesday in March

On Tuesday, 3 March 2026, Revathi Krishnamoorthy, head of product at Hastakshar Claims Cloud, a Pune-based software company that runs claim-support desks for health insurers, opened the results of a six-week pilot sent by her engineering lead, Hemant Bhagwat. Hastakshar had built an assistant, which the team called Sahayak, that drafted replies to policyholders' health-insurance claim messages. The insurer was ready to switch it on for about 1,20,000 claim conversations a month, now answered by human agents at ₹95 each.

Sahayak had been "accurate" on 96 per cent of a sample of test conversations. Hemant's draft product requirements document, the page engineers build against, said only: Sahayak shall answer claim queries accurately. Revathi read the sentence three times. Accurate on which queries? What happened to the other four in a hundred? If they included a widow being told, wrongly and cheerfully, that her husband's claim was rejected, would the insurer call 96 per cent good?

The launch was set for 1 April. The insurer's chief operating officer, Harsimran Dutta, had made clear that one publicised wrong answer to a bereaved family would end the contract, worth roughly ₹9 crore a year to Hastakshar. Revathi's decision was what, precisely, she was asking the team to ship. The instrument was a behavioural specification, and she had never written one.

2. The idea

A conventional product requirements document, or PRD, describes what a feature does: when the user taps "Pay", the balance is debited. The feature either does this or has a bug. An AI feature may give two different outputs to the same input, some wrong in ways nobody wrote a rule to prevent. There is no single correct behaviour, only a spread of behaviours, some acceptable.

A behavioural specification is the requirements document for that situation. It states, in advance and in measurable terms, which outputs are acceptable, how often the feature may fall short, how it must fail when it does, what it must cost and how fast it must respond, and when it must stop and hand the user to a person. It replaces "the feature does X" with "the feature's behaviour falls within these bounds across this population of inputs".

No single person invented the idea. It descends from site-reliability engineers at large web companies, who from the mid-2000s set numeric service-level objectives such as "99.9 per cent of requests answered within 300 milliseconds", and from machine-learning researchers who from about 2018 published model cards, short documents stating what a model was built for and where it should not be used. AI product management joined the two.

"Sahayak does not have to be right every time; it has to be right often enough on the questions it answers, and it must know which questions it should not answer."

That sentence, which Revathi wrote on the whiteboard that afternoon, is the whole idea. Its two halves are how good answers must be, and whether to answer at all.

3. How it actually works

Revathi worked through the specification in six steps. Some are usually left implicit, and those are where specifications fail.

Step one: divide the inputs into classes by consequence. Hemant pulled 2,000 real conversations and, with two senior agents, sorted them by what a wrong answer would cost. Routine status questions ("where is my claim?") were 60 per cent, document-requirement questions 25 per cent, disputed or denied claims 10 per cent, and bereavement, grievance and ombudsman messages 5 per cent.

Step two: define "acceptable" per class, in words a reviewer can apply. For a denial question, acceptable means the reason matches the insurer's letter and the appeal route is named. Otherwise two reviewers grade the same reply differently.

Step three: set a target rate per class and a way to measure it. Step four: set the operating envelope: latency, cost and tone limits. Step five: define the answer-or-escalate rule, the confidence threshold below which Sahayak passes the case to a human. Step six: define failure behaviour: what happens on timeout, and how a human takes over without the customer repeating everything.

Figure 1 shows the six steps as one path. A feature that may decline chooses among many points on a quality curve, and the threshold selects one. Escalation is an intended outcome with its own cost, latency and quality bar.

4. A worked example, line by line

Revathi needed to know whether the threshold in the diamond was sensible. Shares of 60, 25, 10 and 5 per cent of 1,20,000 monthly conversations give 72,000, 30,000, 12,000 and 6,000. The team proposed a threshold under which Sahayak answers 40 per cent of denial queries, the 40 per cent it is most sure about, which is 4,800; the remaining 7,200 go to a human. If each wrong answer on a denied claim costs the insurer an average of ₹2,500 in rework, complaints and ombudsman handling (an assumption), the 864 extra errors cost 864 × 2,500 = ₹21,60,000. The change loses ₹21,60,000 − ₹3,27,600 = ₹18,32,400 a month. One changed input reversed the answer.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Acceptable is not the same as correct

A reply can be factually right yet unacceptable: correct about status but curt to a grieving customer. Acceptability is a reviewer's checklist; correctness is one line of it.

A rate needs its population

"95 per cent" describes a test set, not the world. If the test set over-represents easy queries, the number flatters the feature, and live traffic drifts when IRDAI issues a circular.

Confidence is not probability of being right

The score a model reports about its own answer is not automatically a probability. An overconfident model saying 90 per cent may be right 75 per cent of the time. The threshold in Figure 1 is trustworthy only after calibration, meaning checking, on labelled data, how often answers at each confidence level are actually acceptable and adjusting accordingly.

Average latency hides the customer who waits

A median of 2 seconds is compatible with one customer in twenty waiting a minute, so Table 1 also bounds the 95th percentile. The 95th percentile is the value below which 95 per cent of responses fall.

A specification is not an evaluation, and neither is a guardrail

The specification says what is required. An evaluation is the recurring test that measures whether it is met. A guardrail is a runtime check, such as a filter blocking mention of legal outcomes, that enforces part of it. A team with a guardrail but no written bound cannot tell whether it is enough.

What it cannot tell you

A specification cannot tell you whether customers want the feature, nor whether the bounds are the right ones. It cannot foresee failures no one imagined. Ask who was missing from the room when the classes were drawn.

6. How it differs across contexts

In consumer products, stakes per error are usually low, so specifications lean on sampling, with hard rules for small severe classes. In B2B products the specification often becomes part of the contract: Hastakshar's agreement will quote Table 1. In marketplace products an AI feature affects two sides at once, so the specification needs bounds on each and a statement of whose interest prevails.

An early-stage company may have one engineer as reviewer and a one-page specification with two classes. A large company adds risk, legal and data teams and pays in slower change. The small firm risks having no bounds; the large one, so many that nobody knows which binds.

7. Common mistakes

The single accuracy number. Symptom: a launch review quotes 96 per cent and no one can say who is in the other 4. Misunderstanding: quality is a scalar. Diagnostic: ask for the number split by consequence class; if it takes more than a day, no specification exists.

Escalation as an afterthought. Symptom: agents complain that handed-over cases arrive without context. Misunderstanding: a person is a free backstop. Diagnostic: could a new agent act on ten escalated transcripts without asking the customer anything?

Optimising cost before the tail. Symptom: the threshold creeps upward each quarter and complaints follow with a lag. Misunderstanding: cost and quality trade on averages. Diagnostic: recompute Table 4 with a real cost per wrong answer before approving any change.

The frozen specification. Symptom: the document is dated launch week and the inputs have shifted. Misunderstanding: it is a deliverable rather than a control. Diagnostic: when was the test set last refreshed from live traffic?

8. What good looks like

Consider the same Tuesday handled well. By Friday, Revathi has a two-page specification like Table 1, signed by the insurer's claims head and compliance officer as well as by Hemant. The classes come from real conversations, and the reviewers' checklist is attached. The pilot's "96 per cent" appears nowhere.

The launch is staged: two weeks of routine and document queries only, with all denials escalated, then the denial threshold opens in steps as the reviewed sample holds the tolerated rate. Any team member can say which number would make them pause the feature.

9. What Revathi decided

She asked Harsimran Dutta for a one-month delay to 1 May, offering the staged launch in return. The delay cost roughly ₹75 lakh of the contract's annual ₹9 crore, the price of proving the bounds rather than promising them. He agreed after seeing Table 4, because ₹18,32,400 a month of avoidable cost was a number his finance team could recompute.

The pilot had measured the feature, not the product. What would ship was a policy: which questions are answered, how well, and how the rest are handled.

What to learn next. The specification is only as good as the tests that check it, so study designing evaluations next, then specifying AI features in general.

Two questions to sit with. First, in a product you know, which class of input would you never allow an AI to answer, and could you defend the boundary to the person on the wrong side of it? Second, if you were forced to publish one number from your specification to customers, which would it be, and what would it reveal about your priorities?
case40v1-aipm.behavioural.spec:
Rasaayan Plant Systems: Signing for a Machine That Changes Its Mind

Teaching case. Rasaayan Plant Systems, Riyada Petrochemical and the other named companies and people are fictional. Real firms and regulators appear only as market context.

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday, 18 October 2026, Radhika Sundaresan sat at her kitchen table in Aundh, Pune, with two documents open: a fourteen-page paper titled Rahbar Behavioural Specification, version 2, and its signature block, three names typed in, none signed.

In the morning the steering committee of Rasaayan Plant Systems would decide whether Rahbar — its natural-language shift assistant, embedded in plant control rooms — went live at a petrochemical complex in Jubail on 1 December. On 15 December the model underneath Rahbar would cease to exist.

Radhika had spent eleven years shipping software whose behaviour she could draw on a whiteboard. Rahbar was not that: asked twice why a compressor had tripped, it gave two differently worded answers, one of which might be wrong in a way that mattered to a man standing before a live column. Her engineers had written a specification to bound this. Her safety head would not sign it; her sales president had already sold it.

2. How the company got here

Rasaayan Plant Systems was founded in Pune in 2013 by two instrumentation engineers. Its product was never the control layer — that belongs to Honeywell, Yokogawa, ABB and Siemens — but the layer above, pulling tags, procedures and shift logs into one searchable place. By FY2026 revenue was ₹384 crore across 61 industrial clients.

One decision from 2021 shapes everything Radhika now faces. Competing against global vendors, the founders promised what incumbents would not: they warranted their outputs. Clause 9.3 of the standard agreement, carried by 54 of the 61 clients, obliges Rasaayan to deliver "accurate and complete" information from the plant record, with a service credit of 4 per cent of the quarterly fee per validated incident of materially incorrect output, capped at 20 per cent of that fee. Clause 14.2 permits termination for cause if the cap is reached in three consecutive quarters.

For five years it was a weapon: the suite returned the right document or nothing, and credits had been paid twice, both for indexing failures. Nobody then imagined a feature whose correct behaviour was a distribution rather than a rule, and Clause 9.3 is now the paper under which a probabilistic system must ship.

3. The industry

Indian plants of this size run safety management systems audited against the Factories Act 1948, the hazardous-chemicals rules of 1989 and, in petroleum, PESO. Each turns on one idea: a named competent person authorises hazardous work. No statute contemplates software in that role, and none forbids software from advising the person who holds it.

Pressure comes from two directions. AVEVA and Aspen Technology bundle generative assistants into their own layers at licence prices Rasaayan cannot match, while Freshworks, Zoho and the integration arms of Infosys and TCS have made talent expensive: a Bengaluru machine-learning engineer with retrieval experience costs about ₹52 lakh a year against ₹31 lakh for a platform engineer.

Exposure abroad matters more than its size suggests. Five accounts, in Exhibit 5, contribute ₹59.0 crore a year — 15.4 per cent of revenue — and the largest, Riyada Petrochemical Industries in Jubail, has been the reference in every Gulf pitch. Indian plants ask about Rahbar; Riyada asked for a date. Jubail's conversations cannot be pooled into a Pune evaluation set, and Indian operator logs carry obligations under the DPDP Act 2023.

Figure 1. Pune overlaps Melbourne about four hours a day, Austin about one.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The board approved an AI programme on 14 January 2026. On 2 March came a choice that looked purely technical: rather than self-host, Rahbar would call a vendor's hosted frontier model, then at release M4, saving six weeks. It also meant Rasaayan did not own the release calendar.

On 11 May, Rehan Qureshi and Rishi Ananthakrishnan produced specification version 1: six classes of operator question and, for each, what an acceptable answer contained, a minimum correctness rate, a confidence threshold below which Rahbar must decline, and a latency ceiling. Raghavendra Mahabal signed it. Rupali Chitnis, who runs safety assurance from Vadodara, was not in the chain and first read it on 9 July.

A thirteen-week shadow trial ran from Monday 1 June to Sunday 30 August at Rohtas Minerals in Chandrapur, Rangoli Specialty in Dahej and Raibagh Fertiliser in Kakinada. Every answer went first to the shift engineer, who accepted or rejected it before the operator saw it. Over the trial 41,000 questions were logged; Exhibit 1 is what the team carried into September. Three beliefs have since come apart.

The first was that the accept-or-reject click measured correctness. On 9 September Rishi's team finished an independent adjudication of 1,200 answers against the plant record. Exhibit 2 is the result: engineers had been accepting answers that were plausible rather than right.

The second was that a specification, once written, holds. On Friday 4 September the vendor released M5 and announced M4's withdrawal on 15 December. Seventeen days later Rehan re-ran the frozen 2,400-case suite on both. Exhibit 4 shows M5 passing more cases — and answering, rather than declining, in 118 of the 260 cases where the specification requires abstention, against 31 for M4. The newer model is better at what the trial measured and worse at what the specification exists to guarantee.

The third was that abstention is free. Of 1,043 operators refused twice in one shift, 636 — 61.0 per cent — asked Rahbar nothing further that shift; the questions go to the control-room telephone, unlogged.

On 25 September Rajat Khemka converted Riyada's August letter of intent into a signed order: live at Jubail on 1 December 2026, Clause 9.3 unamended, ₹2.48 crore payable on acceptance. On 6 October Rupali wrote that she could not sign version 1. On 14 October Rehan delivered version 2, Exhibit 3, replacing thresholds with tolerance bands.

Figure 2. Fourteen days between go-live and the withdrawal of the model the specification was written for.

5. The people

Radhika Sundaresan, Vice-President, Product, Pune, owns the recommendation. Position: Rahbar ships only under a specification someone will sign. Incentive: an executive-committee seat the Riyada reference would settle. Unsaid: she does not fully believe Exhibit 2 either — its adjudicators were her own team.

Raghavendra Mahabal, Chief Technology Officer and founder, Pune. Position: move to M5 now; holding a dying model is not engineering. Incentive: the hosting decision was his. Unsaid: no self-hosted fallback has been costed.

Rupali Chitnis, Head of Safety Assurance, Vadodara, twenty-two years in process safety. Position: the interlock class must not reach an operator without a competent person in the loop, whatever the rate. Incentive: she signs the assurance letters clients file with their auditors. Unsaid: she thinks the real risk is a confident answer that displaces the operator's judgement, which she cannot measure.

Rehan Qureshi, Machine Learning Lead, Bengaluru, wrote both specifications. Position: bands are the honest form, because a band admits the number moves. Incentive: the document is his case for promotion. Unsaid: the class boundaries were drawn to fit the trial data.

Rishi Ananthakrishnan, Principal Data Scientist, Melbourne. Position: no number in Exhibit 1 should be quoted again, and nothing ships until adjudication is weekly and standing. Incentive: budget for the panel. Unsaid: his sample covered two of the three plants; Kakinada, with the oldest documents, is absent.

Reema Sohal, Principal Designer, Amsterdam. Position: abstention must be designed, not merely specified. Incentive: to own the escalation journey. Unsaid: of 400 logged questions she reviewed, 88 — 22.0 per cent — sat in a class that did not describe what the operator wanted.

Rupinder Gill, Head of Customer Success, Kuala Lumpur. Position: ship narrow and early; the four Indian accounts have been shown it. Incentive: a renewal book weighted on gross retention. Unsaid: two of them have asked whether Rahbar can be switched off without touching their platform fee.

Rajat Khemka, President, International Sales, Austin, signed the order on standard paper. Position: reopening the warranty signals doubt. Incentive: commission on acceptance, not renewal. Unsaid: Rashed Al Subai asked in August whether the answers were "deterministic"; he replied they were "grounded in the plant record".

7. Voices

"Ninety-three per cent, near enough, and they have watched it work for three months. I am not going back to Rashed to say our own people grade us differently from our engineers."

Rajat Khemka, steering call, 12 October.

"Every number in it is a band. A band is an admission of uncertainty. What more would you like us to admit?"

Raghavendra Mahabal to Rupali Chitnis, 15 October.

"What I am asked to sign is not the bands. It is the sentence saying an engineer releases each interlock answer. I have been in a control room at three in the morning during an upset. He will release all of them. Who signs for that?"

Rupali Chitnis, reply, 15 October.

"Please confirm in writing that from 1 December the assistant's answers on interlocks and trips are accurate and complete within the meaning of Clause 9.3; our safety team needs it for the management-of-change file. We are happy to accept a defined scope."

Rashed Al Subai, Operations Technology, Riyada Petrochemical, email, 12 October.

"He has offered us a defined scope. Nobody on this call has noticed."

Rupinder Gill, steering call, 12 October.

8. The options as Radhika sees them

A. Ship on 1 December on M4, under version 1. The specification was written against M4 and the trial ran on M4, so Exhibits 1 and 4 describe what would ship. It buys fourteen days, then a migration under production pressure.

B. Ship on 1 December on M5, under version 2's bands. M5 has a future and the better average, and bands accommodate movement. But Exhibit 4's abstention finding is not a band problem: every escalation rule in Exhibit 3 assumes the model knows when to stop, and M5 declines correctly in 142 of 260 required cases against M4's 229.

C. Ship narrow. Release only the three classes Exhibit 3 treats as autonomous, hold the rest behind a human, and go to Riyada to convert Clause 9.3 into a behavioural annexe: per-class bands, an agreed adjudication method, a rollback trigger. Rashed's email offers a defined scope; Rajat believes reopening the clause costs the account.

D. Delay to 1 March 2027 and rebuild on a model Rasaayan controls, forfeiting the ₹2.48 crore acceptance payment, the reference, and probably Rupinder's two wavering renewals.

None of the four addresses whether the six classes are the right unit of specification at all: Reema's 88 of 400 means every band in Exhibit 3 surrounds a quantity that may not exist. Nor does any say who holds the specification once it is live. Exhibit 3 names sign-off owners for classes, but nobody owns the document, nobody owns the decision to revert a class, and nothing says what happens the day the vendor ships M6. Every conversation, too, has been with Rashed, not the engineers who would press the release button.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Go-live at Jubail is contracted for 1 December 2026, ₹2.48 crore payable on acceptance. M4 is withdrawn on 15 December. The audit committee, chaired by Ruchira Devasthali, meets on 24 November and wants Rasaayan's position on Clause 9.3 across all 54 agreements.

Of the ₹22 crore approved in January, ₹13.6 crore had gone by 30 September, leaving ₹8.4 crore; operating the specification as Exhibit 6 describes consumes ₹4.80 crore a year, more than half the remainder, for one year's assurance on eleven plants.

People are tighter. The Vadodara reviewer pool that Options B and C both assume — nine process-domain reviewers — takes about ten weeks to hire and train. Begun on 19 October, it is ready on 28 December, four weeks after go-live. Rupali will not sign the interlock class without it; Raghavendra notes that her signature is an internal practice, not a contractual requirement.

Regulation constrains form rather than function: the management-of-change file must name a human. And Jubail's conversations cannot join the Pune evaluation set, so the panel will measure Indian answers and extrapolate to Saudi ones.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibits 1 and 2 describe the same thirteen weeks and disagree by about eight percentage points once volume-weighted, thirteen on the unweighted figure. Which number, if any, belongs in a document Rasaayan signs, and how should the others be disclosed?
  2. Version 2 replaced thresholds with bands. What does a band buy that a threshold does not, and what does it give away? What must Exhibit 3 add before a band is enforceable rather than decorative?
  3. Exhibit 4 shows a model better on average and worse at abstaining. Write the clause that governs a model upgrade: who tests it, against what, and what may ship before that test completes?
  4. Take Reema's two findings in turn — 61.0 per cent of twice-refused operators going quiet, and 22.0 per cent of sampled questions misclassified. What does each do to Exhibits 1, 2 and 3?
  5. Draft the behavioural annexe that would replace Clause 9.3. What does Rasaayan lose by no longer warranting its answers?
  6. It is Monday morning, 19 October. What does Radhika put to the committee, in what order, and what does she ask each of the eight people in Section 5 to commit to before she leaves the room? And on 24 November, what does she tell Ruchira Devasthali about the other 53 agreements, and what does she not yet know?

Back at the kitchen table

Radhika opened the signature block again. Three names: Raghavendra's, Rupali's, her own. Rehan had left a comment in the margin, in the flat tone engineers use for what frightens them: Should this be re-signed on every model release, or does the signature travel?

She thought about the phrase Rajat had used with Rashed — grounded in the plant record — and how reasonable it sounded, and how it was not the same as accurate, and how nobody had asked which he meant. She thought about the engineer at Dahej on 12 August who had caught a purge sequence with an isolation step missing, whose catch was now one item in a sample of two hundred.

Outside, a truck went past on the Mula road. It was twenty past one. The committee met at half past nine.

Behavioural specification for AI products

The requirements document for a feature with no deterministic answer — and why the hard part is how the bounds interact.

1. Two rooms, one week

On Wednesday, 11 February 2026, in a converted mill off Bengaluru's Magadi Road, Lalitha Yerneni held a two-page draft her chief medical officer would not sign. Yerneni led product at Lochan Diagnostics Cloud, whose Lakshan Triage read chest radiographs and marked the unremarkable ones so that no radiologist opened them. The customer, Lokhit Hospitals Network, produced 60,000 chest X-rays a month across forty-one hospitals, each read today at a fully loaded ₹180. Lokendra Yadav, the machine-learning lead, could auto-report any share of that volume: the model emitted a confidence score and the business chose where to cut.

The draft said Lakshan Triage shall identify normal studies with at least 99.6 per cent accuracy. Dr Yashasvi Lele, whose registration number would sit beside it, had written in the margin: accurate on whom, measured how, and what happens to the ones it gets wrong? Yogita Lamture, Lokhit's group chief operating officer, objected from the other side: at the coverage proposed, the savings did not justify the integration. Yerneni could answer neither, because the document described a model and both were asking about a system.

The next day, in Gurugram, Yashodeep Lonkar faced the same instrument and the opposite politics. Lonkar ran seller-experience product at Yatharth Commerce Exchange, a marketplace with about 4.1 lakh active sellers. Yantra Reply drafted answers to buyer questions on product pages and, above a confidence of 0.90, posted them in the seller's name. Growth wanted 0.85; Lavleen Yende, who ran trust and safety, had a panel reading a weekly sample and would not agree. The seller council had begun asking who was liable when an answer in a seller's name was wrong.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A behavioural specification is a written, measurable statement of the distribution of outputs a probabilistic feature may produce over a defined population of inputs; the policy deciding which inputs receive an output at all; the cost and latency envelope; and the behaviour required when the feature declines or fails. A conventional requirements document asserts a function; this asserts a constraint on a distribution and a policy over a population.

Four ancestors, and today's schools are those ancestors still arguing. The reliability school descends from service-level objectives and error budgets as practised at Google from the mid-2000s: quality is a budget you spend deliberately. It signs "a zero error rate is a refusal to choose", and will not accept that some errors must be argued out of existence rather than budgeted, an unbudgeted category being an unmeasured one.

The assurance school descends from functional safety and medical-device regulation — hazard analysis in Nancy Leveson's tradition, safety cases in the form Tim Kelly formalised. A specification is an argument from hazards to evidence, and some hazards are eliminated by design rather than tolerated. It signs "name what must never happen and show the mechanism", refuses to reduce every constraint to a number, and regards an aggregate accuracy figure as evidence of nothing.

The evaluation school descends from disaggregated measurement: datasheets and model cards from about 2018, Ribeiro's CheckList in 2020, batteries such as HELM from 2022. A specification is a test suite, and bounds written before the failure taxonomy exists are fiction. It signs "you cannot specify what you have not watched the feature do", and so rejects the spec-first sequence the others recommend.

The decision-theoretic school is the oldest and the least heard in product meetings. C. K. Chow published the reject option in 1970: abstain when the expected loss of answering exceeds that of abstaining. Charles Elkan's 2001 work on cost-sensitive learning made the corollary explicit — every threshold already prices each kind of error, written down or not. It signs "make the price legible", and refuses prohibitions, since an absolute ban is an infinite loss and infinities usually mean somebody declined to estimate.

One school says: name what must never happen. The other: name the price. A specification that does both without noticing is the commonest bad document there is.

3. Mechanics: the surface, not the dials

Competent practitioners write four bounds — quality, coverage, cost, latency — and treat them as four dials. Experts know they are one surface: move the confidence threshold and all four move together, in a relationship the risk–coverage curve already fixes. The specification's real content is the point chosen on that surface, and why.

Yadav's curve came from eighteen months of held-out studies in which 18 per cent of images carried an actionable abnormality: of 60,000 a month, 10,800 abnormal and 49,200 normal.

A bound you cannot afford to verify is a wish.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Three testable conditions. The output space defeats enumeration: Lakshan passes narrowly, its output binary but its inputs unbounded; Yantra Reply overwhelmingly. Consequences are unequal across inputs: both pass, which is what makes the class structure the important part. Abstention exists and has a defined cost: Lochan passes cleanly at ₹180 a read; Yatharth awkwardly, its fallback being seller time it neither pays for nor can compel.

It misleads where abstention is not truly available — a pricing engine must return a price, so "escalate" means "return the fallback", whose own error distribution teams treat as free and correct. It misleads where the population has moved unwatched, because it then manufactures confidence. And it misleads where value is a portfolio property: bounding each recommendation in a strip is beside the point.

And the four bounds are owned by four functions — quality by data science, coverage by growth, cost by finance, latency by platform — while the surface is owned by nobody. Mature companies make one named person sign the operating point.

6. The nuances that separate an expert

Confidence is a number, not a probability. A score of 0.90 means nine times in ten only after calibration against labelled data from the live population. The tell: an expert wants a reliability table before discussing thresholds, and treats an uncalibrated score as an ordering — good for ranking, useless for pricing.

The population is part of the bound. A rate without a stated population is a boast. An expert's specification names the sampling frame — which hospitals, months, languages — and how it is refreshed. The subtle version is Exhibit 3: stratification yields per-band rates you can trust and an aggregate you must not quote. A blend can improve while every component worsens, whenever the easy class grows.

Acceptability is a judgement, not a fact. Two reviewers grading one output disagree more than teams expect, and inter-rater agreement below about 0.7 means the central term is undefined and every downstream number noise. The tell: an expert asks the disagreement rate before the acceptance rate.

The fallback has its own specification. Escalation is a product with its own latency, cost, capacity and error rate. Yatharth's is unpaid seller labour answering in hours; Lochan's a radiologist queue that lengthens as coverage falls. The tell: an expert asks what it does in the worst hour of the worst week.

Human review is not automatically a control. Bainbridge's ironies of automation in 1983, and the automation-bias work since, say one thing: a reviewer who sees a correct answer ninety-seven times in a hundred stops reviewing. The tell: an expert measures the catch rate by seeding known-bad outputs.

Bounds must be affordable to verify. Exhibit 2 is the general case. The tell: an expert prices the audit in the same document as the bound, and refuses a tolerance the review period cannot resolve.

The specification is a control, not a deliverable. Its value lies in the moments it changes a decision — someone wants to move the threshold and cannot, or a number crosses a line and the feature pauses. The tell: an expert can name the date it last blocked something. If never, it is documentation.

Prices and prohibitions are different instruments, both legitimate. A price accepts a harm at a rate; a prohibition refuses it at any rate and names the mechanism. Experts price where harm is linear in events, and prohibit where one event is categorically unacceptable or the price cannot honestly be estimated. The tell: they can say which each clause is.

7. How the practice changes with product type and stage

In consumer products per-error cost is low and volume enormous, so specifications are statistical and the interesting clauses concern tail behaviour and the small severe classes carved out as prohibitions. In business and enterprise software it migrates into the contract and becomes a document written to be enforced against you, which tempts everyone towards vagueness; Lochan's counsel wanted "commercially reasonable accuracy", and Yerneni argued that vagueness defers the argument to the incident, when the customer is strongest. In platforms and marketplaces it must bound both sides and say whose interest prevails, because otherwise that sentence is written by whoever controls the threshold. In hardware-plus-software it must bound the input. For AI-native products it is the product definition; there is nothing else to describe.

By stage the difference is real but smaller than claimed. A seed-stage company can write a useful one-page specification with two input classes, one bound and a named escalation path; it cannot verify finely, so its bounds should be coarse and its review manual. A large company's problem is the reverse: many bounds, several owners, nobody able to say which binds. That specifications slow early companies down is usually a claim about bad specifications.

8. Three worked examples

Lakshan Triage, in Exhibits 1 and 2, is the case where the arithmetic produced a counter-intuitive answer: ship at lower coverage than the model permits. Yantra Reply, in Exhibits 3 to 5, is the case where the aggregate quality number was mismeasured and irrelevant, and the real content was a statement about which side of a market absorbs an error.

The third is Lakeer Reader, built by Yashodhan Field Services of Nagpur, and it failed. Yashodhan held an outsourced meter-reading contract: field agents photographed 8,00,000 electricity meters a month on Android handsets and Lakeer Reader read the index off the image. The specification, written by founder Yuvraj Lakdawala in one line, required at least 99.2 per cent reading accuracy. At launch it measured 99.3 per cent, and was met every month for five months while the product failed.

The 5,600 monthly errors were not spread evenly. Twelve per cent of meters were old electromechanical dials, often in unlit stairwells, with an error rate of 4.5 per cent against 0.18 per cent on digital displays; because they clustered in the older wards, wrong bills arrived monthly from the same few localities. About 3,240 of the 4,320 wrong bills drew a formal dispute at ₹620 each, ₹20,08,800 a month, a pattern legible enough for the state electricity regulatory commission's grievance machinery to notice. A blended figure could not show it. That is the failure: not a bad model, but a specification with no input classes, which made the product's only serious problem invisible in the only number anyone read.

Recovery took eleven weeks. Meter class became an input class with its own bound; a capture-quality gate prompted a re-shoot and sent a second failure to manual entry; and the gate's pass rate became a specified quantity, because a gate that quietly loosens is a specification that quietly lapses. Of the 96,000 hard meters, 60,000 then passed the gate and were auto-read with 720 errors, and 36,000 went to manual entry with 144 — the 864 in Exhibit 6. Disputes fell to about 648 a month, ₹4,01,760: a saving of ₹16,07,040 against extra field cost of ₹6,30,000, a net ₹9,77,040. Accuracy rose from 99.30 to 99.76 per cent, but Lakdawala says the headline is not why it worked.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The single number. Warning: the same figure in the board pack three quarters running. Diagnostic: split it by input class with volumes; if that takes over a day, no specification exists. Late cost: Yashodhan's five months.

Threshold creep. Warning: coverage rises quarter on quarter with no documented decision. Diagnostic: who signed the current operating point, and when? Late cost: creep shows only in complaint data lagging a quarter, so by discovery you are several steps down the curve.

The unmeasurable bound. Warning: a tolerance to two decimal places on a sample of two hundred. Diagnostic: what change would this review detect, at what power? Late cost: a commitment nobody can prove or disprove, which in a dispute favours the other side.

The decorative human. Warning: reviewer approval above 98 per cent with falling review times. Diagnostic: seed known-bad outputs and measure the catch rate. Late cost: a compensating control the safety case rests on, which does not work.

The frozen population. Warning: an evaluation set unrefreshed since launch. Diagnostic: what fraction of last month's traffic resembles nothing in the test set? Late cost: quality fine on paper and visibly poor in the field.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Specify first, or evaluate first. Spec-first holds that without a written bound no evaluation result can be called good, and that teams which evaluate first rationalise whatever they measured; its evidence is how regularly launch criteria get set after the launch data arrives. Evaluate-first holds that you cannot bound failure modes you have not seen, and that almost every real class structure emerged from the first month in production. Spec-first is wrong if early bounds are routinely revised rather than defended; evaluate-first, if measure-first teams converge on bounds rather than narratives. Both patterns occur, which is why the argument survives.

Prohibitions, or prices all the way down. The decision theorist says a prohibition is an unpriced infinity, and that a firm refusing one harm at any cost while tolerating a larger expected harm elsewhere is not careful but inconsistent. The assurance engineer says some harms are not commensurable with money, that pricing them corrodes the will to prevent them, and that naming a mechanism produces better engineering than naming a number. The first is wrong if firms that price severe harms prevent them better; the second, if prohibitions conceal larger tolerated harms. The evidence is mixed and anecdotal.

Bound the model, or bound the system. One camp specifies the model alone, because only then is a bound attributable, testable and portable. The other specifies end to end, because users experience systems and model-level bounds let every layer point at another. The first is right that system bounds are hard to attribute when they break; the second, that model-level bounds were met in every documented case where the product still harmed someone.

Whether output bounds belong at all. A minority, strongest in consumer organisations, holds that the acceptability of individual outputs is the wrong object, and that specifications should bound business outcomes — resolution rate, repeat contact — leaving the model free. The objection is that outcome metrics are slow, confounded and blind to rare severe failures; the rejoinder, that output acceptability was chosen for convenience and tracks nothing anyone cares about.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this writes a good document. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four ways. They ask for the risk–coverage row before the accuracy number, knowing the number alone is uninterpretable. They price the audit in the same breath as the bound, and refuse a tolerance they cannot verify. They can say of every clause whether it is a price or a prohibition, and notice when a colleague wrote one while meaning the other. And they treat the document as what makes disagreement productive: Lamture and Lele were pricing one event at ₹22,000 and at infinity — a discussable disagreement rather than a mood.

12. What each of them decided

Yerneni shipped at P2: 45 per cent auto-reported, a bound of 0.20 per cent missed abnormals in that bucket, a monthly re-read of 4,013 studies powered to detect a doubling, and a prohibition — written as a mechanism, not a rate — on auto-reporting any study flagged paediatric or portable. She gave up ₹10,80,000 a month against P3, on the hospital's own arithmetic rather than Lochan's caution, which is why Lamture signed. Lele signed because the document named the hazard and showed the gate.

Lonkar did not lower the threshold. He kept 0.90 for sellers below a listing-completeness score and opened 0.85 above it, turning a single number into a policy over a population — the move this topic is about. He also wrote the sentence nobody at Yatharth had written: where buyer and seller interests conflict, an auto-posted answer must fail towards saying less rather than towards being helpful, and that is a company's choice rather than a consequence of the model.

Three questions. First: Lokhit priced a missed finding at ₹22,000. If Lochan sells the same product to a group that prices it at ₹80,000, should the specification differ — and if so, what is Lochan selling? Second: the change is worth ₹24.28 lakh a month to sellers and costs Yatharth ₹7.02 lakh. On what principle would you decide, and would you write it where the seller council could read it? Third: Lakeer Reader met its specification while failing. What would the original line have needed for that to show in month one?

13. Going deeper

Quality as a distribution is the foundation: until output quality is a spread rather than a score, none of these bounds parse. PRD structure is what this replaces, and knowing the deterministic form shows which clauses fail. Specifying AI features carries these bounds into ordinary scoping. Problem–model fit asks whether a model belongs at all, where abstention-cost analysis begins. The ML lifecycle locates where the specification is written and re-tested. Data strategy and data acquisition fixes the population your bounds cover, the usual reason a bound stops being true. Labelling and annotation operationalises "acceptable". Model metrics: precision, recall, AUC lets you read a risk–coverage curve without a vendor steering you. What's different when the feature is a model extends this to release, support, pricing and liability.

Human-in-the-Loop vs Autonomy: where a person must confirm, and where the system may act

1. Two rooms, ten days apart

At 2:14 on the morning of 18 August 2026, an alert fired in the card-authorisation cluster of a mid-sized private bank in Chennai. The bank runs its operations on software from Lagaam Systems, a Bengaluru company whose product is an agent that watches infrastructure telemetry, diagnoses incidents and proposes a remediation — restart a stateless service, roll back a deployment, expand a volume, fail over a database. The agent diagnosed the fault in nineteen seconds and proposed a rollback. Then it waited. Lagaam's contract with each of its thirty-eight bank and NBFC customers requires an on-call engineer to approve every action before it executes. The engineer acknowledged the page at 2:21 and approved at 2:23. Authorisation failures ran for nine minutes, eight of them spent waiting for a person to agree with a conclusion the machine had reached in nineteen seconds.

Aniruddh Sathe, Lagaam's vice-president of product, had been assembling the case for a change all year. The agent proposed 5,900 remediations last quarter; engineers approved 94.4% of them at a median of twelve seconds from page to click. Median approval latency was 91 seconds in business hours and 7 minutes 40 seconds after midnight. An audit of 4,600 approved actions found 31 a senior reviewer later judged wrong — 0.67% — of which nine caused a second incident. Sathe's problem was not whether the agent was good enough, but that "good enough" is not one number: a wrong restart costs a few thousand rupees of latency; a wrong database failover costs twenty-two lakh and a data-loss conversation with the Reserve Bank's supervisors.

Ten days later, Dr. Shalini Bhagat faced the same question in another currency in Nashik. She is chief product officer of Muhaafiz Diagnostics, which runs sixty-two radiography vans and a hundred and forty partner labs screening for tuberculosis across Maharashtra and Telangana. Its model scores every chest film; eleven radiologists then read every film again and sign every report. At 1,900 scans a day the backlog had reached 4.5 days. Bhagat proposed auto-releasing as normal the 61% of films scoring below 0.05, which would cut the backlog under a day and put abnormal films in front of a radiologist three and a half days sooner. Dr. Ashok Rane, who leads the panel, refused to sign — not because the model was bad, but because a diagnostic conclusion goes out under a registered practitioner's name, and a missed cavitary lesion in a mill worker in Malegaon is not a rupee figure to trade against reporting latency.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Define the terms precisely, because the looseness in ordinary usage is where the bad decisions hide. Human-in-the-loop means an action does not take effect until a person acts: the output is a proposal and human assent is a precondition of execution. Human-on-the-loop means the system acts while a person monitors, retaining the ability to intervene or reverse within a window. Human-out-of-the-loop, or autonomy, means the system acts and nobody is positioned to intervene before the consequence lands; review, if any, is retrospective. The move that separates practitioners who settle this from those who argue about it forever is that these are settings for an action, not for a product — and one product routinely holds all three at once.

The vocabulary is borrowed. Sheridan and Verplank's 1978 taxonomy of levels of automation ran from "the computer offers no assistance" to "the computer acts autonomously and ignores the human." Lisanne Bainbridge's 1983 paper Ironies of Automation supplied the finding that still does most of the analytic work: automating the easy parts leaves the human responsible for the hard remainder while removing the practice that made them competent, and asks them to monitor a process that is almost never wrong — a task human attention performs badly. Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens generalised it in 2000 by splitting any task into four stages — acquire, analyse, decide, act — each automatable to a different degree. The framing entered AI product management when models began producing outputs finished enough to act on, and arrived carrying regulatory weight: the EU AI Act's Article 14, GDPR Article 22's right against solely automated decisions of legal effect, and in India a DPDP Act with no equivalent clause, leaving the RBI, CDSCO and the ICMR's biomedical AI guidance to set the expectation sectorally.

Four schools disagree, about propositions rather than vibes. The human-factors school after Bainbridge and Dekker signs: partial automation degrades the operator's ability to catch what it leaves behind, so a reviewer's catch rate depends on how much is automated; not adding an approval step makes a system safe. The function-allocation school signs: autonomy is set per stage and action class; not there is a correct level for a system as a whole. The expected-cost school signs: the boundary sits where expected cost of an uncaught error exceeds the full cost of review, including the cost imposed on whoever waits; not some decisions need a human signature whatever the arithmetic shows. The due-process school — Article 22, and Madeleine Elish's "moral crumple zone," the nominal human who absorbs blame without holding control — signs: a materially affected person is owed a human decision-maker; not beating the median human justifies autonomy. Sathe is an expected-cost man with function-allocation instincts; Rane is a due-process man being handed arithmetic.

3. Mechanics: the arithmetic experts actually run

Start with the naive break-even, then break it, because breaking it is where the expertise lives. For a class of actions let p be the probability the proposed action is wrong, C the cost when a wrong action executes uncaught, d the fraction of wrong proposals a reviewer actually catches, and cr the all-in cost of routing one case through review — reviewer time plus the cost borne by whoever waits. Review pays when d · p · C > cr, so the break-even error rate is p* = cr / (d · C). Two terms surprise people. d is never 1: Lagaam's shadow study put the on-call catch rate at 0.55 for restarts. And cr is dominated by latency, not salary — about ₹9,400 per night-time incident against ₹180 of engineer time.

The table is what a good practitioner can reconstruct; four refinements separate them from an expert. First, d is not constant but falls as automation rises: the proposals still reaching a human become a thinner slice, the reviewer's prior shifts toward "this will be fine," and vigilance decays. Lagaam has the measurement — where 40% of proposals ran unattended the catch rate on the rest was 0.71; in the two customers already at 85% it was 0.38. A declining d(a) makes total cost non-monotone in automation share, with its minimum well short of where the naive model puts it.

Second, the cases routed to humans are by construction the hard ones: if the gate triggers on low confidence, the human's accuracy on the deferred subset is their accuracy on cases the model found difficult, which are usually the cases people find difficult too. Muhaafiz measured it — on a blinded re-read of 2,400 archived films, radiologist miss rate was 2.9% above a score of 0.4 against 1.1% below 0.05. Deferral is itself a prediction, and needs its own metric: the risk–coverage curve. A team that cannot draw it does not know what its gate buys.

Third, the residual error rate inside an autonomous band must be measured, and measurement is priced: estimating a 0.6% rate to within ±0.3 points at 95% confidence needs about 2,550 blind re-reads per band per period, which Muhaafiz costed at ₹2.4 lakh a quarter. That is the price of the claim that autonomy is safe; a team unwilling to pay it is asserting rather than knowing. Fourth, instrument the boundary: override rate, time-to-decision, the share of overrides later judged correct, and drift in the case mix crossing the threshold. Lagaam's twelve-second median approval was Sathe's most informative number, and it appeared on no dashboard until he built one.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

State the conditions as testable claims. One: the action decomposes into classes with materially different costs of being wrong. True at Lagaam, where a factor of 370 separates a restart from a failover; only partly true at Muhaafiz, where cost varies less by action than by patient, which argues for gating on population rather than score. Two: the reviewer has information the system lacks. True for failover, where the engineer knows about the unlogged migration in another team's window; largely false for Muhaafiz's normal band, where the radiologist sees exactly the pixels the model saw — which is why Rane's objection must rest on accountability rather than accuracy. Three: review is fast relative to the cost of delay. False for both, and this is the condition teams most often assume without checking: eight minutes of authorisation failure and 4.5 days of tuberculosis backlog are review costs no business case had carried.

The idea actively misleads in three situations. At low volume — a hundred cases a day reviewed by the people who built the system — the value of the labelled disagreement swamps the arithmetic. When failures are correlated rather than independent, expected cost understates the tail: a hundred wrong actions from one bad deploy is one outage, not a hundred ₹6,000 events. And when the real question is who is answerable, a threshold produces a number that satisfies nobody and collapses the first time a case reaches a regulator.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Two-sided products break the symmetry the framework assumes. Peshkar Commerce, a Bengaluru marketplace for home-furnishing sellers, autonomously approves buyer refunds below ₹2,500 — cheap and reversible for the buyer, and simply a debit for the seller, who never reviewed it. The sum is clean only once you decide whose costs are in it. Peshkar kept buyer refunds autonomous but required review of any action debiting a seller more than 2% of trailing monthly payout, reasoning that its leverage over the two sides is unequal and the framework does not supply that judgement.

Regulated products relocate the question rather than answering it. CDSCO registration, the ICMR's biomedical AI guidance and the NMC's telemedicine framework all point at practitioner accountability; none forbids an auto-released normal result outright, but together they make the signature, not the accuracy, the contested object. The mature response is not to argue that the model beats a tired radiologist at 11 p.m. but to redesign the artifact: Muhaafiz's draft policy releases low-score films as a screening result with no abnormality detected rather than a diagnostic report, with a named radiologist accountable for the band policy instead of each film. Whether a regulator accepts that distinction is genuinely unsettled.

Hardware adds physics. Hukum Robotics runs autonomous mobile robots in third-party warehouses with one remote operator to fourteen units; on escalation the operator has about nine seconds to take control. Bainbridge's irony arrives literally — nine seconds cannot rebuild the awareness the robot accumulated over two minutes, so intervention is often worse than its default of stopping. Hukum's fix was to stop calling it supervision: the operator now picks among three pre-computed options, converting an unachievable control task into an achievable decision task.

At the organisational seam the pattern is consistent and rarely matches stated policy. The threshold is a number in a model team's config; the staffing that makes review real sits in an operations budget; "a human approves" is written by legal; nobody owns the joint object. What good companies actually do is give one named person the autonomy register — a row per action class, with its authority level, measured in-band error rate, date of last audit, and who would answer for it.

6. Nine things experts see that competent practitioners miss

Reviewer vigilance is endogenous. The obvious reading treats the gate as a filter with a fixed catch rate; its efficiency in fact depends on how much you automate. The tell-tale sign is median time-to-approval: when it collapses toward the time needed to read a summary line and click, the gate is a formality and its catch rate is far below the business case. Lagaam's twelve seconds is that sign, and it implies d must be re-measured whenever the threshold moves — which almost nobody does.

Review's cost lands on someone not in the room. Teams price review in staff-hours because staff-hours appear in a budget. Muhaafiz's 4.5-day backlog is a review cost borne by patients whose treatment starts later, and in expectation it is larger than the misses autonomy would add. The tell-tale sign is a business case whose review-cost line contains only salary. The obvious reading — that keeping a human is the cautious choice — fails wherever waiting is itself harmful, which covers most of health care, most of credit, and all of incident response.

Confidence and cost are different axes. Most gates trigger on model confidence, which orders cases by difficulty; what matters is the cost of being wrong, often uncorrelated with it. Lagaam's failover proposals are among the agent's most confident, because the diagnostic pattern is clear, and they are the ones that must stay gated. The tell-tale sign is one confidence threshold spanning action types. An expert gates on cost first and uses confidence to subdivide within a cost class.

Deferral is a prediction needing its own evaluation. Any team can produce a model's error rate; ask for the error rate among cases they route to humans, and the humans' accuracy on that subset, and most cannot. Without both, the gate's value is unknown — it may route hard cases to people who are also bad at them. The tell-tale sign is the missing risk–coverage curve; the safety-net reading assumes a competence nobody measured on the relevant population.

The unwatched band is the attacked band. From an adversary's view autonomy is published policy that says where to aim. Peshkar's in-band refund abuse moved from 0.8% to 6.2% in nine weeks while the overall rate barely twitched, because abuse migrated rather than grew. The tell-tale sign is divergence between in-band and out-of-band adverse rates; the obvious reading, that low-value actions are low-risk, ignores that value to the attacker is cumulative while the threshold is per transaction.

A nominal human relocates liability without conferring control. This is the moral crumple zone, common where approval exists because a customer's risk committee asked for it. The tell-tale sign: the approver sees the conclusion and a confidence score but not the evidence, cannot investigate in the time allowed, and is named in the audit trail anyway. The obvious reading is that the organisation retained control. It retained a defendant.

Reversibility is a property of the path, not the action. On paper a wrongly auto-released normal report is reversible, since the film is archived; in practice nobody re-reads a closed normal report, so that channel's utilisation is near zero. The tell-tale sign is a team that can describe how reversal would work but cannot say what share of wrong actions were actually reversed last quarter, and how fast. Design for the reversal that happens, not the one in the runbook.

Autonomy composes, and a gate at the end sees nothing. An agent chaining three steps each 99% correct is right end-to-end 97% of the time, and whoever approves only the final action reads an artifact whose provenance is invisible — they cannot distinguish a good conclusion from a good-looking one built on a bad step. The tell-tale sign is a single approval at the end of a chain. Experts gate where the evidence is still legible.

The gate's most valuable output is often data, not safety. Every override is a labelled disagreement between model and expert on a case that mattered — the scarcest evaluation data a team can get — and organisations that treat review purely as cost pay the reviewer and discard the label. The tell-tale sign is an override rate nobody reports and nobody has broken down by segment. Seen this way, review is sometimes worth keeping where the cost arithmetic says remove it, which is why early-stage teams should automate their gates away more slowly than the formula suggests.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the cost of a wrong autonomous action lands one user at a time and is usually reversible through support, which permits a further-right default: Ijazat Pay auto-schedules recurring bill payments below ₹5,000 and absorbs the rare wrong one as goodwill, because the alternative is a confirmation prompt 94% of users approve unread. In B2B and enterprise the buyer, not the user, sets the level, and enterprise autonomy limits are often procurement artifacts rather than risk judgements — Lagaam's approval clause began in a 2023 bank contract and was never revisited against evidence. Marketplaces add Peshkar's asymmetry: an autonomous action for one side creates an obligation for the other. In hardware, handover latency rather than cost sets the boundary. In AI-native products the distinctive feature is chaining, where the question shifts from "does a person approve this action" to "at which step is the evidence still legible."

Stage matters more than teams admit, and in the counter-intuitive direction. Early-stage companies should be slower to automate gates: volume is low, reviewers are the domain experts, and the disagreement data is worth more than the throughput. Growth-stage companies hit the transition where review cost dominates and the register must be built. Late-stage regulated companies earn each move rightward with audited evidence, and usually find the expensive part is not the model but the measurement apparatus nobody budgets for at the moment of decision.

8. Three worked examples

Lagaam, restarts. Moving 3,410 stateless-restart proposals a quarter to unattended execution removed a 91-second daytime and 7-minute-40-second night-time wait. Expected additional uncaught errors: 0.9% of 3,410 is 30.7 wrong restarts, of which review would have caught 55%, leaving 16.9 extra wrong restarts at ₹6,000 each, about ₹1.01 lakh. Latency saved, at ₹9,400 per gated night incident and less by day, came to roughly ₹94 lakh a quarter across the fleet. The decision was not close — and its not being close is the point, because teams argue hardest where the answer is most obvious.

Muhaafiz, the normal band. Of 1,900 daily scans, 61% (1,159) score below 0.05. Audited abnormal rate inside that band is 0.6%, about 7 missed abnormalities a day if auto-released; radiologist miss rate on the same band in blinded re-read is 1.1%, about 12.7 a day. Auto-release is therefore expected to reduce misses by roughly 5.7 a day while advancing every genuine abnormal read by 3.6 days. The panel still refused, because the model's misses cluster — under-exposed films from three vans, paediatric chests — where human misses scatter, and a systematic, attributable failure is a different institutional object from a scattered one even when it is smaller.

Peshkar, the failure. Auto-refunds below ₹2,500 launched in January 2026 at 11,400 a month, saving about ₹31 lakh a quarter in support cost. By late March an organised group had learned the threshold and was running ₹2,400 claims across thousands of accounts; in-band abuse went from 0.8% to 6.2% in nine weeks and leakage reached ₹1.1 crore before a finance reconciliation caught it. The failure was not the autonomy decision but that the threshold was per transaction while the exposure was per account and cumulative, and nobody watched the in-band rate separately. The recovery went the other way: instead of restoring review, Peshkar added a per-account autonomy budget capped against lifetime GMV, a weekly in-band anomaly review, and a rule dropping any account crossing its budget to human review for a quarter. Seven weeks later the product ran more autonomously than before, at a third of the abuse rate.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

The ceremonial gate. Warning sign: median approval time falls below the time needed to read the evidence and override rate drifts under 2%. Diagnostic question: what would an approver have to see to reject this, and can they see it in the time they have? Caught late, the cost is the credibility loss when a regulator finds the documented control never functioned.

Threshold decay. Warning sign: the case mix crossing the boundary shifts — more thin-file applicants, films from a newly commissioned van — while the threshold stays put. Diagnostic question: what is the audited in-band error rate this quarter against the quarter the threshold was justified? Caught late, it surfaces as an external complaint, after which every historical decision in the band becomes suspect.

Aggregate safety, segment harm. Warning sign: nobody can produce the in-band error rate for the segment least able to absorb a wrong outcome. Diagnostic question: for whom is this threshold least safe? Caught late, the cost is a fairness finding that is both true and unanswerable, because the data to rebut it was never collected.

Adversarial migration. Warning sign: in-band and out-of-band adverse rates diverge while the aggregate stays flat. Diagnostic question: if I knew your threshold, how would I make money? Caught late, as at Peshkar, the result is a crore-scale reconciliation surprise rather than a monitored cost.

Correlated autonomous failure. Warning sign: autonomous actions of one class cluster in time just after a model or prompt change. Diagnostic question: what is the blast radius of one bad deploy in the fifteen minutes before anyone notices? Caught late, a risk budget sized for independent events turns out to have been guarding events that were never independent.

10. Where the disagreement is real

The expected-cost position, steelmanned: every gate rations a scarce resource — expert attention — and refusing to quantify it hides the trade-off rather than avoiding it. Muhaafiz's backlog is the evidence: a policy justified as caution was producing measurable harm nobody counted. It rests on harms being commensurable, and would be wrong if some are genuinely lexical, or if the error distributions differ in kind — which is exactly Rane's claim.

The due-process position, steelmanned: who is answerable is prior to what fails more often, because institutions run on attributable responsibility and a statistical claim cannot be cross-examined. The evidence is a long record of automated systems whose accountability was never located failing in ways an accountable person would have been forced to anticipate. It would be wrong if the signature is fictional — if a radiologist signing 1,900 reports a day exercises no per-film judgement — in which case the honest move is to relocate accountability to the policy level and say so.

The autonomy-first position, steelmanned: pre-action approval is a weak, expensive control next to reversibility, sandboxing, blast-radius limits and fast detection; teams reach for gates because gates are cheap to specify, not because they work. Lagaam's own data supports it — a catch rate of 0.55 is a coin flip with a bill attached, while a rollback executing in four seconds recovers most of the cost of being wrong. It would be wrong wherever reversal is unavailable: a disbursed loan, a released clinical result, a collision. Which is why the camps talk past each other — they describe different action classes as though describing one product.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this argues about the product's autonomy level and quotes the spectrum. Someone who has internalised it asks within thirty seconds for the list of discrete actions the system can take, and will not discuss policy until the list exists. They ask the cost of being wrong before the accuracy number, because accuracy is uninterpretable without it. They treat the reviewer's catch rate as a measured quantity and are uncomfortable when it is assumed. They ask what review costs the person waiting. They know their override rate and read a falling one as a warning. They budget for the audit that substantiates the autonomy claim. Most tellingly, they can name who would answer for each band — and when they cannot, they treat that, not the threshold, as the open item.

12. What they decided

Sathe took the register to Lagaam's customer advisory board on 9 September. Restarts and node-pool scaling moved to unattended execution with a fifteen-minute blast-radius cap and automatic rollback; deployment rollbacks moved to unattended only where in-band error rate had been audited for two consecutive quarters; failover stayed gated regardless of confidence, with the approval screen rebuilt to show the three signals behind the diagnosis. He also began publishing median approval time and override rate to each customer's risk committee monthly, arguing that a gate whose effectiveness goes unreported is one nobody can defend.

Bhagat did not get her policy. What she got, on 11 September, was a six-month instrumented pilot in two districts: low-score films released as a screening result rather than a diagnostic report, a named radiologist accountable for the band policy, 2,550 blind re-reads a quarter, three under-performing vans excluded until their exposure calibration was fixed, and paediatric films excluded entirely. Rane's condition was that the pilot report miss rate by district and by van, never as a fleet average. It is not obvious that either of them has conceded anything.

Discussion question 1. Muhaafiz's data suggests auto-release would reduce total missed abnormalities. Is Rane's refusal a failure of nerve, or is he defending something the arithmetic cannot represent? What evidence would change your answer?

Discussion question 2. Lagaam's approval requirement came from a customer contract, not a risk analysis. Whose job is it to reopen a control that has become ceremonial, and what would you put in front of a bank's risk committee to do it?

Discussion question 3. Peshkar recovered by increasing autonomy while bounding cumulative exposure. Which of your own checkpoints are per-transaction controls guarding a cumulative risk, and what would the budgeted version look like?

13. Going deeper

  • AI product design choices — autonomy is one axis among several; the others stop you solving a trust problem with a gate.
  • Agent autonomy and consent — what changes when actions chain and the checkpoint has nowhere legible to sit.
  • Workflow design over interface design — the gate is a workflow decision; designing the screen first yields ceremonial approval.
  • Human review operations — staffing, queueing and fatigue set the catch rate the whole calculation rests on.
  • Reviewing work you did not write — the skill that makes a checkpoint real rather than a signature.
  • Disclosure, consent and what users are owed — knowing an action was autonomous changes the obligation, independent of accuracy.
  • Problem–model fit — no autonomy policy rescues a model aimed at the wrong prediction task.
  • The ML lifecycle — thresholds decay as data drifts; the lifecycle is where recalibration lives.
  • Data strategy and data acquisition — override data is often the highest-value data a team owns.
  • Labelling and annotation — the audited re-reads behind an autonomy claim are a labelling programme with a budget.
  • Model metrics: precision, recall, AUC — the operating point is the autonomy boundary in another vocabulary.
  • What's different when the feature is a model — probabilistic behaviour is why the boundary is re-argued every release.

Janmitra Network: Who Presses the Refund Button?

A teaching case on human-in-the-loop design versus autonomy

1. Opening

On Monday, 5 October 2026, Ananya Krishnan walked into the glass-walled steering room on the fourth floor of Janmitra Network's Bengaluru office with a single slide and a deadline. As head of product, she had to tell the steering committee by the end of the day whether the company's new AI dispute agent would be allowed to issue refunds on its own. If the answer was yes, the agent would go live on Monday, 19 October. That date mattered. Diwali fell on Sunday, 8 November, twenty days after go-live, and the festive weeks bring the year's heaviest dispute volumes.

The agent had just finished a thirty-day shadow pilot. It had read tickets, checked ledgers and written decisions, but a human had made every final call. Ananya had to decide where a person must confirm and where the system may simply act.

2. Company background

Janmitra Network, founded in 2019, sells UPI acceptance to small merchants: QR codes, voice-announcing soundbox devices, and next-day settlement into a bank account. Its 6.2 lakh merchants are mostly kirana stores, chemists, tea stalls and small restaurants across Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns. The company competes with PhonePe and Paytm on the counter, and with Razorpay for merchants who also sell online. All operate inside NPCI's rails and the RBI's turnaround-time norms for failed transactions.

The product is cheap, so the economics depend on cheap support. Merchants write in about double debits, payments that show on a customer's phone but not in the merchant's settlement, and wrongly deducted charges. In September 2026 the company received 48,000 refund-related tickets. A team of 26 agents in Jaipur resolved them with a median turnaround of nine hours (the AI agent needs under two minutes).

3. The situation

Six months earlier, the product team had built an AI agent on a large language model. For each ticket the agent reads the merchant's message, pulls the transaction trail from the ledger, decides whether to refund, reject or escalate, and, if permitted, triggers the payout. During the pilot, from 1 to 30 September, it did everything except the payout. A human reviewer compared its decision with the case file and made the final call.

Exhibit 1 shows what the team found. The pilot defined an error as a recommended payout that was wrong in amount or in eligibility, and treated a wrongly paid refund as unrecoverable, because the money leaves to a customer's bank account. Across 48,000 tickets the agent made 908 such errors, an overall rate of 1.89 per cent. But the rate was not flat. Small refunds under ₹500 went wrong one time in a hundred; refunds above ₹10,000 went wrong eight times in a hundred, and those few cases carried most of the money at risk.

In Mumbai, the risk team worried about the tail: one wrongly paid ₹22,000 refund can become a regulatory conversation, and the DPDP Act adds duties around automated decisions.

4. The people

Arvind Menon, chief executive, Bengaluru. He wants full autonomy before Diwali. Zomato and Swiggy have taught Indians to expect instant resolution, and he fears a nine-hour wait pushes merchants to PhonePe.

Anirudh Pillai, machine-learning lead, Pune. He wants the agent to act wherever it is reliably right.

Rukmini Nambiar, head of risk and compliance, Mumbai. She wants a person to confirm any payout whose failure she could not explain to the RBI or to an angry merchant, and she wants an audit trail either way.

Rohit Bhatia, head of support operations, Jaipur. He wants his team's judgement used where it matters, and is candid that reviewing 72,000 tickets in a festive month would turn careful people into people who click “approve” without reading.
