Design A runs cheapest but carries the largest losses; design B breaks just as Diwali arrives; design C costs least but needs someone to decide where the line sits.

6. The options

Option 1: Full autonomy from 19 October. The agent issues every refund. Merchants get answers in minutes. The cost is ₹45.17 lakh a month of expected leakage, concentrated in a few large cases, and an audit trail that shows no human judgement behind errors.

Option 2: Keep a human on every refund. The agent drafts and a person confirms. Leakage falls to ₹4.52 lakh and Rukmini sleeps well. But the design costs ₹18.24 lakh a month in review, leaves the team 13 agents short in the festive month, and the nine-hour wait would shrink only modestly. Rubber-stamping threatens the assumed 90 per cent catch rate.

Option 3: Split by stakes. The agent acts alone on refunds up to ₹2,000 and queues the larger ones for a person. This captures most of the speed, 85 per cent of tickets resolved in minutes, and puts human attention on the 15 per cent that hold about 91 per cent of the money at risk. The cost is a judgement call that must be defended: the threshold, who owns it, and how it changes as evidence accumulates.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Why does the average error rate of 1.89 per cent mislead, and what does Exhibit 1 show that the average hides?

2. Using Exhibits 3 and 4, why does Option 2 fail in the festive month even though it is the safest on paper?

3. Beyond rupees, what makes an action one a person should confirm: reversibility, regulatory exposure, the customer's vulnerability, or the agent's own confidence? Rank them for Janmitra.

4. If you chose Option 3, what would you monitor in the first thirty days, and what result would make you move the threshold up or down?

8. A note for the learner

This topic frames autonomy as a design choice made per action, not per product: how costly is a wrong action, can it be undone, how often is the system wrong at each level of stakes, and what does a reviewer add? A person in the loop helps when looking at cases that matter and harms when asked to approve everything.

A defensible path is Option 3, introduced as a staged rollout. Go live on 19 October with autonomy for refunds up to ₹2,000, where Exhibit 1 shows error rates of 1 to 2 per cent and each mistake costs ₹300 to ₹1,200. Route everything above ₹2,000 to the Jaipur team, who will see 10,800 tickets in the festive month and need only about six agents. Audit 2 per cent of autonomous decisions: 1,224 checks of 61,200 festive tickets, under one agent's load. At September volumes, 816 audits at ₹38 add about ₹0.31 lakh a month. Monthly cost becomes about ₹11.39 lakh, still a quarter of the ₹45.17 lakh that full autonomy risks.

The reasoning is that human judgement is scarce, so it should go where one error costs ₹22,000, not ₹300. Rukmini gets an explainable boundary, Arvind gets minutes-level resolution for most merchants, Anirudh gets a route to a higher threshold, and Rohit's team does the work needing judgement. The line is a hypothesis: if audited accuracy in the ₹501 to ₹2,000 band holds near 98 per cent through Diwali, test a higher ceiling; if it slips, lower it.

Human-in-the-Loop vs Autonomy

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Meher Chalke, head of product for lending decisions at Faisla Credit, a Pune-based non-banking financial company, sat in a glass conference room with a spreadsheet she had built at eleven the night before. Faisla had spent fourteen months building an underwriting assistant: a large language model that read salary slips, bank statements and GST filings, drafted a credit memo, and recommended approve, decline or refer. Loan officers had used it as a co-pilot since March, reading every memo before acting on it. Volume was the problem now. Faisla's application count had grown from forty a day to just under four hundred, and the fourteen underwriters on staff were reading memos, not writing them, at a pace that made the assistant feel like theatre rather than help. The chief risk officer wanted the system to auto-approve the applications it was confident about and route only the rest to a human. The head of the underwriting desk wanted every decision touched by a person, full stop, citing a wrongful-decline complaint that had reached the Reserve Bank of India's ombudsman channel two months earlier. Both were right about something. Meher's job that week was to decide, loan-bucket by loan-bucket, where the system could act on its own and where a person had to look first — and to be able to defend that line to the board, to the regulator and to the underwriters whose jobs would change because of it.

The idea

Human-in-the-loop versus autonomy is the design decision about which actions an AI system may take by itself and which actions require a person to review, approve or reject them before they take effect. It is not a binary switch. It is a spectrum of how much of the loop — sense, decide, act — a machine is allowed to close without a human in it, and the decision is made separately for every action a system can take, not once for the whole product. The idea has a long lineage in aviation and industrial automation, where "human-in-the-loop," "human-on-the-loop" and "human-out-of-the-loop" were used from the 1990s onward to describe how much a pilot or operator supervised an automated system versus monitored it versus was absent from it entirely. The framing was imported wholesale into AI product management once generative models became capable of producing outputs — text, code, decisions — that looked finished enough to act on directly, and product teams needed a disciplined way to decide when "looks finished" was good enough to skip a human check. The sentence Meher could say in the boardroom without sounding glib is this: autonomy should be granted action by action, in proportion to how wrong the system can be and how expensive that wrongness is, not granted to the product as a whole.

How it actually works

Practitioners who use this idea well move through four steps, and the two that get skipped are the third and the fourth. First, they decompose the product into discrete actions rather than treating "the AI feature" as one thing — for Faisla that meant separating "draft the credit memo," "approve a loan," "decline a loan" and "flag for fraud review" into four actions, each capable of sitting at a different point on the spectrum. Second, for each action they score two independent variables: reversibility, meaning how cheaply a wrong outcome can be undone once it has happened, and stakes, meaning what a wrong outcome costs in money, safety or trust if it is not caught. A drafted memo a human reads before anything happens is fully reversible and low stakes; an approved loan already disbursed is expensive to reverse and high stakes if the applicant defaults or the approval was discriminatory. Third — the step people skip — they set an explicit confidence or evidence threshold deciding which cases even qualify for reduced human involvement, because "the model is usually right" is not a policy, a number is. Fourth, also frequently skipped, they instrument the boundary itself: every case that crosses from automatic to human-reviewed, and every case a human overrides, gets logged and looked at on a cadence, because a threshold correct in March is not guaranteed to still be correct in September once the applicant mix or fraud patterns have changed. Skipping steps three and four is how a "human-in-the-loop" system quietly becomes an unaccountable autonomous one: the human is nominally there, but no one has defined what triggers their attention, so they rubber-stamp everything the model already decided.

A worked example

Faisla's assistant scores every application with a confidence number between 0 and 1, built from how well the extracted financial data matched the applicant's stated income and how similar the case was to historical loans with a known good or bad outcome. Meher's spreadsheet started with the policy already running informally at a 0.92 threshold: cases scoring 0.92 or above were auto-approved with no human read, cases below were sent to an underwriter. Of the 400 daily applications, 210 scored at or above 0.92. Faisla's own audit of the model's decisions over the prior eight weeks found that 1.4% of cases in that top band were later found to be wrong on manual re-check — mostly income mismatches the model had waved through. Applying 1.4% to 210 gives roughly 2.9 wrongly auto-approved loans a day, each averaging ₹1.8 lakh in disbursed principal, for an expected daily bad-loan exposure near ₹5.3 lakh, against a fully-staffed review cost of roughly ₹350 per case saved. The remaining 190 applications went to fourteen underwriters, each reading twelve to fourteen memos a day at an average eleven minutes per case — workable, but it left no slack for the fraud-flagged cases that needed twenty minutes each. Meher then ran a second pass at a 0.85 threshold, the number the risk officer had proposed. At 0.85, 274 applications qualified for auto-approval, freeing underwriter time, but the same audit data showed the error rate in the 0.85–0.92 band was 4.1%, more than double the top band's rate; applied to the additional 64 auto-approved cases, that is roughly 2.6 more wrong approvals a day, pushing expected daily bad-loan exposure to about ₹9.8 lakh — nearly double — while saving nineteen underwriter-hours across the desk. The arithmetic showed the two policies were not "safer" and "faster" in the abstract; they were two different, quantified trades between rupees at risk and hours saved, and the board could pick one only once it had both numbers in front of it, not a vague sense that 0.85 "should be fine."

The nuances

Reversibility is not the same as low stakes

A drafted email a person reads before sending is reversible and usually low stakes, but a drafted credit memo that a distracted underwriter approves without a careful read is reversible in principle — someone could revisit the file — and high stakes in practice, because no one actually revisits closed loan files. Design the human checkpoint for how reversal actually happens, not how it could theoretically happen.

"Human-in-the-loop" is routinely confused with "human-reviewed-eventually"

A system that logs every auto-decision for a monthly audit has a human near the loop, not in it; the loan has already disbursed by the time anyone looks. True human-in-the-loop means the action does not complete until the person acts. Anything after the action completes is oversight, a different and weaker control.

Thresholds decay

A confidence score calibrated on March's applicant mix drifts as the mix changes — more gig-economy income statements, a new fraud pattern, a festival-season surge of first-time borrowers. A threshold is a hypothesis about the present, not a permanent setting; it needs a recalibration date on the calendar, not just a value in a config file.

Model confidence is not the same as correctness

A language model can be highly confident and wrong, especially on cases that resemble its training data in surface form but differ in the fact that matters — a salary slip formatted like a hundred genuine ones but attached to a fabricated employer. Confidence measures pattern familiarity, not truth, so the threshold should be validated against audited outcomes, never against the model's own stated certainty alone.

Autonomy on one action can quietly expand autonomy on another

Faisla's fraud team assumed the 0.92-and-above bucket was low-risk, but a fraud ring that learns what a clean-looking application looks like will target exactly that bucket, because it is the one nobody reads. Raising autonomy on an approval decision without separately re-examining the fraud-detection action attached to it is how a system's weakest control becomes its most exploited one.

Who bears the cost of a wrong autonomous action is a design input, not an afterthought

If the applicant bears the cost of a wrongful decline — a missed festival-season working-capital loan — the bar for autonomy should be higher than if Faisla alone bears the cost of a wrongful approval it can absorb. The Reserve Bank of India's Fair Practices Code and the fair-lending expectations built into it exist precisely because that cost has historically landed asymmetrically on the applicant.

A single autonomy setting cannot be right for every applicant segment

The 1.4% and 4.1% error rates were desk-wide averages; Faisla's later analysis found the error rate for first-time borrowers with thin credit files was nearly three times the desk average inside the very same confidence band, because the model had less reliable historical pattern to match against. A threshold that looks safe in aggregate can be quietly unsafe for the segment with the least ability to absorb a wrong decision.

The idea tells you where to put the checkpoint, not what a good decision looks like

Human-in-the-loop versus autonomy is a governance framework, not a quality framework. Getting the boundary right does not make the underlying model good at underwriting; it only ensures that when the model is wrong, someone is positioned to catch it before the loan disburses. The two problems — is the model good, and is the boundary right — have to be solved separately.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace, and company stage

In a consumer product, the cost of a wrong autonomous action is usually borne one user at a time and is often reversible by a support ticket — a mis-recommended playlist or a wrongly auto-filled address is annoying, not ruinous — so consumer products can typically tolerate a further-right position on the spectrum, provided the failure mode is never physical or financial harm. In a B2B product like Faisla's, one wrong action can carry regulatory exposure and a customer relationship, which pushes the sensible default left, toward human approval, especially for anything that disburses money or touches a regulated disclosure. In a marketplace product the calculus gets a third layer: an autonomous action taken on behalf of one side — auto-matching a buyer to a seller, auto-adjusting a price — creates an obligation to the other side that neither end necessarily reviewed, so marketplaces often need a checkpoint because the platform itself is exposed. Company stage matters too: an early-stage team with thin support capacity can often justify pushing further toward autonomy earlier, accepting a higher error rate in exchange for speed and the labelled data that reviewing every case would not generate fast enough, while an established company with a regulator relationship and a fixed error budget typically has to earn the right to move right on the spectrum, action by action, with an audit trail to show for it.

Common mistakes

Treating "human-in-the-loop" as a single product-wide badge. Symptom: a team says "we're human-in-the-loop" as if that settles every action in the product. Underlying error: autonomy was never decomposed to the action level, so some genuinely low-stakes step gets a human bottleneck it doesn't need, while a genuinely high-stakes step hides inside the same badge unexamined. Cheapest diagnostic: list every action the system can take and ask, for each one, who currently reviews it and what triggers that review — a badge that cannot answer this for every row on the list is not a policy.

Setting the threshold once and never revisiting it. Symptom: the error rate inside the auto-approved band creeps upward over successive months without anyone noticing until an external complaint surfaces it. Underlying error: the threshold was treated as a launch decision rather than a live control. Cheapest diagnostic: pull the audited error rate inside the auto-approved band every month and compare it to the number that justified the threshold at launch.

Confusing a human reading the output with a human able to catch the error. Symptom: underwriters approve nearly everything the model recommends, so the human step exists on paper but changes nothing in practice. Underlying error: the reviewer was given the model's conclusion and its confidence, not the raw evidence, so they have nothing independent to check it against. Cheapest diagnostic: measure the override rate — the share of cases where the human's decision differs from the model's recommendation; a rate near zero for months usually means review, not judgment, is happening.

What good looks like

A comparable NBFC handled this well the year before: it kept every loan-approval decision above ₹5 lakh in the human-approve band regardless of model confidence, moved only the memo-drafting step to full autonomy, and built the underwriter's screen to show the three numbers the model's confidence score was built from — income-match score, document-anomaly score and applicant history match — rather than a single confidence percentage, so a reviewer could see which input was weak and use judgment specific to that weakness. It recalibrated its threshold quarterly against audited outcomes, published the override rate to its own board every month, and treated a rising override rate as a signal to investigate the model rather than a nuisance to route around. Nothing about that setup eliminated errors; it made every remaining error visible to someone positioned to catch it before it became a disbursed rupee.

Closing

Meher's decision, presented to the board that Thursday, kept memo-drafting fully autonomous, moved loan approval under ₹3 lakh to an approve-to-act model with a 0.94 threshold recalibrated monthly against audited outcomes, and kept every approval above ₹3 lakh and every first-time-borrower case in the human-approve band regardless of score, with the override rate reported to the risk committee monthly. The reasoning she gave was not that 0.94 was safer than 0.85 in the abstract, but that Faisla could not yet show the board an error rate broken out by applicant segment, and until it could, the more conservative line was the only one she could defend to a regulator asking why a first-time borrower with a thin file had been auto-declined. The next idea worth her attention is agent autonomy and consent — what changes once the system is not just deciding but acting across multiple steps and systems, chaining actions in a way that makes the checkpoint harder to place at all. Two questions worth sitting with: for an action in your own product, do you know the audited error rate inside the band you have already made autonomous, broken out by the segment least able to absorb a wrong decision — and if a regulator or a customer asked you to justify where you drew that line, could you show them a number, or only a feeling?

Yugantar Industries: What Kasauti May Do Alone

A teaching case on autonomy and the human in the loop, set in Indian contract food manufacturing. The case does not resolve.

1. Sunday night, Pune

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday, 11 October 2026, Sharmila Raikar was still at the dining table of her flat in Baner, Pune, with three printouts weighted down by a cold cup of chai. She was Chief Product Officer of Yugantar Industries, and in ten hours she had to tell the board's operations sub-committee what the company's inline inspection system, Kasauti, would be permitted to do without a human pressing anything.

The question had a precise shape. Kasauti looked at every pack on four lines across three plants and wrote an opinion on every batch: hold, or release. Today an officer read that opinion and signed. Tomorrow Sharmila had to say where the signature was worth its cost and where the machine should simply act — on a pack, on a batch, and on the line itself, which Kasauti could halt.

The timing was not hers to choose. Yugantar made other companies' biscuits, sauces and beverage powders, and its customers' last festive dispatch date was Sunday, 25 October — fourteen days away. Diwali fell on Sunday, 8 November, twenty-seven days after the meeting. Between now and then the plants would run the heaviest fortnight of their year.

2. How Yugantar got here

Yugantar Industries began in 1996 as a job-work unit in Nashik, filling pickle jars for a Mumbai trading house. Thirty years later it ran three plants — sauces at Nashik, biscuits and extruded snacks at Hosur, beverage powders at Indore — on revenue of ₹1,340 crore in the year to 31 March 2026 at an EBITDA margin of 9.2 per cent, or ₹123.28 crore. Almost all of it was other people's brands. Contract manufacturing runs on thin margins and borrowed reputation: a defect that reaches a shelf damages a customer's brand, and the remedy is written into the contract.

One decision from 2021 shaped everything Sharmila could now propose. To standardise the plants cheaply, Yugantar signed a seven-year exclusive supply agreement with Drishtikon Edge Systems for cameras and edge controllers, running to 31 March 2028. It locked in two-megapixel sensors on the two Hosur lines, commissioned first; Nashik and Indore were later fitted with five-megapixel heads under a variation clause Drishtikon has declined to extend. Hosur also still ran the 2019 manufacturing-execution system, which exported batch genealogy once a day at 06:00, while Nashik and Indore moved to a streaming data layer in 2024. Kasauti therefore saw Hosur through older glass and yesterday's records — and Hosur was more than half the company's batches.

3. The industry around the decision

Indian packaged food had been reorganised by speed. Quick-commerce platforms such as Zepto, Swiggy Instamart and BigBasket had compressed replenishment cycles, and brand owners pushed that compression onto their contract manufacturers. Reliance Retail's private labels, Amul's ambient range and the shadow of Parle and Britannia on the biscuit shelf meant a brand owner with a short-dated consignment had alternatives within a week.

Regulation pulled the other way. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India licensed every plant and required documented release under its hygiene schedules; the company's BRCGS certification, needed for export listings, required release to be authorised by a named, trained person with authority to withhold. Nothing said a model could not form the opinion; everything assumed somebody signed.

Yugantar's exposure went beyond India. Private-label sauces and snack packs moved through Safwan Foods Trading, a distributor in Jeddah, and a British grocery chain was qualifying a Manchester-warehoused listing. The quality system was audited by people in another time zone who read procedures, not dashboards.

Figure A. Sites, teams and markets. The two lines on older cameras sit at the plant that carries most of the volume.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The board approved ₹7.40 crore of capex for Kasauti in July 2025, on a case promising fewer escapes and a smaller quality-assurance headcount. By 30 September 2026 ₹6.15 crore had been spent, leaving ₹1.25 crore that lapses on 31 March 2027.

A pilot ran at Nashik from January 2026 and looked excellent. The team then ran a shadow trial on all four lines for the sixty-one days from 1 August to 30 September 2026. Kasauti inspected every pack and wrote a verdict on every batch, but an officer adjudicated each flag and signed every release. Exhibit 1 reports the pack-level results, Exhibit 2 the batch-level ones.

Three beliefs held in August did not survive September. The first was that precision would be roughly uniform. It was not: Kasauti was right about eighty-five per cent of the packs it flagged on the five-megapixel lines and about sixty per cent at Hosur, where crumb shadow on printed film reads like a seal defect at two megapixels. The second was that the trial produced clean labels. In mid-September Vikram Sabharwal's team found the adjudication screen showed Kasauti's verdict and confidence to the officer before she recorded her own, so every agreement number in Exhibit 2 may be agreement with a suggestion. The screen changed on 21 September, nine days before the trial ended — too little data to measure the difference.

The third belief was that the holds Kasauti recommended were nearly all real. They were not. Of the 254 batch holds Kasauti recommended in the window, quality assurance confirmed 146, or 57.5 per cent, and overturned the rest after retesting. Each overturned hold still cost a retest, a repack and a day of delay. And two counts of the same thing disagree, unresolved — see the footnote to Exhibit 2.

Figure B. The shadow window ran 61 days, from 1 August to 30 September 2026.

5. The people

Sharmila Raikar, Chief Product Officer, Pune. She owns Kasauti and must recommend on Monday. Her position: autonomy is decided action by action, not plant by plant. She has not told the committee that the FY2027 plan she signed assumes a ₹9 crore run-rate benefit from Kasauti, nor that she believes the shadow labels are contaminated.

Satyen Dholakia, Managing Director, Pune. He wants full autonomy on at least two lines before the festive fortnight, and speaks of the Manchester listing needing "a digital quality story". He is not saying that a minority investor's exit talks lean on the digitisation narrative.

Vandana Kirtane, Head of Quality Assurance, Nashik. She insists a qualified person releases every batch, citing BRCGS and the customer contract. Her incentive is her department's survival. She is not saying eleven of her twenty-six officers are on contracts ending 31 December 2026, nor that her time study, if accepted, would prove her nine officers short — a case she has lost twice.

He is not saying the model version was fine-tuned partly on Kasauti's own accepted verdicts, so its agreement with past human decisions is not independent.

7. Voices

"Sixty per cent precision is not a model failure, it is a two-megapixel sensor failure. Give me the cameras the 2021 contract will not let us buy and this argument disappears. Until then, do not ask me to defend Hosur."

Vikram Sabharwal, Bengaluru, in the architecture review of 6 October 2026

"The contract says a qualified person releases. Not a qualified system. If we automate release at Hosur and the Rotterdam auditor reads the procedure in January, the finding is not a slap on the wrist, it is the Manchester listing."

Vandana Kirtane, email to Sharmila Raikar and Satyen Dholakia, 8 October 2026

"Thirty unjustified stops in two months. The operators have started calling Kasauti the nervous uncle. Take the stop button away from it and I will support everything else."

Sushant Talwalkar, Hosur, on the operations call of 9 October 2026

"Please do not read Exhibit 5 as a ranking. Change one in three to one in six and design A beats design C. I cannot tell you which is right. I can tell you the number was not measured."

Vaishnavi Dandekar, chat thread, 10 October 2026

"Jeddah does not care about our seal-defect curve. They care that the stock arrived with four weeks of shelf life. Holding more batches would have made that worse, not better."

Shireen Contractor, Mumbai, replying to the same thread

"We have spent six crore. I have told the board it pays back next year. I am not asking you to be reckless. I am asking you to be done."

Virendra Pathak, Pune, to Sharmila Raikar, 10 October 2026

8. The options as Sharmila currently frames them

Design A — full autonomy on all four lines. Kasauti holds and releases, and quality assurance audits a sample afterwards. It is the only design that frees the department before the festive fortnight. Exhibit 5 puts it at ₹230.57 lakh for October, the dearest of the four, and almost two-thirds of that is the escape line, which rests on Vaishnavi's unmeasured assumption. It may also be unavailable: contract and certification both speak of a person.

Design B — the status quo. Exhibit 5 makes it the cheapest at ₹92.52 lakh, which is the most uncomfortable fact in the pack, because ₹138.05 lakh a month separates it from design A. But Exhibit 4 says it needs 53.2 per cent of the department's October hours for sign-off alone, on top of 62 per cent of other work. The design that costs least on paper cannot be staffed, and an officer signing a hundred batches a day is not reviewing them.

Design C — autonomy where the cameras are good. Autonomy at Nashik and Indore, human sign-off at Hosur: ₹119.11 lakh, and it halves the sign-off burden. Its logic is that trust follows measured precision. Its weakness is that the boundary was drawn in 2021 by a procurement decision, not by any judgement about which batches matter. Hosur also makes the lowest-value batches, so the design puts human attention on the cheapest product.

Design D — the machine may stop, only a person may start. Kasauti holds autonomously everywhere and quality assurance decides every release. It is the most conservative reading of the asymmetry between a reversible action and an irreversible one, and at ₹142.36 lakh it buys nothing: it keeps the whole sign-off load and adds ₹49.83 lakh of holds a person then undoes. Exhibit 6 suggests it would also stop the Hosur lines about thirty times in two months for no reason.

Sharmila's note at the bottom of the third printout read: all four are organised by plant or by direction, none by what the action costs if wrong. Nothing in the pack asked whether a defect on a bottle of chilli sauce for a Nashik depot deserves the same ceremony as one on a beverage powder going to Jeddah, or whether the reviewer should see Kasauti's verdict at all.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The sub-committee meets at 9:30 a.m. on Monday, 12 October 2026, with Sharmila's recommendation the second item. Whatever is agreed must be configured and validated before the last festive dispatch on 25 October, thirteen days later.

The constraints do not move. The Drishtikon agreement runs to 31 March 2028, so Hosur keeps two-megapixel cameras. The Hosur manufacturing-execution system exports once a day at 06:00, so any autonomous batch decision there is made on a stale genealogy. The master supply agreement with Madhurima Foods, renewed for three years on 1 April 2026, allows six quality incidents a contract year before a two per cent rebate on annual billings; Yugantar billed Madhurima ₹412 crore in FY2026, so the rebate is worth ₹8.24 crore, and four incidents are already logged in the six months to 30 September 2026. Eleven of twenty-six quality-assurance officers hold contracts expiring 31 December 2026, and renewing them will be read as a verdict on Kasauti. The unspent ₹1.25 crore of capex lapses on 31 March 2027.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1's blended precision of 68.3 per cent conceal, and which single row of that exhibit should change the design most?
  2. Exhibit 5 makes design B the cheapest and Exhibit 4 makes it unstaffable. Which exhibit is the more reliable guide, and what would you need to see to settle it?
  3. The adjudication screen showed Kasauti's verdict before the officer recorded hers. What does that do to the 57.5 per cent agreement figure in Exhibit 2, and to the 86.5 per cent recall in Exhibit 1?
  4. Design D treats "hold" as the safe direction. Is a hold reversible in a plant running at festive volume with a dispatch date thirteen days away? What would make the asymmetry hold or fail?
  5. Autonomy here is split by plant. Propose a different axis — action, value, reversibility, customer, confidence — and say what it would cost Yugantar to measure well enough to defend to the Rotterdam auditor.
  6. What should Sharmila recommend on Monday morning, given that Exhibit 2's own counts disagree by twenty-five batches, and what exactly should she say to the board about what she does not know?

Sunday night, continued

At a quarter to one Sharmila wrote out a fifth design, drawing the line by batch value and customer rather than by plant, then stopped: she had no measurement of Kasauti's precision at that cut, and thirteen days to find one. She thought about Vandana's eleven contracts, about the word person in the customer agreement, and about the cheapest column in Exhibit 5 belonging to the design nobody believed could survive Diwali. She turned off the lamp without writing a recommendation.
case40v1-aipm.ml.lifecycle:
Ganana Services: The Sieve That Stopped Catching

The companies named are fictional; the market and regulation around them are real.

1. Sunday night, 18 October 2026, Hyderabad

The board sub-committee call was at nine the next morning, and Nalini Vasireddy had been staring at the same two charts since dinner. She was chief product officer of Ganana Services, and both charts described one product, from one database, over the same nine months. One said the model had wobbled and was recovering; the other that it had slid every month since January, faster each month. Both came from her own team.

Twelve days earlier, on Tuesday 6 October, Chambal Power Distribution Nigam had invoked clause 9.4: two consecutive quarters below a 35 per cent strike rate gave it the right to terminate on sixty days' notice. Counted from 6 October, that notice expires on 5 December 2026. Chambal pays ₹350 lakh a year. Rohilkhand Vidyut Vitaran Nigam, at ₹456 lakh, renews on 31 December, seventy-four days after tonight; its strike rate has also fallen below its 40 per cent guarantee in two successive quarters, though not below 35.

Niteen Abhyankar, her co-founder and chief executive, wanted one slide: what are we doing, what does it cost, when does the number turn. Nalini had four answers and no confidence in the question. What she could not yet say aloud was that she no longer trusted the measurement the argument rested on. If the strike rate was computed across mismatched windows, every meeting since July had argued about an artefact.

2. Ganana Services, 2017 to 2026

Ganana was founded in Hyderabad in March 2017 by Abhyankar, a former distribution-loss consultant, and a data scientist who left in 2020. Its single product, Chhanni — a sieve — scores every metered connection a utility monitors and returns a monthly ranked list where consumption suggests meter tampering, direct hooking, or an unmetered commercial load behind a domestic meter. The vigilance cell inspects; on a confirmed irregularity the utility raises an assessment under the Electricity Act, 2003 and recovers arrears. Chhanni costs ₹19 to ₹26 per monitored connection a year; a confirmed case yields an average assessment of ₹18,400. Exhibit 1 sets out the eleven contracts, 86 lakh monitored connections and ₹1,821 lakh of annual recurring revenue.

One decision from 2021 shapes everything available tonight. To win Rohilkhand — then transformative for a forty-person company — Ganana agreed to run Chhanni inside the utility's own data centre, with no consumption data leaving it. Four later contracts copied the clause. So there is no central training corpus, only nine on-premise installations exporting a monthly aggregate file: counts, bucketed feature distributions and inspection outcomes at feeder level, never connection level. Bengaluru has never seen a row from the two largest clients. Retraining the model means something different at each client, and at two it means asking a utility's IT staff to run a script on a Thursday evening (Figure 2).

3. The industry

Cutting distribution losses has been national policy for a decade, and the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme has funded a very large prepaid smart-meter rollout through REC and PFC. That rollout created Ganana's market: interval consumption data arriving daily, where before a monthly reading on a card. Between April 2024 and March 2026 the connections Ganana monitored rose from 31 lakh to 86 lakh, up 177 per cent, most of it newly metered.

The field is uneven. Private licensees such as Tata Power and Torrent Power run their own loss analytics and are not customers. Integrators — Infosys, TCS, L&T — bid for the whole metering stack and treat analytics as a line item, so Ganana sometimes sub-contracts on tenders it would rather win. Meter makers bundle crude tamper alerts free, so a chairman may ask why he pays ₹21 a connection for a second opinion. Ganana's answer is empirical: the list converts. On the June cohort in Exhibit 2, the month's fee was ₹151.75 lakh and assessments against confirmed cases from that month's flags came to ₹2,203.22 lakh, 14.5 times the fee.

Two regulatory facts bear on tonight. Consumption data is personal data under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which made the on-premise clause easy to insist on and hard to argue away. And state commissions watch closely how vigilance inspections are conducted; a disputed inspection becomes a consumer-forum matter, and an embarrassed utility turns cautious about whom it visits. That is the thread running through June. Abroad, Prabodh Chitale, the international lead in Amsterdam, has a paid pilot with a privately operated utility in Manila and an invitation to a tender in Accra; both want a documented, auditable retraining process, and neither has asked what the architecture is. What Prabodh has not told Bengaluru is that his Manila pilot runs on a model a Pune contractor built for him privately, outside Prashant Dandekar's team.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Chhanni 3, running today at every client, was trained in January 2024 on data to 31 December 2023. Since then it has had calibration refreshes — the cutoff moved, features and weights untouched — most recently in October 2025 at some clients, later at others, as Exhibit 6 records. Nobody inside the company calls that a retrain; until September every slide did.

On Saturday 14 February 2026 Rohilkhand's metering head completed a firmware upgrade across 9.2 lakh connections, 38 per cent of that utility's 24 lakh, changing interval data from 30-minute to 15-minute blocks. Ganana's pipeline, which expects 30-minute blocks, averaged each pair — and averaging halves the measured variance of the night-time spikiness feature Chhanni weights most heavily. Nobody noticed for 223 days (Figure 1). Pranali Sirsikar found it on Friday 25 September, writing a data-quality script for an unrelated purpose.

On Tuesday 9 June a consumer forum heard a complaint about a Chambal inspection at a small commercial premises. The matter was procedural and the utility handled it properly, but from 1 July Chambal's vigilance cell required a second approval before inspecting commercial and industrial connections on the list, which in practice stopped them. Those were 9 per cent of Chambal's flags and confirmed at roughly twice the domestic rate. Rohilkhand restricted similarly in July. Across the portfolio the share of flags dispatched fell from 70 per cent in the first half to 61 per cent from July — visible in Exhibit 4, invisible in Exhibit 3, which is what clients see.

On Friday 24 July Nupur Sathaye escalated in writing: three clients had raised the strike rate in reviews. Prashant replied that July looked soft because inspections close late in the monsoon. On the dashboard, in August, the rate did recover, from 38.5 to 39.4 per cent. On 3 September Chambal's quarterly review put its first-quarter figure at 34.6 per cent; on 6 October the letter arrived. The team now believes, and cannot prove, that August was no recovery: Lucknow's backlog cleared in the second week and a block of older, better cases closed then. Exhibit 3 divides confirmations by inspections closed in the same calendar month, whatever month the flag was issued; Exhibit 4 groups the same inspections by flag month. Measured the second way, no month since January has improved on the one before.

5. The people

Nalini Vasireddy, chief product officer, Hyderabad, owns the recommendation. She holds that the company cannot fix what it cannot measure, and has argued for two years that her group be funded as a platform, not a run of rescues. Not saying: she signed off the October 2025 refresh as a retrain in a board paper now in the Series C data room.

Prashant Dandekar, head of machine learning, Bengaluru, has wanted the central platform since 2023. Retraining on the exports, he argues, teaches the model to imitate its own past flags: the only labelled connections are ones Chhanni flagged and a utility inspected. His team of eleven loses people to firms that retrain weekly. Not saying: his July explanation was a guess, and he has not back-tested since March.

Pranali Sirsikar, data platform lead, Pune, found the averaging bug and thinks it explains much of the Rohilkhand decline and none of Chambal's. She wants two months to instrument the pipeline before anyone retrains. Not saying: she does not know whether the bug touched the training-time features too, in which case the model was never right on those connections rather than decayed.

Nivedita Chaubey, head of field enablement, Lucknow, says the model is being blamed for a dispatch problem: at Chambal the restriction removed the most productive 9 per cent of the list. Her team's standing with vigilance cells is the company's real distribution channel. Not saying: her team advised two utilities to deprioritise commercial flags after June.

Nupur Sathaye, key accounts lead, Jaipur, wants a visible change at Chambal within three weeks and would take Option C; most of her variable pay rides on renewal. Not saying: Chambal's chief engineer told her in September that the real objection is how many inspections the utility funds per confirmed case, not the contract percentage.

Nikhil Thatte, chief financial officer, Hyderabad, has approved ₹53.5 lakh of rebates this year and wants a ceiling. He will fund Option A or C now and calls B a Series C item. Not saying: he has modelled Chambal and Rohilkhand both leaving, and in that case B is unaffordable in any year.

Padmanabhan Ramanathan, general counsel, Chennai, notes that renegotiating the guarantee reopens each contract's whole schedule, price included, and that two utilities want a cut. No contract, he adds, obliges a utility to inspect what Ganana flags. Not saying: on the clients' figures he reads the clause 9.4 breach as established, whatever Exhibit 4 shows.

Option B builds what the company has never had: instrumented feature pipelines, drift monitoring on inputs and not only outcomes, a scheduled retrain, a release gate. It would have caught the February firmware change in February. It arrives 15 May 2027, five months after Rohilkhand's renewal.

Option C raises the score cutoff. On September's basis flags fall 40 per cent, from 53,900 to 32,340 a month, and Prashant estimates the shorter list strikes at 48 per cent. A fifth option — repair the dispatch, the pipeline and the measurement, and leave the model alone until it can be honestly evaluated — is nowhere in Exhibit 7: nobody costed it.

Chambal's notice expires on 5 December 2026 on a contract worth ₹350 lakh; Rohilkhand renews on 31 December 2026 at ₹456 lakh. Together that is ₹806 lakh, 44.3 per cent of ₹1,821 lakh. Nikhil's budget for unplanned product spend to 31 March 2027 is ₹110 lakh, against which ₹53.5 lakh of rebates has accrued. Prashant has eleven people and two notice periods running. The on-premise clauses cannot be varied before renewal, and between the DPDP Act and each utility's IT policy a central training corpus is a negotiation, not an engineering task. No contract obliges a utility to inspect what Ganana flags. The Series C data room is open.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. State precisely what Exhibits 3 and 4 each measure. Which belongs in a contract, and what must be added to make the other computable?
  2. Exhibit 2 follows one month's flags to collection. Which stages does Ganana control, which the utility, and where did the 2021 decision blind it?
  3. Decompose the fall from 46.1 per cent in January to 37.1 per cent in September into the causes offered: firmware averaging, the dispatch restriction, new feeders, decay. What here lets you size each, and what is missing?
  4. Option C improves the contracted metric and cuts the arrears utilities raise by about ₹11.03 crore a quarter. Is that a product decision, a commercial one or an ethical one, and who should take it?
  5. Prashant argues that retraining on inspection outcomes teaches the model to agree with itself. Design an evaluation that tests him within the constraints of Section 9, and price it for a utility.
  6. It is Monday morning. Nalini has one slide and fifteen minutes. What does it say, which option — or which fifth — does she commit to, what does she tell the board she got wrong, and what does she ask them to decide rather than approve?

At a quarter to twelve she shut the laptop and opened it again. The September cohort was 14 per cent complete; in three weeks it would be perhaps half complete, and she would know whether 35.2 per cent was the floor or the beginning. The call was in nine hours, and the one thing she was sure of was that waiting three weeks for a number she could defend was itself a decision, and not obviously the wrong one.
case20v1-aipm.ml.lifecycle:
Upaya Works and the Model That Stopped Learning

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 12 October 2026, Divya Awasthi, chief product officer of Upaya Works, stood at the whiteboard of the company's Pune office with a marker in one hand and a printed dashboard in the other. Diwali was twenty-seven days away. Every year, the weeks before the festival were when Upaya's customers, regional FMCG distributors, placed their largest stock orders of the year, and every year the company's demand-forecasting product was most visible to them in exactly these weeks.

This year the forecasts were wrong, and had been getting steadily worse since June. The distributor clients had started to notice. By the end of the day Divya had to tell her chief executive which of three courses of action to fund, because the engineering plan for the festive quarter had to be frozen on Friday, 16 October.

2. Company background

Upaya Works was founded in 2019 by two former supply-chain consultants. It sells a subscription forecasting tool to mid-sized distributors who buy from consumer-goods manufacturers and sell on to thousands of kirana stores. The product predicts, store cluster by store cluster and week by week, how many cases of each product a distributor should hold. Customers pay an average of ₹3.6 lakh a year. The company has 220 distributor clients across Maharashtra, Gujarat, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh, which makes annual recurring revenue of ₹792 lakh, or ₹7.92 crore.

The competitive field is crowded from several directions. Udaan and Jumbotail sell to the same kirana stores and increasingly offer inventory advice to their suppliers. Reliance Retail's JioMart Partner programme has a large in-house data team, and manufacturers such as Amul run their own dealer planning software. Upaya's niche is the independent distributor too small for any of these, and its pitch is simple: its forecast is better than a clerk's spreadsheet and cheaper than an enterprise planning suite.

The forecasting model went live in August 2025, fourteen months before this scene. Its contracts carry a service commitment: monthly mean absolute percentage error, or MAPE, below 15 per cent. MAPE is the average gap between forecast and actual sales, expressed as a percentage of actual sales, so a lower figure is better.

3. The situation

Exhibit 1 shows where the fourteen months' ₹140 lakh went across the stages of the machine-learning lifecycle: data, training, evaluation, deployment, monitoring and retraining. Data preparation consumed the largest share, ₹48 lakh, which is 34.3 per cent of the total. Monitoring received ₹4 lakh, or 2.9 per cent, and retraining received nothing, because nobody had planned for it.

Exhibit 2 shows what the one manual report revealed. In April the error stood at 11.2 per cent, close to the 11 per cent measured at launch. By September it was 19.8 per cent, a rise of 8.6 percentage points, or about 77 per cent in relative terms. The model first breached the contractual 15 per cent line in August. Nobody inside noticed until a client did.

Exhibit 2. Monthly forecast error. July's 14.6 per cent sits just inside the line, but August and September breach it. Source: manual accuracy reports.

Why had it decayed? Kiran Hosur, Upaya's head of data science, who works from Bengaluru, had a clear diagnosis. The model was trained on sales that pre-date two shifts. First, quick-commerce players such as Zepto and Swiggy Instamart had pulled small-pack demand away from many kirana stores in the larger cities. Second, a monsoon that arrived late in several districts changed the seasonal pattern the model had learned. The world had moved away from the data the model was trained on.

Kiran's team had a rough retraining script, but it ran on one engineer's laptop and was untested. In Chennai, Kalpana Iyyer, who leads customer success, was fielding the consequences. Thirty-one clients, whose renewals fall within the next six months, had complained about forecasts that were off. Their combined subscriptions come to ₹111.6 lakh, which is about 14 per cent of annual recurring revenue.

The Delhi-based sales head had his own view of the clock. He wanted the problem gone before the festive orders landed, because distributors judge a forecasting vendor by its Diwali stock calls. Retraining must also respect the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the consent terms in each contract.

4. The people

Divya Awasthi, chief product officer, Pune. She owns the product and must recommend a plan. She wants the Diwali quarter protected without repeating this crisis next year.

Kiran Hosur, head of data science, Bengaluru. He wants time to build things properly. He is wary of a quick retrain that treats a symptom, and says a retrained model will decay again within two quarters if nothing else changes.

Kalpana Iyyer, customer success lead, Chennai. She wants clients to see an improvement before Diwali, and she wants honest communication about what went wrong.

Deepak Sethi, sales head, Delhi. He wants no new commitments that risk the festive pipeline and would prefer the fastest fix, since renewals fall on his target.

5. Exhibits and the options

Divya asked Kiran to price three courses of action. His estimates appear in Exhibit 3. They run to 31 March 2027, so that the comparison includes the cost of keeping the model healthy and not just of the first repair.

Exhibit 3. Cost and timing of the three options (₹ lakh)
OptionSpend nowFurther spend to 31 Mar 2027Total to 31 Mar 2027First fix liveExpected MAPE at Diwali
A. Retrain now, by hand1818362 Nov 202613%
B. Build the full pipeline first6206221 Dec 202619.8% (unchanged)
C. Retrain now, then build the pipeline1830482 Nov 202613%

Option A's further spend is two more manual retrains at ₹9 lakh each. Totals are the sum of the two spend columns. Dates: three weeks from 12 October is 2 November; ten weeks is 21 December.

Option A: retrain now, by hand. The team assembles the latest six months of data, retrains, tests against the most recent quarter and ships by 2 November, six days before Diwali on 8 November. The upside is speed and low cost. The drawback is that every later repair is another emergency, and the company would still not know when the model is going wrong until a client says so.

Option B: build the full pipeline first. Kiran's team puts in place automated data checks, monitoring dashboards, scheduled retraining and a controlled rollout. It is the complete answer and costs ₹62 lakh. But it takes ten weeks, so the current model, at 19.8 per cent error, serves the entire festive season.

Option C: retrain now, then build the pipeline. The team does Option A's retrain under a stricter test, then uses the quiet period after Diwali to build monitoring and automated retraining over the following months, for a further ₹30 lakh. The total is ₹48 lakh, which is ₹14 lakh less than Option B, though ₹12 lakh more than Option A. Its risk is discipline: the second phase can easily slip once the crisis passes.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, which stages of the lifecycle did Upaya fund, and which did it leave out? What did that omission cost?
  2. Exhibit 2 shows a gradual decline. At what month should an alert have fired, and what would the team have needed to measure to fire it?
  3. Compare Options A, B and C in Exhibit 3 on cost, timing and risk to the 31 clients with pending renewals. Which cost matters most to each of the four stakeholders?
  4. What would you say to clients, and when, about the breach of the 15 per cent commitment, and how would you test the retrained model before release?

7. A note for the learner

This case turns on a single idea: a model is not a deliverable but a process that has to keep running. The lifecycle runs from data to training, evaluation, deployment, monitoring and retraining, and then loops back to data. Upaya funded the first four stages and treated the loop as someone else's problem. The result was predictable. The world changed, and the model was never designed to notice.

A well-reasoned answer separates two questions that the stakeholders blur together. The first is the repair: what restores accuracy before the festive quarter? The second is the system: what keeps accuracy from decaying again? Option B answers only the second and gives up the festive season to do it. Option A answers only the first and guarantees a repeat. Option C answers both in sequence.

One defensible path is Option C, with three conditions. First, the retrain is not a rush job: it is tested against the most recent quarter, region by region, and released only if the error is below the 15 per cent commitment in every region. Second, the first and cheapest part of the monitoring work, an automated weekly MAPE report with an alert at 14 per cent, is pulled forward into the October sprint, because it costs little and would have flagged the problem in July. Third, the ₹30 lakh second phase is approved today, with a named owner and a date of 31 January 2027 for the first automated retrain, so that it cannot be quietly deferred.

Kalpana should tell the 31 clients plainly what happened and when the fix arrives, before the sales team reaches them. Deepak gets the faster fix he wants; Kiran gets the durable system he wants, later but funded.
exp20v2-aipm.ml.lifecycle:
The ML lifecycle

AI & Data Products, AI & ML Product Management. Question: what does it take to get a model from data to production, and keep it there?

1. A model that got worse while nobody touched it

On 12 March 2026, Nandini Rajagopalan, head of product at Ambuj Lending Cloud in Bengaluru, opened a spreadsheet that her machine-learning lead, Anirudh Sethuraman, had sent from Pune the night before. Ambuj sells a lending platform to non-bank lenders, and its centrepiece is Nirnay Score, a model that estimates whether an applicant will default within 90 days of receiving a personal loan. Nirnay Score had gone live on 3 November 2025. At validation it had caught 75 per cent of the loans that later defaulted. Anirudh's spreadsheet covered the first cohort of loans whose 90 days had elapsed, and the figure was 60 per cent.

Nothing in the code had changed. What had changed was the applicants: a partner lender had begun serving gig workers in smaller cities, a group the training data barely contained. A model is a frozen description of the past, and the past had stopped resembling the present. Two proposals now sat on Nandini's desk, and both concerned the process around the model, not the model itself.

ItemFigure
Nirnay Score live date3 November 2025
Share of eventual defaults caught, at validation75 per cent
Share caught on first matured live cohort60 per cent
Proposal one: contractor retrain, once₹35 lakh
Proposal two: build a repeatable lifecycle pipeline₹2.4 crore

The first proposal was cheap and would work for a few months. The second was expensive and would keep working. Anirudh had also warned her that the honest cost of the first was not ₹35 lakh but the next surprise, which nobody had scheduled. Her decision turned on whether she believed the model was a product or a process.

2. The idea

The machine-learning lifecycle is the repeating sequence by which a model is built and kept useful: assemble data, train a model on it, evaluate it against something that matters, deploy it into the product, monitor how it behaves once real users meet it, and retrain when monitoring shows it has fallen behind. The last step feeds the first, so the sequence is a loop and not a line.

The lifecycle was invented to solve a mismatch. Ordinary software fails when someone changes it; a model can fail when the world changes. The earliest widely used description, CRISP-DM, was written in the late 1990s by a consortium of industrial firms for data-mining projects, and it already drew a cycle. The sharper statement came in 2015, when Google engineers D. Sculley and colleagues published Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems, arguing that the model code is a small box surrounded by the much larger machinery of data collection, serving and monitoring. By around 2018 the practice of running that machinery had acquired the name MLOps (machine-learning operations, a borrowing from DevOps).

The sentence Nandini could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: a model is not something we ship, it is something we run, and running it has a cost that recurs.

3. How it actually works

Follow Nirnay Score through the loop. Data means more than collecting records. Ambuj had to define the label, the outcome the model predicts: here, a missed payment within 90 days. That definition creates a delay, because a loan disbursed today reveals its label only in three months. Each feature (an input the model reads, such as income band or number of bureau enquiries) also had to be computed exactly as it would have been known on the application date, not as it looks now. Using later information by accident is called leakage, and it makes a model look brilliant on paper and useless in life.

Train means letting an algorithm search for the pattern linking features to labels. Anirudh's team trained on loans from January to September 2025 and held back the later months. Splitting by time, not at random, is one of the implicit steps: it imitates the real situation of predicting the future from the past.

Evaluate means measuring the model on data it has not seen, against a baseline. Two terms matter. Recall is the share of actual defaulters the model flags. Precision is the share of flagged applicants who really would have defaulted. A third implicit step belongs here: converting those rates into rupees before deciding, which the next section does.

Deploy moves the model into the live approval path. The quiet requirement is that the features must be computed identically online and in training; when they differ, the gap is called training-serving skew. Ambuj ran Nirnay Score in shadow first, scoring applicants without acting on the score, then switched it on. Monitor watches two things: the inputs (do today's applicants look like the training data?) and the outcomes (are the predictions still right?). The outcomes arrive 90 days late, so inputs are the early warning. Retrain repeats the loop with newer data and, crucially, a rule for when to do it and who approves the replacement.

StageFirst build (weeks)Repeat cycle (weeks)
Data62

Evaluate21
Deploy31
Total145

Table 1. Elapsed weeks per stage. The 14-week first build is Anirudh's record of the 2025 project; the 5-week repeat cycle is his estimate for a pipeline that automates data assembly and deployment.

The table carries the argument of the second proposal. The first trip round the loop is dominated by building things that never get rebuilt. Every later trip is short only if someone paid to make it short.

4. A worked example

Take 1,00,000 loan applications, of which 6 per cent, or 6,000, would default. Each loan is ₹40,000; a default loses 70 per cent of that, or ₹28,000; each good loan earns ₹3,000 net of costs. Without a model, every applicant is approved: 94,000 good loans earn 94,000 × ₹3,000 = ₹28.20 crore, and 6,000 defaults lose 6,000 × ₹28,000 = ₹16.80 crore, a net of ₹11.40 crore.

Now apply Nirnay Score as validated: it catches 75 per cent of defaulters, so 4,500 are rejected and 1,500 slip through. It also wrongly rejects 10 per cent of good applicants, 9,400. It rejects 13,900 people in all, of whom 4,500 are true defaulters, a precision of 32.4 per cent. Approved: 86,100, of which 84,600 are good. Earnings are 84,600 × ₹3,000 = ₹25.38 crore; losses are 1,500 × ₹28,000 = ₹4.20 crore; net ₹21.18 crore.

Second pass: change one input. Leave everything alone but let recall fall from 75 to 60 per cent, as the live cohort suggested. Now 3,600 defaulters are caught and 2,400 pass. Rejections number 3,600 + 9,400 = 13,000; approvals 87,000; good approved loans remain 84,600. Losses rise to 2,400 × ₹28,000 = ₹6.72 crore and the net falls to ₹25.38 crore − ₹6.72 crore = ₹18.66 crore.

The model still beats no model at 60 per cent recall, which is why drift is easy to ignore. But the slide costs ₹2.52 crore per 1,00,000 applications (₹21.18 crore minus ₹18.66 crore), which is 900 extra missed defaulters at ₹28,000 each. Ambuj processes about 3,00,000 applications a quarter, so the leak is ₹7.56 crore a quarter. Against that, ₹35 lakh for a retrain looks trivial, and so does ₹2.4 crore for a pipeline that makes retraining routine.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

The lifecycle is a loop, and the loop is the product

Teams that treat deployment as the finish line budget for stages one to four and nothing after. Monitoring and retraining are recurring costs, not overruns.

Offline and online performance are different claims

The 75 per cent figure was true of a historical test set. It is a forecast about live traffic, and it holds only while live traffic resembles that set.

Labels arrive late, so monitoring has two clocks

Input checks are fast and indirect; outcome checks are slow and decisive. Mature teams also track a proxy, such as missed first instalments at 30 days, which trades certainty for speed.

Data drift is not concept drift

Data drift means the inputs change (more gig workers). Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and outcome changes (the same income now predicts repayment differently). The remedies differ: new data may fix the first; the second may need new features.

Retraining is not automatically improvement

A retrained model can be worse, for instance if the newest months are incomplete. The discipline is champion-challenger: the challenger must beat the incumbent on a fixed evaluation set before it replaces it.

Selective labels bias the data

Rejected applicants never receive a loan, so their outcomes are never observed. The model learns only from people it, or its predecessor, approved. Nothing in the lifecycle fixes this automatically; it needs deliberate exploration, such as approving a small random slice.

The model metric is not the business metric

Recall and precision are instruments. Table 2 showed that rupees, weighted by loss size and margin, decide the threshold. Ask whose cost each error carries.

The lifecycle cannot tell you whether to use ML

It assumes that problem–model fit already exists. A well-run lifecycle around a poor fit only produces reliable disappointment.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; early and large

In a consumer product, feedback is fast and plentiful: a recommendation is judged by a click in seconds, so retraining can be daily. In B2B, as at Ambuj, feedback is slow and lives inside customers' systems, and each customer's data may differ. Ambuj must decide whether one model serves every lender or each gets its own. In a marketplace, the model's decisions change the behaviour of both sides, so today's data is partly a product of yesterday's model, and monitoring must watch for that feedback loop.

An early-stage company should run the loop by hand, with a written checklist, a notebook and a person on call, because automation before the loop is understood freezes the wrong steps. A large company has the opposite problem: many models, many owners, and no one who knows which are still running. There the scarce asset is a register of models, owners and retraining rules.

7. Common mistakes

Shipping without a baseline. Symptom: everyone praises the model but no one can say what the business would earn without it. Misunderstanding: accuracy is treated as value. Cheapest diagnostic: fill in a table like Table 2 with the no-model column first.

Monitoring only uptime. Symptom: the dashboard is green while approvals worsen. Misunderstanding: a model that responds is assumed to be a model that is right. Diagnostic: ask what alert fires if recall falls 15 points, and who reads it.

Random splits on time-ordered data. Symptom: spectacular validation, mediocre launch. Misunderstanding: shuffling is harmless. Diagnostic: re-run evaluation on the latest month only.

Retraining without a promotion rule. Symptom: performance wobbles after each refresh. Misunderstanding: newer data is assumed better. Diagnostic: ask for the fixed test on which each replacement was approved.

8. What good looks like

Suppose Ambuj had handled the launch well. Before 3 November, the team would have written down that the model was expected to keep at least 70 per cent recall, and that a fall below it would trigger a retrain. Shadow scoring would have shown the partner's gig-worker share rising, and the input alert would have fired weeks before the outcomes matured. A challenger would have been trained in a 5-week cycle, tested against the incumbent on a fixed set, and promoted by a named owner. Nandini would have read about drift in a routine report, not a March spreadsheet.

9. Closing

Nandini approved the ₹2.4 crore pipeline, staged so that its first deliverable was monitoring and a promotion rule, not automation. Her reasoning was arithmetic and structure together: a recall slide of 15 points leaks ₹7.56 crore a quarter, so the pipeline pays for itself in about four weeks of a 13-week quarter, and the same loop that would be retrained by hand would otherwise be rediscovered by accident each time. She also asked Anirudh to include a random approval slice, to address the missing labels of rejected applicants. The contractor retrain went ahead too, as a bridge.

To go further, study data strategy and data acquisition, because every loop starts with data and the selective-label problem is a data-acquisition problem; and model monitoring and drift, which turns stage five from a slogan into a set of thresholds.

Two questions to sit with. First, in a product you know, which stage of the loop has no named owner? Second, if outcomes reach you 90 days late, what would you watch on day one to decide that the model is going wrong?

The ML lifecycle

AI & Data Products › AI & ML Product Management. What it takes to get a model from data into production, and keep it there.

1. Two decisions, taken a fortnight apart

On 18 August 2026 Eshita Emani, vice-president of product at Ekagra Inspection Systems in Pune, was reading a debit note. Ekagra sells machine-vision inspection cells to auto-component plants: a camera tunnel over the conveyor, an industrial computer called Ekagra Edge, and a model family, Eklavya-3, that decides in 40 milliseconds whether a forged part goes to despatch or to the reject chute. By July 2026, 240 cells ran across 37 plants, some supplying tier-one houses that serve Bajaj Auto.

The note came from Eshanya Forge Works, which had cells on eleven lines at Chakan and Hosur. Its quality manager, Eswari Etikala, had approved a new bar-stock supplier in June, and the new stock had a slightly different sheen. No code had changed and no camera had moved, yet on 26 affected lines Ezhil Elangovan, Ekagra's machine-learning lead in Coimbatore, measured recall down from 90 to 75 per cent and false rejects doubled.

Exhibit 1. The gap is ₹48,060 per cell per day; on 26 cells over a 26-day month, ₹3.25 crore (₹3,24,88,560) of quality cost that did not exist in May.

Her decision was not whether to retrain but what the unit of retraining should be: Ezhil wanted one global model with a per-cell calibration step, while field engineering wanted 240 per-cell models, each fine-tuned on its own images, because a cell has its own lens, lighting and part mix.

Fourteen days later Qamar Qureshi met the same question at Qalam Resale Exchange in Bengaluru, a marketplace for pre-owned smartphones. A seller photographs a handset; Qalam Grade reads the photographs and diagnostics and assigns a condition grade; Qalam Quote turns the grade into a firm price. If the seller accepts, the handset reaches an inspection centre, where a grader issues the true grade within 4.2 days. The model was retrained automatically every Monday.

In July 2026, 20 per cent of received devices were downgraded at inspection, against 13 per cent in April. Qudsia Qazi, the data-science lead in Hyderabad, traced part of the rise to a new annotation guideline redefining screen micro-scratches, and part to something worse: the model learned only from devices whose quotes were accepted, so rejected quotes produced no label. Qaiser Qasmi, who ran trust and operations from Gurugram, wanted the retrain stopped until a human gate existed; Qudsia wanted an exploration budget.

2. The idea, and the people who disagree about it

The machine-learning lifecycle is the repeating, versioned process by which a learned artefact is produced, served, watched and replaced — for a product manager, a control loop whose output is a decision rule and whose feedback signal is delayed. Four artefacts must be versioned together: a data snapshot, the feature code that turns records into inputs, the training code and configuration, and the evaluation set against which candidates are judged. The model is a fifth thing, and it is derived. Name the four and the fifth is reproducible; otherwise you are running an artefact of unknown provenance.

Ordinary software engineering assumes failure follows change. Models violate that: correctness is a claim about a distribution, and distributions move, so a model can rot while every line of code stays frozen. CRISP-DM, published in 1999, already drew a cycle. The decisive statement was Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (D. Sculley and colleagues, 2015), with its tiny “ML code” box surrounded by configuration, data collection, serving and monitoring, and its CACE principle: changing anything changes everything. By 2018 the practice had a name, MLOps. In 2021 Nithya Sambasivan and colleagues, studying high-stakes deployments in India, added that practitioners want the model work, not the data work, and the resulting data cascades surface late.

At least five schools sign different propositions. Pipeline-first: the unit of delivery is the pipeline, because if retraining needs a named person's afternoon it will not happen when it matters; it will not sign that every promotion needs approval. Data-centric, after Andrew Ng's 2021 campaign: most remaining improvement comes from label consistency and thin-slice coverage, not modelling; it denies that a dashboard of model outputs is the main defence. Evaluation-first, after Ribeiro's CheckList (2020): no aggregate number can authorise a release. Reliability, importing site-reliability practice: a model with no owner and no rollback path is an outage awaiting a date; it refuses automation without hard staleness bounds. Minimalist, rare at conferences and common in profitable companies: retrain on evidence or on incident, not on a calendar.

3. Mechanics, including the steps usually left implicit

Begin with the step missing from every diagram: point-in-time correctness. A feature must be computed from information that existed when the decision was made. At Qalam, “prior listings by this seller” is easy to get wrong, because the obvious query counts listings as of today; train on that and the model learns to read the future. Temporal leakage is the commonest reason a model validates at 0.94 and lands at 0.71, and the defence is an as-of join written once, in shared feature code, used by training and serving alike.

Then evaluation protocol. A random split on time-ordered data flatters the model. Experts use rolling-origin backtesting — train on weeks 1–20, test on 21–24; then train on 1–24, test on 25–28 — and report a distribution of scores. Expanding windows assume the past stays relevant; sliding windows assume it does not.

Third, the threshold is a business object. Eklavya-3 emits a crack probability; the product decides where to cut. Ekagra prices an escape at ₹1,200 and a scrapped good part at ₹180, about 6.7 to 1, so the optimum lies where preventing one escape costs more than 6.7 extra good parts. Exhibit 1 is that calculation made explicit.

Fourth, drift statistics. During L the only evidence is the shape of the inputs. The workhorse is the population stability index, PSI = Σ (ai − ei) ln(ai/ei) over bins of a feature, e being the training share and a the share seen now. Below 0.10 reads as stable, above 0.25 as a different population.

PSI is a smoke alarm, not a verdict: an input shift may be harmless, since a bright part is still a sound part, or it may be the mechanism of failure. Only the delayed loop can say which, so the fast loop's output is an investigation, not a deployment.

Fifth, and least discussed, cadence is an inventory problem with a closed-form answer. Suppose staleness cost grows linearly after a retrain, so week w costs δ·w, and one retrain of one cell costs C.
