Sixth, promotion. A candidate is a challenger: it must beat the incumbent on the frozen set, survive shadow scoring without acting, then a canary, then full rollout, under an owner who can revert. Reverting a model needs the old snapshot, the old feature code and a schema that still parses.

4. When the lifecycle applies, stated as tests

Five conditions, each checkable. One: the inputs move measurably. Ekagra passes at 0.1740 on brightness alone, driven by a purchasing decision nobody told the vendor about; Qalam passes emphatically, its device mix turning over each launch season. Two: labels arrive, and you know how late. Qalam's L is 4.2 days; Ekagra's is 26 days, plus a destructive audit of 300 parts per cell per week. Three: the decision is repeated and priced. Both pass. Four: each cycle brings enough fresh signal. Ekagra fails at single-cell level. Five: the model's actions do not determine the next training set. Ekagra passes, since a rejected part is still inspected by hand; Qalam fails badly.

The idea is actively misleading in three cases. Where the task is a converged physical measurement in controlled conditions, retraining injects variance into a stable system and the right cadence is never. Where problem–model fit does not hold, a good loop produces reliable, well-monitored disappointment. And where model risk is formally regulated, change itself costs, because each promotion triggers revalidation.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature firms actually do

In multi-product companies the seam is shared features: one team's redefinition of “active seller” silently changes three models trained elsewhere. Mature firms answer with a registry recording which models consume which feature, not with documentation. In two-sided markets the output alters the population it will next train on; Qalam is the pure case. In regulated settings the artefact list grows — model cards, challenger evidence, a monitoring plan, an audit trail — and such firms retrain far less often than their policies imply.

Hardware-plus-software is Ekagra's world and breaks the diagram three ways. The fleet is heterogeneous: 240 cells run some distribution of versions, so a rollout is a migration. Bandwidth is scarce, making data selection a product decision — Ekagra uploads only frames scoring between 0.3 and 0.7, plus a 1-in-200 random sample. And rollback must work for an engineer on a shop floor at 2 a.m. In AI-native products on bought foundation models — Qissa Assist Cloud, a support-agent product — the train step disappears and the loop reassembles around prompts, retrieval corpora and evals: the artefacts change names, not their number, and the vendor's silent update is an uncontrolled retrain that happens to you.

6. Nine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The evaluation set ages too

A frozen golden set is the right instrument and a wasting asset, drawn from a receding distribution. The tell-tale is three or four challengers in a row that win offline and disappoint online. The obvious reading — overfitting — is usually wrong: the set has stopped representing traffic.

Aggregate stability hides segment collapse

With 89 per cent of volume at 93 per cent recall and 11 per cent, the new bar stock, at 62 per cent, blended recall is 0.89 × 0.93 + 0.11 × 0.62 = 0.8959, or 89.6 per cent against a 90 per cent baseline: a 0.4-point move concealing a 31-point collapse. Alert on the worst slice above a volume floor, never on the mean.

Drift statistics answer a different question

PSI says the inputs moved, not that the model got worse, so a team retraining on PSI alone refreshes on harmless seasonality and misses silent concept drift, where inputs hold steady and their relation to the outcome changes. The tell-tale is a retraining log full of refreshes that produced no measurable gain.

Cadence is inventory, not virtue

“We retrain quarterly” describes a calendar, not the world, and the tell-tale is that nobody can estimate δ. Once δ exists, Exhibit 3 delivers the surprise: the optimum is flat, so precision about cadence is worth little while an order-of-magnitude error is expensive. The real prize is cutting C.

The label pipeline has its own lifecycle

Qalam's downgrade spike was partly a guideline change about micro-scratches. Annotator cohorts turn over and agreement drifts. The tell-tale is a step change dated to an onboarding or guideline release rather than to anything in the world. Version guidelines like code, and re-label a fixed audit sample under each.

Your metrics become self-fulfilling

Where the model gates what happens next, it gates what you can learn: Qalam observes outcomes only above the acceptance threshold. The tell-tale is precision improving while coverage quietly narrows. The remedy costs money: randomised exploration, to buy labels where you are blind.

"The model" in production is a distribution of versions

Ask a fleet operator which model is live and the competent answer is a histogram. The tell-tale is an incident review that cannot establish which version served the failing request. Log model version, feature-code version and snapshot identifier with every prediction; without that triple a rollback is a guess.

Rollback is not redeploying the previous container

Reverting needs the old snapshot, the old feature code and a schema that still parses today's records; if a feature was deprecated meanwhile, the old model cannot be served at all. The tell-tale is a rollback plan written by someone who has only reverted stateless services.

The maturation window bounds the honest learning rate

If truth arrives in 26 days, no honest weekly improvement claim exists; weekly reports can only describe proxies. The tell-tale is a roadmap iterating faster than L. Name the proxy and state its measured correlation with the outcome.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

The real differences are in L, volume and feedback. Consumer products have short L and abundant data, so the binding constraint is the feedback loop and the work is exploration design. B2B and enterprise products have long L, low volume per customer and data inside customer systems, forcing Eshita's question: one model for all, one per tenant, or a shared trunk with local calibration. The middle answer usually wins because per-tenant models starve. Marketplaces make the model a policy affecting supply as well as demand, so offline replay overstates gains.

What does not differ, though exemption is often claimed: point-in-time correctness, a promotion gate, priced errors. A team claiming exemption by product type is usually describing an absence of capability.

By stage the shift is real but narrower than the tooling market suggests. One model and six engineers should run the loop by hand from a written runbook, because automating a loop you have not understood freezes the wrong steps. At five to fifteen models the scarce asset is the register: which models exist, who owns each, what triggers a retrain.

8. Three worked examples

Qalam, and the value of a narrower grading gap. In July 2026 Qalam issued 7,50,000 quotes. Acceptance ran at 24 per cent, giving 1,80,000 shipments, of which 95 per cent arrived: 1,71,000 devices. At a 20 per cent downgrade rate 34,200 were regraded downward, and 30 per cent of those sellers refused the revised offer, so 10,260 went back.

Against that, Qudsia's proposal is cheap. A randomised 4 per cent uplift on 1 per cent of quotes — 7,500 of them — at a mean quote of ₹9,400 adds ₹376 per accepted device; at 29 per cent acceptance, 2,175 devices, the bill is ₹8.18 lakh a month, about an eighth of the prize.

Ekagra, and the arithmetic that settled a design argument. The per-cell option had intuitive appeal and a fatal statistic: a cell running 6,000 parts a day at a 2 per cent defect rate produces 120 defects, but only the 12 escapes and a weekly destructive audit of 300 parts yield confirmed labels, so one cell cannot gather enough rare-defect examples per cycle to fine-tune safely. Pooling 240 cells multiplies the defect evidence by two orders of magnitude. Ezhil's compromise was a shared trunk on the 12-week cadence, plus a per-cell normalisation layer refitted from 200 unlabelled images whenever brightness PSI exceeds 0.15 — which the 0.1740 reading would have crossed three weeks before the debit note.

Qandeel Power Systems, where the approach failed. Qandeel, in Jaipur, sells day-ahead load forecasting to distribution utilities; Ekavali Erram is its product head. One urban circle averaging 9.5 million units of daily load ran the model with a nightly automatic retrain and no human gate — the pipeline-first ideal. In March 2026 a metering concentrator failed on a group of feeders and wrote zeros rather than nulls for three weeks. The retrain read the zeros as genuine low demand, and each night's model learned the error more thoroughly. Forecast error rose from 3.4 per cent of daily load to 6.9 per cent — an extra 0.3325 million units a day, or 3,32,500 units, which at a deviation charge of ₹1.35 per unit cost ₹4,48,875 daily. Over 21 days, ₹94.26 lakh.

The failure was not the automation but its bareness: no input validation, so a data fault entered training as evidence, and no outcome gate, so each silent degradation was promoted. Recovery had three parts. A data-quality gate aborts the retrain and holds the incumbent whenever a feeder group's record count falls more than 15 per cent from its trailing median. A staleness bound escalates a held model after 35 days. And a promotion gate requires approval whenever a challenger's backtested error differs from the incumbent's by more than 0.4 percentage points either way, a suspiciously large improvement being as informative as a degradation. The gate cost ₹22 lakh to build and ₹1.6 lakh a month: ₹41.2 lakh in year one, against one ₹94.26 lakh incident.

9. Failure modes, with their early warnings

Silent data-fault ingestion. Early sign: a feature's null rate falls to zero, which rarely happens naturally. Diagnostic: what would abort tonight's retrain? Late, this is Qandeel: ₹94.26 lakh. Promotion without a gate. Early sign: nobody can name the fixed set that approved the last replacement. Diagnostic: who signed, against what? Monitoring only availability. Early sign: the dashboard is green while a customer escalates. Diagnostic: which alert fires if recall falls 15 points on one segment, and who reads it? Unbounded staleness. Early sign: a model held “temporarily” still serves four months later. Diagnostic: what is the oldest model live? Feature-change collateral damage. Early sign: behaviour changes on a date with no release. Diagnostic: which models read this feature?

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Automate promotion, or gate it. The pipeline-first case is that human gates are theatre — reviewers approve what they cannot evaluate, and queues mean stale models during the excursions that matter — and in high-volume consumer systems most degradation is indeed found by monitoring. The reliability case replies with Qandeel, where automation propagated one data fault for twenty-one nights that a gate would have caught on the second.

Is input monitoring worth its cost? The sceptic says PSI alarms are mostly noise, teams learn to mute them, and the money is better spent shortening L. The steelman is Ekagra: the shift was visible in week 31, the debit note came in week 34, and three weeks at ₹48,060 per cell per day across 26 cells is real money. The rejoinder is that the decisive statistic — the share of investigated alarms that mattered — is one almost nobody computes.

One model or many. Per-tenant models fit local idiosyncrasy and starve for data; a global model pools evidence and is wrong the same way everywhere. The middle path is widely adopted and defended by nobody as a principle, which should make a careful reader suspect a compromise rather than an answer.

Does a training lifecycle survive foundation models? One camp holds the train step is gone for most application teams, so the loop is now curation, retrieval, prompts and evals. The other holds only the artefact names have moved, with the vendor now retraining on your behalf without telling you. Both have two years of evidence; neither has five.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied the lifecycle can draw the loop and name the stages. Someone who has internalised it does three things differently. They ask for L before asking for accuracy, because L bounds what any report can mean. They ask what the model prevented them from observing. And they treat every claimed improvement as needing a stated comparison — against which incumbent, on which frozen set, promoted by whom.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Eshita chose the shared trunk with per-cell normalisation, a 12-week fleet cadence and a PSI trigger at 0.15 that can pull a retrain forward, rejecting 240 per-cell models because one cell cannot supply enough confirmed defects per cycle. She also added a contract clause requiring customers to notify a raw-material change — her most effective intervention was not technical.

Qamar kept the weekly automatic retrain but subordinated it to a data-quality and annotation-version gate modelled on Qandeel's, and to Qudsia's ₹8.18 lakh a month exploration band. He rejected human approval for every weekly promotion, since with L at 4.2 days and 7,50,000 quotes a month a reviewer could add no information — but conceded the principle after a guideline change, where a reviewer certainly can.

Discussion questions. First: Ekagra and Qandeel drew opposite conclusions about automatic promotion from the same body of practice. What feature of each business makes each answer right, and what would have to change for them to swap? Second: Qalam spends ₹8.18 lakh a month to buy labels it is blind to, against a ₹67.31 lakh prize — at what point does exploration stop paying? Third: take a model you rely on. What is its L, who owns its rollback, and which frozen set authorised its last promotion?

13. Going deeper

Problem–model fit comes first: a good loop around a bad fit yields well-documented failure. Data strategy and data acquisition is where Qalam's exploration band and Ekagra's frame-selection rule live. Model monitoring and drift turns PSI and slice alerts into thresholds with owners. Labelling and annotation explains the guideline version that moved Qalam's downgrade rate. Model metrics: precision, recall, AUC supplies the instruments Exhibit 1 converts into rupees. What's different when the feature is a model carries the loop into product design; quality as a distribution formalises segment collapse; what evals are and why PMs own them extends it to foundation-model products; and building a golden set from real usage answers the ageing evaluation set.

Error Analysis and Iteration

Reading failures, naming clusters and fixing the largest one is the easy half. The expert half is knowing how much of what you read is signal, what the ranking is worth, what the fix will actually remove, and what the fix will break.

1Two rooms, one week apart

On 4 March 2026, Arundhati Bose, Head of Product at Tehreer Claims Cloud in Mumbai, had three days to settle an argument with her engineering lead. Tehreer sold a pre-adjudication assistant to health insurers: it read discharge summaries, hospital bills and policy wordings and drafted a recommendation — approve, query, or partially settle — that a human adjudicator accepted or overturned. Three insurers ran it across roughly 62,000 claims a month. The overturn rate — Tehreer's headline quality number, and the trigger for a service-credit clause in two of the three contracts — stood at 11.0%, about 6,800 claims. Her engineering lead wanted six weeks on optical character recognition for Tier-2 hospital scans, the most visible source of complaints. Arundhati had read 120 overturned claims herself and thought OCR the wrong place to start, but "I read the transcripts and disagree" is not an argument that survives a steering committee.

Seven days later and 980 kilometres south, Zoya Qureshi, VP Product at Bisaat Bazaar in Bengaluru, faced the mirror image. Bisaat ran a vernacular marketplace: buyers searched in Hindi, Marathi, Kannada or code-mixed English across goods listed by 1.4 lakh small sellers, and a model interpreted the query and ranked the catalogue, across roughly 38 lakh AI-assisted sessions a month. Zoya's team had clustered buyer complaints cleanly, found a dominant failure — regional product names matched to the wrong category — and built the fix. What stopped her was a memo from the supply team: the tightening would suppress exactly the loosely-titled listings on which 60% of long-tail sellers depended. Her cluster was real. It was also one side of a two-sided ledger, and her analysis could not, by construction, see the other.

Both were turning a pile of bad outputs into a defensible plan. Both had reached the point at which the textbook procedure — sample, read, tag, cluster, size, fix the biggest, re-run — stops giving answers and starts demanding judgement.

2The idea, and who disagrees about it

Error analysis is the practice of drawing a sample of a system's failures, labelling each by reading the artefact rather than the score, aggregating those labels into a small set of distinguishable clusters, costing each cluster against the whole population, acting on one, and re-measuring against a set frozen before the reading began. Iteration is the commitment that this runs on a cadence rather than as incident response.

Three lineages, and the field's disagreements are inherited from them. Industrial quality control — Juran's "vital few", Ishikawa's cause diagrams — supplied the Pareto instinct that a handful of causes explain most defects. Software reliability, specifically Ram Chillarege's Orthogonal Defect Classification at IBM in 1992, argued the opposite of the grounded-theory instinct: categories should be fixed, orthogonal and defined in advance, because only a stable scheme lets you compare this release with the last. Applied machine learning, principally Andrew Ng's Machine Learning Yearning (2018), told engineers to stop theorising and count a hundred misclassifications by hand. Language-model practice added a fourth strand after 2023, when the artefact became free text, the grader became another model, and categories began moving faster than any fixed scheme could track — what Shreya Shankar and colleagues named criteria drift in 2024.

Four positions are held by serious practitioners, and they do not reconcile by splitting the difference.

The emergent school.
Signs: no taxonomy survives a model upgrade, and a reused taxonomy is a machine for not noticing new failures. Will not sign: cluster shares are comparable across quarters.
The orthogonal-taxonomy school, descended from ODC.
Signs: comparability beats fidelity; a slightly wrong stable scheme beats a perfect unstable one, because only the stable scheme says whether you are improving. Will not sign: each team invents its own labels each sprint.
The scale school.
Signs: an imperfect automated clustering applied to 100% of failures beats an excellent manual one applied to 1%. Will not sign: the product manager must personally read every trace.
The specification school.
Signs: most things logged as model errors are underspecified requirements; error analysis is requirements elicitation wearing a lab coat. Will not sign: the fix for a large cluster is usually a model change.

Arundhati is specification-school by instinct: she suspects adjudicators overturn recommendations because Tehreer never defined what "partially settle" means when a room-rent sub-limit meets a proportionate-deduction clause. Zoya is scale-school by necessity — 38 lakh sessions cannot be read. Neither argument is about method; each is about which school's assumption holds in that product.

3Mechanics, worked through

Four quantities separate expert practice from the procedure as taught: the precision of the sample, the contamination of the flag, the expected value of the fix, and the coverage of the taxonomy. Each has arithmetic.

How much does a rank order from sixty reads actually tell you?

Arundhati read 120 overturned claims and produced five clusters, the largest — sub-limit arithmetic — at 31%. The standard error of a proportion is √(p(1−p)/n) = √(0.31 × 0.69 / 120) = 0.042, so the 95% interval runs roughly 23% to 39%: tolerable for a single share. What teams do next is not. They compare it with the 24% cluster and declare a winner, but for two categories from the same multinomial sample the standard error of the difference is √((p₁ + p₂ − (p₁ − p₂)²)/n) = √(0.5451/120) = 0.067, so the seven-point gap is well inside noise. Separating a 30% cluster from a 22% one takes roughly 310 reads, not 60. The consequence is not "read more": the top two or three clusters are a tied set whose tie is broken on cost, which is what an expert does anyway. The imprecision bites in one place — when a leader asks whether cluster A grew from 22% to 31% since last month, and the honest answer is that both readings are consistent with no change.

Figure 1. Tehreer's five clusters at two sample sizes. At n = 120 the intervals for A, B and D overlap heavily: the observed rank order is one of several the data support. Tripling the read still does not separate B from D.

What fraction of your "failures" are failures?

Every cluster count inherits the error rate of whatever flagged the failure. Treat the flag as a diagnostic test: 10,000 responses, a true failure rate of 6%, a judge catching 90% of real failures and wrongly flagging 8% of good ones. Real failures caught, 0.90 × 600 = 540; good responses wrongly flagged, 0.08 × 9,400 = 752. The pile holds 1,292 items, of which 42% are genuine. Fifty-eight per cent of what the team is about to cluster is not a failure — and those false positives are not random, they concentrate where the judge systematically misunderstands, forming convincing clusters of their own. The remedy is trivial and almost never done: before clustering, audit thirty flagged items by hand. Below about 70% precision, the correct first fix is the judge.

Figure 2. Judge contamination. At a 6% true failure rate, even a good judge — 90% recall, 8% false positives — hands the team a pile in which most items are not failures, and those false positives cluster convincingly enough to outrank every genuine cluster.

Ranking by expected value, not by size

The quantity worth ranking on is monthly recoverable cost: cluster share × failure volume × cost per failure × expected fix efficacy, divided by engineering effort. Efficacy is the term teams omit, and it is rarely above 0.7. Arundhati's five clusters, sized against 6,800 monthly overturns, produce a ranking that inverts the frequency order.

Cluster B, the one engineering wanted six weeks for, ranks last per engineer-day. The frequency ranking and the value ranking agree on nothing except that D is small, and that is the ordinary case, not an exotic one.

Have you seen the taxonomy, or only part of it?

The last quantity is coverage. Arundhati's cluster E — fourteen items, none with a sibling — is usually read as noise. It is an estimate. The Good–Turing intuition is that a sample's singleton share approximates the probability mass belonging to categories not yet seen: fourteen singletons in 120 reads implies roughly 12% of Tehreer's failures come from types the taxonomy does not contain. A low, stable share means saturation; a share above a fifth, or one growing cycle over cycle, means the distribution is moving faster than the reading, and the response is more reading, not more fixing.

One mechanic is missing from most descriptions of the loop: inter-annotator agreement. When two people tag the same 100 failures and agree on 78, with chance agreement of 0.31, Cohen's kappa is (0.78 − 0.31)/(1 − 0.31) = 0.68. Below roughly 0.6 the problem is almost never the annotators' care; it is that two clusters are indistinguishable and should merge, or one holds two causes and should split. Kappa diagnoses the taxonomy, not the people.

4When the method applies, stated as tests

Error analysis is not universally appropriate, and its conditions can be written as claims a team can check in an afternoon.

ConditionThe testTehreerBisaat
Failures repeatDoes the top cluster hold ≥15% in a second, independent read?Passes: sub-limit reappeared at 28%Passes: mismatch at 26%
The flag is trustworthyHand-audit 30 flagged items; ≥70% genuine?Passes: an overturn is a human actUncertain: silent abandonment is invisible
Causes are modifiableName the artefact each cluster would changePasses for A, C, D; B is vendor-boundPasses for ranking; fails for listing quality
Distribution stable over a cycleDo last month's clusters still exist?Passes: policy logic is slow-movingFails: festival catalogue shifts weekly
Cost roughly linear in countIs the worst instance within ~10× the median?Fails: cluster C has a regulatory tailPasses for search, fails for payments

The last condition is where the method turns from inapplicable to actively misleading. Where cost is heavy-tailed — a wrong settlement reaching an ombudsman, a missed medication interaction, a safety response to a minor — frequency-weighted clustering ranks the catastrophic tail below the merely annoying, with an air of rigour. Those cases need per-incident root-cause analysis with no thresholding; Arundhati's ₹1,900 average for cluster C should be read as a lower bound.

Two other cases mislead. Adversarial failure — fraud on Bisaat, prompt injection anywhere — is not a fixed distribution being sampled; it responds to the fix, so closing the biggest cluster moves attackers to the next and produces a flat headline concealing continuous churn. And thin volume: a B2B product with nineteen failures a month should read all nineteen, weighted by account, and abandon any pretence of statistics.

5Hard edges and organisational seams

The clean loop assumes one product, one model, one owner and a re-runnable world. Each assumption fails somewhere.

Multi-product. When four products share a prompt library and a retrieval index, a cluster's cause sits in the shared layer while its cost sits in one product's P&L: the platform team sees ₹40,000 a month, while the same defect aggregated across products is worth ₹6 lakh. Mature organisations say they handle this with a shared taxonomy and a quarterly review. What they do is more instructive — the product with the loudest customer patches its own prompt, the shared defect survives, and three products accumulate three divergent patches for one cause. The tell is a cluster that keeps being fixed and keeps returning.

Two-sided. A taxonomy built from buyer complaints is blind to seller-side harm, because sellers do not complain about impressions they never received, and running the analysis per side is necessary but insufficient because the clusters interact. Bisaat's fix cut the buyer-side mismatch cluster from 29% to 11% in offline replay and simultaneously cut impressions for loosely-titled listings by 18% — absorbed by long-tail sellers, who write loose titles because they type on phones between deliveries. A marketplace has two error analyses and one decision, and the decision belongs to whoever owns the balance.

Regulated. At Girvi Credit, a lender under RBI's digital lending framework, the taxonomy became a regulated artefact: once a cluster is named and sized in a document, a supervisor may ask what was done about it and when. The rarely-discussed second-order effect is that supervised teams drift towards vaguer names, because "applies an incorrect income multiple to gig-economy applicants" creates an obligation that "assessment variance" does not. A second constraint bites harder: the DPDP Act's data-minimisation expectations sit awkwardly with a practice built on reading raw transcripts of personal data, and redaction degrades the signal — "confuses the borrower's employer with the co-applicant's" is invisible once both are masked to [NAME]. What works is a small, access-controlled, time-boxed reading pool rather than a transcript lake.

Hardware plus software. Machaan Agri Devices ships field nodes with on-device pest classification to cotton and chilli growers, and cannot re-run the world: every failure is entangled with dust, light, crop stage and hour. Its regression set must be stratified by device generation and field condition, and since fixes arrive over the air on a three-week cycle, the loop's period is set by logistics rather than analysis. At three weeks a cycle, picking the wrong cluster costs three times what it costs a weekly team — which justifies far more reading per cycle than a software team would tolerate.

AI-native. The foundation model moves under the product. A cluster closed against version N can reopen at N+1 with no change on the team's side, and the team will blame its own last change; the defence is a frozen regression set re-run on every model version, not only every code change. At the seams, "who owns this cluster" has no good answer: retrieval-caused belongs to data, prompt-caused to product, judge-caused to the eval team, interface-caused to design. Functioning companies assign it to whoever read the transcripts, because that person is the only one who understands the failure.

6Nine things experts see that competent practitioners miss

One: most model errors are specification errors. The tell is that two experienced humans, shown the same failing input, disagree about what the right output would have been. The model did not fail; nobody decided what success was. The obvious reading — this needs a better model — is wrong because no amount of capability resolves an undefined target. A large share of what teams log as model defects dissolves on contact with a decision about what the product should do.

Two: the denominator is the whole argument. Cluster shares are shares of failures, not of traffic. "Cluster A fell from 37% to 12%" may mean nothing was fixed, if total failures fell for other reasons, or that things got worse: 12% of 9,000 is more claims than 37% of 2,800. Experts carry three numbers per cluster — share, absolute count, rate per thousand sessions — and compare only the third across months.

Three: a fix does not shrink a cluster to zero; it moves part of it. Tehreer's sub-limit fix removed 80% of cluster A, but a fifth of the remainder resurfaced inside cluster D as over-explained recommendations, because the fix taught the model to narrate its arithmetic. The tell is a cycle in which the top cluster shrinks by roughly what you predicted and total failures barely move. Catching it means re-tagging the post-fix sample with the pre-fix taxonomy before inducing new categories.

Four: the miscellaneous bucket is a reading, not a residue. Practitioners discard it; experts track its share, because it estimates unseen failure types. A small stable share licenses confidence; one growing from 12% to 24% across three cycles is the earliest signal of distribution shift — new segment, new model version, new use being made of the product — and it appears well before any headline metric moves.

Five: a cluster named after its remedy has stopped being evidence. "Needs better retrieval" is a hypothesis in a cluster's clothing; the tell is a name built from the engineering backlog rather than from what the user saw. Going straight to the fix feels efficient, but it forecloses the possibility that one observable failure has two causes — precisely the case in which the first fix removes a third of the cluster and the team concludes the method does not work.

Six: judge errors and model errors separate before clustering, not after. The tell is a cluster whose examples look fine when a domain expert reads them. Because judge false positives are systematic, they aggregate into plausible, well-populated, fictional clusters that can rank first. Every failure should carry a tag assigned during the read — which system am I disputing, the producer or the grader — and the two populations sized separately.

Seven: patch debt compounds. Each cycle adds a clause to a prompt or a rule to a pipeline. After nine cycles the prompt has gone from 380 to 2,100 tokens, p95 latency is up nearly a second, cost has trebled, and clauses interfere: week two's instruction is overridden by week eight's. The tell is a regression on a cluster closed months ago, appearing after a change to an unrelated one. The discipline is consolidation — every four or five cycles, rewrite the instruction from the accumulated clusters rather than appending — which feels like lost velocity and is the only thing that preserves it.

Eight: you cannot cluster what was never flagged. The analysis runs on the flagged set, so failures the detector misses are structurally invisible, and they are the interesting ones: the confidently wrong answer no adjudicator questions, the buyer who abandons rather than complains. The tell is a mismatch between churn interviews and the taxonomy. The counter-practice is cheap — each cycle, read twenty items the flag marked passing, purely to estimate what it misses.

Nine: cycle time dominates per-cycle rigour. A weekly loop at seventy per cent rigour closes far more cost in a quarter than a quarterly loop at ninety-five, because each cycle re-orders the queue on fresh information and the ordering is where the value sits. The tell is a team reporting clusters closed per quarter rather than days from sample to shipped fix. The marginal read buys precision on a ranking that will be broken on cost anyway; the marginal week of delay buys nothing.

7What actually changes by product type and stage

The act at the centre — a person reading an artefact and naming what went wrong — does not change across these settings, and claims that it does are usually marketing. What changes is the sampling frame, the ranking weight, and the clock.

SettingSampling frameRanking weightCycle clock
Consumer, high volumeStratified sample of flagged failuresFrequency × cost, projectedDays
B2B / enterpriseCensus per account; no samplingAccount value; one champion outranks twenty anonymous usersWeeks, set by release windows
Platform / marketplaceOne frame per side, plus the interactionNet across sides, including uncomplained harmDays; effects land over months
Hardware + softwareStratified by device generation and field conditionField service cost, not reworkOTA cycle, weeks
AI-nativeFlagged set plus a passing-set auditValue at risk, net of judge contaminationDays; reset by vendor model changes

Stage changes less than people expect. A seed-stage team runs the loop informally — the founder reads fifty transcripts on a Sunday and ships on Monday — and its failure mode is that nothing is written down, so the same cluster is rediscovered three times. A growth-stage company formalises the taxonomy, which is right, and immediately produces that stage's pathology: the taxonomy becomes a fixed vocabulary, new failures are forced into old buckets, and reviewers suppress the misc share because it reflects badly on them. A large company adds a triage rota and an SLA, and its loop slows for organisational rather than technical reasons, because a cluster spanning two teams needs a meeting. What does not change is the reading: a hundred transcripts take one person about four hours at any size.

8Three runs of the loop, one of them a failure

Tehreer, March to April 2026. Arundhati took the expected-value table to the steering committee and won the argument on cluster C rather than on her reading. Eight engineer-days went into versioning the policy-wording index by endorsement date. Overturns from stale wordings fell from 950 a month to 90, and two open ombudsman matters at the largest insurer closed with a documented root cause. The headline overturn rate moved only from 11.0% to 9.8%, because cluster C was small. Service-credit exposure fell by far more than the headline implies, which is the point: the metric that moved was the one attached to money, not to volume.

Bisaat, April 2026. Zoya ran the disambiguation fix as a two-sided experiment rather than a release, holding out 15% of sessions. Buyer-side mismatch fell from 29% to 11% of buyer failures and buyer repeat rate rose 1.4 points; impressions to sellers in the bottom two quintiles of listing quality fell 18%, and their ninety-day retention fell 3.1 points. Net GMV in the treatment arm was up 0.4% — thin, and bought by concentrating demand on sellers who already had it. She shipped a weakened version restoring loose-title listings below the fold, and opened a workstream on seller listing assistance, reasoning that the fix for a seller-quality cluster is a seller tool, not a ranking penalty.

Malaah Freight Systems, the failure. Malaah extracted consignment details from e-way bills and lorry receipts for a road-freight network. Through the first nine weeks of 2026 its team ran a textbook loop: sample the judge-flagged exceptions, cluster, fix the largest, re-run. Three fixes shipped. The exception rate moved from 7.9% to 7.8%. The team concluded the model was at its ceiling and scoped a fine-tune worth an estimated ₹40 lakh. A reviewer asked to audit before the spend was approved hand-checked 200 flagged exceptions and found 108 of them — 54% — were correct extractions the rubric had misjudged, because it required an exact string match on consignee names that legitimately varied across GSTIN registrations. Two of the three shipped fixes had been aimed at clusters that did not exist. Recovery took five weeks: rewrite the rubric to normalise entity names, re-audit until judge precision passed 85%, re-cluster the genuine 92 failures, and find the real top cluster — multi-consignment lorry receipts parsed as single consignments, 41% of true exceptions. The exception rate fell to 3.9%. The detour cost roughly ₹34 lakh in engineering time and a delayed pilot, and produced a one-line runbook entry: audit the judge before you believe the pile.

Figure 3. Malaah's exception rate. The flat line through nine weeks is the signature of iterating against a contaminated pile: real work, shipped on schedule, aimed at artefacts of the rubric. Nothing inside the loop reports this; only an audit of the flag does.

9Failure modes and their early warnings

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Clustering a contaminated pileHeadline rate flat despite shipped fixesWhat share of flagged items did a human confirm?A quarter of misdirected engineering — Malaah's ₹34 lakh
Ranking by frequency aloneThe prioritised cluster is always the most commonRecoverable rupees per engineer-day, by cluster?Rework saved while regulatory and churn exposure grows
Un-frozen regression setGains appear only on the sample just readWas this set assembled before anyone read these failures?Regressions found by customers, not the team
Taxonomy calcificationMisc share falls to near zero and staysWhen did a genuinely new cluster last enter?A new failure type grows unnamed for two quarters
Patch debtOld regression items break after unrelated fixesHow many clauses since the last rewrite?Latency and cost creep; a queue that stops converging
Single-side analysis, two-sided productOne side improves, supply or demand quietly thinsWhich side cannot file a complaint?Supply concentration taking quarters to rebuild

The pattern is that the loop cannot audit itself. Every failure above leaves it running, producing clusters, shipping fixes and reporting progress. Each is caught only from outside, by a question about one of the loop's inputs — the flag, the weights, the hold-out, the vocabulary, or the accumulated state of the artefact being edited.

10Where thoughtful people disagree

Read, or automate the reading? The scale position steelmanned: at 38 lakh sessions any human sample is a rounding error, and a model that clusters every failure — imperfectly, at maybe 75% label accuracy — sees what no sample can, including rare clusters a 120-item read will never contain. Its evidence is that automated taxonomies reproduce most human clusters and surface long-tail ones humans miss. It is wrong when the labeller shares the failure modes of the system under test, common when both are the same model family: the labeller is then blind to precisely the failures the system makes. The reading position holds that the real output is the tacit understanding the reader acquires, which no summary transfers, and that teams which stop reading lose the ability to generate hypotheses. It is wrong to the extent that understanding can be written into a rubric — and to that extent the scale school wins on economics.

Stable taxonomy, or emergent? The ODC inheritance holds that without a fixed scheme you cannot say whether the product is improving, only that this month's clusters differ from last month's. The emergent position holds that a fixed scheme, in a domain where the model changes quarterly, is a device for forcing new failures into old names and reporting a stability that does not exist. Each is wrong under the other's conditions, and the conditions are empirical: how fast does your failure distribution actually move? Tehreer's policy logic moves annually and should run a stable taxonomy; Bisaat's catalogue moves weekly and should not. The disagreement resolves per product, not in general.

Fix the model, or remove the task? A minority position, held firmly by some senior designers, is that a large cluster is evidence the product asked the model to do something it should not have been asked, and that the answer to Bisaat's mismatch cluster is a query-refinement step that never lets the ambiguity through. Its evidence is the long history of interface constraints outperforming intelligence. It is wrong where the constraint hands the work back to the user — often exactly the work the product was sold to remove.

Iterate, or wait? The uncomfortable one. A serious argument holds that for many clusters the efficient action is nothing, because the next foundation model removes the cluster for free and engineering spent patching a capability gap is written off at the upgrade; its evidence is the number of 2024 prompt workarounds that were dead weight by 2026. The counter is that nobody can tell in advance which clusters are capability gaps and which are specification gaps, and specification gaps never resolve themselves. The practical middle — tag each cluster as capability or specification during the read, fix specification clusters now, re-test capability clusters at each model upgrade before investing — is what disciplined teams do, and neither camp regards it as settling anything.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four visible ways. They ask what flagged the failures before they look at the clusters, and will spend the first hour of a cycle auditing the judge rather than the model. They speak in rupees per engineer-day rather than percentages, and can be talked out of the biggest cluster by a cost argument without feeling their reading was wasted. They predict in writing, before shipping, how much of a cluster a fix will remove, and treat a miss on that prediction as more informative than the fix — a wrong efficacy estimate means the cause was misdiagnosed. And they protect cycle time above all, defending twelve loops at seventy per cent rigour over three at ninety-five arithmetically rather than as temperament. The person who has merely studied the method produces a beautiful taxonomy, a correct Pareto chart, and a plan six weeks stale by the time it is approved.

12What each of them did

Arundhati presented five clusters with intervals, an expected-value ranking, and a stated prediction: eight engineer-days on the policy-wording index, 90% efficacy, ₹16 lakh a month recoverable, headline overturn rate barely moving. Saying the last part out loud before shipping is why nobody called it a failed quarter when the rate fell 1.2 points. She deferred the OCR work not because it was unimportant but because it returned ₹4,000 per engineer-day against cluster C's ₹2 lakh, and she wrote that comparison into the roadmap so the argument would not be re-fought.

Zoya did something less tidy. She accepted that her analysis was structurally one-sided, ran the fix as a held-out experiment rather than a release, and when the numbers showed a thin GMV gain bought with seller concentration, shipped a weakened version and moved the real work upstream to seller tools. Her cluster was correctly identified and correctly sized, and the right answer was still not to fix it as specified — the case the textbook loop cannot produce on its own.

Question 1. Tehreer's cluster C cost ₹1,900 per instance on average, with a long right tail from ombudsman matters. If the true distribution is heavy-tailed, is the expected-value ranking in the table defensible at all, or does cluster C deserve to be removed from the frequency framework entirely and handled per incident?
Question 2. Malaah's reviewer found 54% contamination after nine weeks. What should have been in place such that this was caught in week one — and what would that control have cost per cycle?
Question 3. Zoya's analysis was blind to sellers because sellers do not complain about impressions they never saw. Name two other product situations where the harmed party cannot generate a failure record, and say what would have to be instrumented to make those failures visible.

13Going deeper

Grading rubrics and LLM-as-judge — the upstream dependency; everything here inherits the rubric's error rate, and Figure 2's arithmetic is unfixable downstream. Evals-driven development — turns this loop from crisis response into the default way releases happen, which is what changes cycle time. Evaluation at scale and eval drift — what happens when the failure distribution moves and yesterday's taxonomy stops describing today's product. Problem–model fit — tells you whether a cluster is a capability gap that closes on the next model or a specification gap that never will. The ML lifecycle — where this loop sits relative to data, training and deployment, and why one cluster gets a different fix at each stage. Data strategy and data acquisition — some clusters resolve only by acquiring data you do not have: a procurement decision with a lead time. Labelling and annotation — the kappa arithmetic here governs training labels too, and a taxonomy nobody can annotate reliably cannot be trained against. Model metrics: precision, recall, AUC — the formal vocabulary for judge contamination and for setting the flag's operating threshold. What's different when the feature is a model — the general case: behaviour measured rather than specified, improved statistically rather than fixed.

Error Analysis and Iteration

Which failures cluster, and which cluster should you fix first? A discipline for turning a pile of bad model outputs into a prioritized, defensible engineering plan.

1. A Tuesday in Pune

On the morning of 9 February 2026, Ananya Rao, Director of AI Product at Uttarpatra Learning, opened a spreadsheet she had been avoiding for a week. Uttarpatra's flagship product, Mains Coach, used a large language model to grade descriptive answers for the UPSC Civil Services Mains examination — the kind of essay-length response where a human evaluator would normally read for content, structure, and argument, and assign a mark out of ten against a published rubric. Roughly 40,000 aspirants used Mains Coach every month, uploading handwritten or typed answers and receiving a score with written feedback within minutes instead of the weeks a human mentor would take.

The spreadsheet tracked a number that mattered a great deal to Ananya's quarter: the share of graded answers flagged as low-confidence or disputed by students, which had crept from 6.1% in the first week of January to 9.5% by the first week of February. Refund requests were up. A coaching partner whose brand appeared inside the app — worth roughly ₹3 crore in annual contract value up for renewal in six weeks — had sent two escalation emails asking, not unreasonably, whether the grader could be trusted. Ananya had three days before a leadership review at which she was expected to say not "we're looking into it" but exactly what was broken, how much of the problem it explained, and what she intended to fix first.

Figure 1. The disputed-grade rate Ananya was tracking each week. A rising line tells her something is wrong; it tells her nothing about what, how much of it is one thing versus many things, or which fix would move the line fastest. That gap is exactly what error analysis closes.

2. The idea

Error analysis and iteration is the practice of reading a sample of a system's actual failures, sorting them into a small number of named groups by shared root cause, sizing each group against the full population of failures, and fixing the group that costs the most before touching anything else — then re-running the evaluation to confirm the group actually shrank. It is downstream of a grading rubric: a rubric or an LLM-as-judge is what flags an output as a failure in the first place, and error analysis is what you do with the pile of failures once they exist.

The habit has two lineages. One is manufacturing quality control — Pareto and root-cause clustering of defects, formalized through Six Sigma programs from the 1980s onward, where the rule was always "find the vital few causes behind the trivial many symptoms." The other is Andrew Ng's teaching on applied machine learning, particularly the 2018 booklet Machine Learning Yearning, which argued that engineers waste months building the wrong fix because they never sat down and manually counted what kinds of mistakes a model was actually making. LLM product teams inherited both lineages directly: the failures are now free-text transcripts instead of misclassified images, but the discipline of counting before fixing is unchanged.

The sentence Ananya could say in the leadership review without sounding glib: "Don't fix bugs one at a time — read enough failures to see the shape of the cluster, fix the cluster that's costing the most, and re-run to prove it shrank."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics run in a fixed order, and the order is the discipline — skipping a step is how teams end up "fixing" things that were never the biggest problem. First, pull a sample of failures only, not a random sample of all traffic: if 9.5% of gradings are disputed, you want fifty to a hundred of those disputed cases, stratified across exam tracks so no single track dominates the read. Second, open the raw transcripts — the actual student answer, the actual model output, the actual score — rather than trusting the rubric score alone; a score of "3/10, weak structure" tells you almost nothing about why the model produced that score.

Third comes open coding: for each failure, write a one-line description of what went wrong in your own words, resisting the urge to force it into a pre-existing category. Fourth, after twenty or thirty tags accumulate, do axial coding — step back and group similar one-liners into a handful of named clusters, typically four to eight for a mature product. Fifth, count each cluster's share of the sample and extrapolate that share to the full failure population to estimate how many real gradings, and how much real cost, it represents. Sixth, prioritize by frequency multiplied by severity multiplied by how cheap the fix is — not by frequency alone, and not by whichever failure a stakeholder happened to see. Seventh, fix only the top cluster. Eighth, re-run the evaluation against a regression set that was frozen before this round of reading began, to confirm the cluster actually shrank and that no new cluster appeared in its place. Practitioners routinely skip two things here: reading raw transcripts instead of scores, and freezing the regression set before they start staring at failures, which is the step that keeps the next iteration honest rather than self-congratulatory.

Figure 2. The loop is cyclic by design. Re-running on a set frozen before the reading began is what stops the team from grading its own homework.

4. Ananya's worked example

Of the 40,000 answers Mains Coach graded in the last week of January, 3,800 were flagged as disputed or low-confidence — a failure rate of 9.5%. Ananya's team pulled a stratified sample of 60 of those 3,800 and read every transcript. Open coding produced dozens of one-line notes; axial coding collapsed them into four named clusters.

ClusterRoot cause (one line)SampleShareProjected / month
AGrader penalizes correct answers written in bullet form instead of essay prose22 of 6036.7%≈ 1,394
BOCR mis-reads handwriting; grader marks facts "missing" that were present but garbled15 of 6025.0%≈ 950
CRubric is silent on partial credit for a correct conclusion built on a weak body11 of 6018.3%≈ 695
DMiscellaneous, no repeating cause in this sample12 of 6020.0%≈ 760

Cluster A, projected across the month, touches roughly 1,394 answers. Uttarpatra's finance team estimates each disputed grading costs about ₹150 in support handling and partial refunds — 1,394 × ₹150 ≈ ₹2.09 lakh a month, before counting the churn risk to the coaching partner's renewal. Cluster A is also the cheapest of the four to fix: it needs a rubric clause explicitly permitting bullet-structured answers and three few-shot exemplars added to the grading prompt, not a new vendor contract. Ananya ranks it first on frequency, cost, and fixability together — not frequency alone, since Cluster D's 20% share is a false signal: it is twelve unrelated one-off failures with no common fix, so no single change touches more than one or two of them.

Her team ships the Cluster A fix and, separately, procurement finalizes a better OCR vendor two weeks later, which was already planned for other reasons and happens to attack Cluster B's root cause. Re-running the same regression logic on the next failure sample of 40 shows the picture has moved: Cluster A falls to about 7.5% of remaining failures, Cluster B falls to about 10%, but Cluster C — untouched — now accounts for roughly half of what is left, because the denominator shrank around it. The arithmetic matters here: fixing the biggest cluster does not just remove failures, it re-orders which cluster is biggest next, which is precisely why the loop re-runs rather than executing a fixed to-do list.

5. Nuances a learner must hold onto

The judge can be the bug, not the model

Some "failures" are cases where the LLM-as-judge disagreed with a human grader who was, on inspection, wrong. Lumping judge errors in with model errors inflates every cluster and points the fix at the wrong system. A disciplined team tags each failure with which side — model output or judge verdict — it disputes, before clustering either.

Frequency is not the only prioritization axis

A cluster affecting 3% of gradings but producing a confidently wrong "9/10" on a factually incorrect answer can outrank a 20% cluster of merely unhelpful feedback, because the cost of false confidence in a high-stakes exam context is not linear with volume.

Naming a cluster precisely implies its fix

"Bad grading" is not a cluster; it is a symptom. "Penalizes bullet-structured answers" is a cluster, because the name alone tells an engineer what to change. If a cluster's name doesn't suggest a fix, it usually isn't finished being split.

Error analysis cannot see what the sample never contained

It reports on the failures you drew, not the ones you didn't. If non-English or code-mixed answers are underrepresented in the sample, a cluster affecting mainly those answers will look smaller than it is, or vanish entirely.

It is not the same discipline as dashboard monitoring

A metrics dashboard tells you the disputed-rate line went up; error analysis is the manual, qualitative act of reading transcripts to learn why. Teams that only watch the dashboard can tell you the problem is growing without being able to say what the problem is.

The regression set must be frozen before you start reading

If the "before/after" comparison uses failures collected after the team has already stared at and half-fixed the obvious cases, the improvement is partly an artifact of hindsight, not a clean measurement of the fix.

Single catastrophic failures deserve individual treatment, not clustering

A one-off case where the grader awarded full marks to a blank answer is worth fixing immediately on its own merits; waiting for it to accumulate into a sizeable cluster before acting would be a misuse of a method built for high-volume, diffuse failure.

6. Where this differs by product shape and by stage

In a high-volume consumer product like Mains Coach, failures are diffuse across tens of thousands of users, so statistical clustering on a modest sample works well and frequency-weighted cost is a reasonable prioritization lens. In a B2B product — an AI drafting assistant sold to a single law firm, say — the failure count in any given week may be small, but each failure sits inside a relationship worth renewing or losing; the practical version of error analysis there is often "read every failure this account reported this month" rather than a statistical sample, and prioritization is account-weighted rather than frequency-weighted. In a marketplace product, failures split by side: a buyer's complaint about a poor match and a seller's complaint about under-ranking can share a root cause or point in opposite directions, so clustering has to run separately per side, and a fix that shrinks the buyer-side cluster can enlarge the seller-side one.

SettingSample sourcePrioritization lens
Consumer (Mains Coach)Stratified sample of flagged failuresFrequency × cost, projected to full volume
B2BEvery failure reported by an accountAccount value and renewal risk
MarketplaceSeparate samples per side (buyer/seller)Net effect across both sides, not just one

Stage matters too. In a five-person startup, one person often writes the prompts, reads the failures, and ships the fix in the same afternoon — the loop is real but informal, running weekly on instinct as much as process. In a larger organization, the same loop formalizes into a standing "eval council," a ticketing queue with a triage SLA, and a shared cluster taxonomy that multiple teams reference — which reduces variance between reviewers but introduces a new failure mode of its own: the loop slows down for political and coordination reasons even when the technical work of clustering a fresh sample takes an afternoon.

7. Common mistakes

MistakeSymptomUnderlying misunderstandingCheap diagnostic
Fixing the loudest failureEngineering drops everything for whatever a leader or a viral post flaggedSalience is mistaken for measured frequencyAsk: of the last 100 sampled failures, how many does this represent?
Reading scores, not transcriptsTeam speculates about causes from a score histogram aloneThe rubric score is treated as self-explanatoryCan anyone name the top three clusters with one real example each, unaided?
No frozen regression setA "fixed" cluster quietly reappears weeks laterIterating directly on the sample just read, rather than a hold-outWas the same regression set re-run and diffed before this release?
Treating cluster names as permanentA taxonomy of fifteen-plus clusters, half no longer relevantClusters are a snapshot of a shifting distribution, not a fixed catalogueDate-stamp clusters; retire any below a floor frequency for two cycles

8. What good looks like

Six weeks after that February review, Ananya's team runs the loop every Friday: a stratified sample of 75 fresh failures, two annotators tagging independently and comparing notes until they agree on at least 80% of tags, clusters ranked by frequency times cost times fixability, the top cluster fixed within the week, and a 500-item regression set re-run before every release with results logged, dated, in a shared sheet. The disputed-grade rate falls from 9.5% to 4.1% over those six weeks — not through one clever prompt, but through six deliberate, measured, sequential fixes, each one closing the cluster that was, at that moment, costing the most.

Figure 3. Six weekly cycles, six closed clusters, one auditable line — the shape a defensible renewal conversation needs.

9. What Ananya decides

At the leadership review, Ananya does not present a plan to "improve the grader." She presents four named clusters with sizes, monthly cost estimates, and fixability, and recommends Cluster A first — the bullet-structure penalty — because it is simultaneously the largest, the cheapest to fix, and requires no external dependency. She commits to freezing a 500-item regression set before the next reading round, and schedules the OCR-dependent Cluster B fix for the following sprint, tied to the vendor evaluation already underway. The coaching partner's renewal conversation, six weeks later, goes well not because the grader became perfect but because Ananya can show, cluster by cluster, exactly what was broken and by how much it shrank.

What she tells her team to learn next is evals-driven development — making this loop the default way the product ships rather than a response to a crisis — and evaluation at scale, including eval drift: what happens when the failure distribution itself moves as the model, the exam syllabus, or the user base changes under you, so that yesterday's clusters stop describing today's failures.

Question 1. The last time you or your team fixed something in a live AI product, could you have said what fraction of the failures that fix actually addressed — or did it just feel like it helped?
Question 2. If a cluster you fixed last quarter came back this quarter, how would you know — and would you know before a customer told you?
